questions.q: What is an amine?
o: An oxygen-containing organic compound that never contains any nitrogen atom
An inorganic nitrogen compound containing no carbon-based groups at all
A compound that by definition never contains a nitrogen atom anywhere
A nitrogen-containing organic compound, an organic derivative of ammonia
questions.e: The lecture defines amines as nitrogen-containing organic compounds or molecules that are organic derivatives of ammonia (NH3).

questions.q: NH3 (ammonia) itself is classified, in the lecture, as:
questions.e: The lecture explicitly states 'NH3 – AMMONIA IS AN INORGANIC COMPOUND', distinguishing it from amines, which are its organic derivatives.

questions.q: What structural feature is shared between ammonia and amines, according to the lecture's introduction?
o: The presence of N-H bonds in ammonia, which become N-C bonds in amines
The presence of S-H bonds in ammonia, which become S-C bonds in thiols
The presence of C=O bonds in both, as seen in aldehydes and ketones
The presence of O-H bonds in both, as seen in alcohols and phenols
questions.e: The lecture highlights 'THE PRESENCE OF N-H BONDS' in ammonia, and later notes that 'THE N-H BONDS ARE NOW CHANGED TO N-C BONDS IN AMINES' once the hydrogens are replaced by carbon-containing groups.

questions.q: In aqueous solution, ammonia behaves as:
o: Neither a base nor a nucleophile
questions.e: The lecture states 'AMMONIA IS BASIC IN NATURE' and 'AMMONIA IS A NUCLEOPHILE'.

questions.q: How does the lecture define a nucleophile?
o: A leaving group in a reaction mechanism
A proton donor only, not an electron pair donor
questions.e: The lecture defines the two key species in organic chemistry as the electrophile ('electron loving species') and the nucleophile ('nucleus loving species').

questions.q: How does the lecture define an electrophile?
o: A species that never reacts with nucleophiles
questions.e: The lecture defines an electrophile as an 'electron loving species', the counterpart of the nucleophile ('nucleus loving species').

questions.q: According to the lecture, the nitrogen atom in ammonia is:
questions.e: The lecture states 'THE N ATOM IN AMMONIA IS TRIVALENT AND THUS sp3 HYBRIDIZED', and advises students to revise hybridization to fully understand this.

questions.q: How are amines classified into primary, secondary and tertiary?
o: By how many of the hydrogens on the nitrogen of ammonia are replaced by organic groups
By their boiling point relative to other similar compounds, not nitrogen substitution
By the color of the compound in solution, not by its nitrogen substituents
By their molecular weight compared to ammonia, not by substitution
questions.e: The lecture states that 'ONE, TWO OR ALL THE THREE Hs ON AMMONIA CAN BE REPLACED WITH DIFFERENT ORGANIC GROUP OF ATOMS', and classification (1°, 2°, 3°) is based on how many are replaced.

questions.q: A primary (1°) amine is one in which:
o: Two of the hydrogens on the nitrogen are replaced by organic groups
No hydrogens are replaced at all, exactly as in ammonia itself
All three hydrogens on the nitrogen are replaced by organic groups
Only one of the hydrogens surrounding the nitrogen is replaced by an organic group
questions.e: The lecture defines: 'PRIMARY – WHEN ONLY ONE OF THE Hs SURROUNDING THE N IS REPLACED'.

questions.q: A secondary (2°) amine is one in which:
o: Two of the hydrogens on nitrogen are replaced by organic groups
Only one hydrogen is replaced by an organic group
All three hydrogens are replaced by organic groups
There is no nitrogen atom present at all
questions.e: The lecture defines: 'SECONDARY WHEN TWO OF THE Hs ARE REPLACED'.

questions.q: A tertiary (3°) amine is one in which:
o: Only one hydrogen is replaced by an organic group
All three hydrogens on nitrogen are replaced by organic groups
Two hydrogens are replaced by organic groups
The nitrogen has no substituents attached to it
questions.e: The lecture defines: 'TERTIARY WHEN ALL THREE OF THE Hs ARE REPLACED'.

questions.q: The symmetrical/unsymmetrical classification of amines is, per the lecture, usually associated with which class(es) of amine?
o: Only aromatic amines, never aliphatic ones
Secondary and tertiary amines, but not primary amines
All three classes equally, without exception
Primary amines only, never secondary or tertiary
questions.e: The lecture states that symmetrical and unsymmetrical classification is 'USUALLY ASSOCIATED WITH 20 and 30 AMINES BUT NOT PRIMARY AMINES' — because a primary amine has only one organic substituent, so the symmetry question does not apply.

questions.q: In a symmetrical secondary or tertiary amine, the organic groups attached to nitrogen are:
o: All identical to one another, as in a symmetrical amine
All different from one another, as in an unsymmetrical amine
Always aromatic rings fused to the nitrogen
questions.e: A symmetrical amine has identical substituent groups on the nitrogen, as opposed to an unsymmetrical amine, whose substituents differ from one another.

questions.q: In an unsymmetrical amine, the organic groups attached to nitrogen are:
o: Identical to one another, as in a symmetrical amine
All hydrogens, with no organic substituents at all
Absent, as in ammonia itself with no substituents
Different from one another, unlike in a symmetrical amine
questions.e: An unsymmetrical amine has two or more different organic groups attached to the nitrogen, contrasting with a symmetrical amine, in which the groups are identical.

questions.q: The lecture presents two compounds that are 'neither aliphatic, aromatic or cyclic' but are instead classified as which type of amine?
o: Primary aliphatic amines with one substituent
Heterocyclic amines containing ring nitrogen atoms
Symmetrical amines with two identical groups
questions.e: The lecture's exercise concludes: 'THE TWO COMPOUNDS ARE NEITHER ALIPHATIC, AROMATIC OR CYCLIC. BOTH COMPOUNDS ARE HETEROCYCLIC AMINES.'

questions.q: A heterocyclic compound is defined, in the lecture, as a cyclic compound in which:
o: The ring contains only carbon atoms
There is no ring structure at all
The ring contains more than one kind of atom
The ring is made entirely of nitrogen atoms
questions.e: The lecture defines heterocyclic compounds as 'CYCLIC COMPOUNDS IN WHICH THE RING CONTAINS MORE THAN ONE KIND OF ATOM', noting that 'IN ADDITION TO CARBON, ONE OR MORE ATOMS OF O, N, S MAY BE PRESENT.'

questions.q: In an alkylamine, the nitrogen atom is attached to:
questions.e: The lecture states: 'Alkylamines — Nitrogen atom is attached to alkyl group.'

questions.q: In an arylamine, the nitrogen atom is attached to:
o: A hydroxyl group, as found in alcohols and phenols
An alkyl group only, never an aromatic ring
An aryl group, such as a substituted benzene ring
questions.e: The lecture states: 'Arylamines — Nitrogen atom is attached to aryl group.'

questions.q: According to the lecture, how many IUPAC naming styles exist for primary alkylamines (RNH2)?
questions.e: The slide heading reads 'Nomenclature of Primary Alkylamines (RNH2) — Two IUPAC styles'.

questions.q: The first IUPAC naming style for a primary alkylamine, analogous to naming alcohols, works by:
o: Using only informal, non-systematic common names for the compound
Replacing the '-e' ending of the corresponding alkane name with '-anamine'
Adding '-ol' to the end of the alkane name, as done for alcohols
Adding '-oic acid' to the end of the alkane name, as for carboxylic acids
questions.e: The lecture states this style is '1) analogous to alcohols: replace –e of an alkane ending by -anamine' — e.g. propane becomes propanamine.

questions.q: The second IUPAC naming style for a primary alkylamine works by:
o: Always using the prefix 'amino-' regardless of the compound
Naming it as if it were a carboxylic acid
Naming the alkyl group and attaching '-amine' as a suffix
questions.e: The lecture states this style is '2) name alkyl group and attach -amine as a suffix' — e.g. propyl + amine = propylamine.

questions.q: Using the two IUPAC styles shown in the lecture, a 3-carbon primary alkylamine (n-propylamine) can also correctly be named:
questions.e: The lecture gives both names for the same 3-carbon primary amine: 'n-propylamine or propanamine'.

questions.q: The cyclic primary amine cyclopentylamine can also correctly be named, following the same two styles:
questions.e: The lecture gives both names for this cyclic amine: 'cyclopentylamine or cyclopetanamine [cyclopentanamine]'.

questions.q: When an amine group co-occurs in a molecule with higher-priority functional groups such as -OH, -COOH or C=O, how is the amine treated for naming purposes?
o: As a group that is ignored completely in the name
As the group of highest priority, always named as the suffix
As a substituent of lower priority than -OH or -COOH groups
As a group that must first be converted to a nitrile
questions.e: The lecture states: 'THE AMINE FUNCTIONAL GROUP IS CONSIDERED OF LOWER PRIORITY WHEN IT IS PRESENT TOGETHER WITH OTHER FUNCTIONAL GROUPS SUCH AS; -OH; -COOH; C=O'.

questions.q: Following the priority rule for competing functional groups, the compound HOCH2CH2NH2 is named in the lecture as:
questions.e: Since -OH outranks -NH2 in naming priority, the parent chain is named as an ethanol with an 'amino' substituent: '2-AMINOETHANOL'.

questions.q: The compound named '1,4-benzenediamine' in the lecture's exercise contains:
o: Two amine groups on the benzene ring, at the 1 and 4 positions
Three amine groups distributed around the benzene ring
One amine group at the 1 position only, with no others
No amine groups at all — it is instead a benzene diol
questions.e: The 'di-' prefix combined with the two locants (1,4) indicates two -NH2 substituents on the benzene ring, at carbons 1 and 4.

questions.q: The compound H2NCH2CH2CH2CH2NH2, which students are asked to name in the lecture, is an example of a:
o: Diamine — a compound bearing two -NH2 groups
Triamine — a compound with three -NH2 groups
Heterocyclic amine containing a ring nitrogen
Monoamine — a compound with a single -NH2 group
questions.e: H2NCH2CH2CH2CH2NH2 carries an -NH2 group at each end of a four-carbon chain, making it a diamine (butane-1,4-diamine), directly comparable to the 1,2-propanediamine and 1,4-benzenediamine naming exercises in the lecture.

questions.q: In solution, how basic are amines generally described as being, in the lecture?
o: Strongly acidic in nearly all aqueous solutions
Strong oxidizing agents toward most organic substrates
Generally weakly basic, acting as mild Lewis bases
questions.e: The lecture states: 'AMINES ARE GENERALLY WEAKLY BASIC (LEWIS BASES) IN SOLUTION.'

questions.q: Comparing NH3, CH3NH2, CH3NHCH3 and (CH3)3N, which is the strongest base according to the lecture's pKb/pKa data?
questions.e: The lecture ranks CH3NHCH3 as order-of-basicity '1' (pKb 3.27, the lowest/least positive value), making the secondary amine the strongest base of the four compared.

questions.q: Comparing the same four compounds, which is the weakest base according to the lecture's data?
questions.e: The lecture ranks NH3 as order-of-basicity '4' (pKb 4.74, the highest/most positive value), making ammonia the weakest base of the four compared.

questions.q: According to the lecture, a stronger base is associated with:
o: No relationship to pKb at all
questions.e: The lecture states: 'STRONGER BASES HAVE THE LEAST +VE VALUES OF pKb.'

questions.q: According to the lecture, a weaker base is associated with:
questions.e: The lecture states: 'Weaker bases have lower pKa VALUES.'

questions.q: What relationship between pKa and base strength does the lecture state?
o: The higher the pKa value, the weaker the base
pKa has no bearing on base strength
The higher the pKa value, the stronger the base
Only pKb — never pKa — determines base strength
questions.e: The lecture states plainly: 'THE HIGHER THE pKa VALUE, THE STRONGER THE BASE.'

questions.q: For simple alkylamines in aqueous solution, what order of basicity does the lecture establish?
questions.e: The lecture states: '20 AMINES ARE MORE BASIC THAN 10 AND 10 MORE BASIC THAN 30 — ORDER OF BASICITY 20 > 10 > 30', i.e. secondary > primary > tertiary.

questions.q: What approximate pH is given for the stomach, as one of the three key compartments for drug absorption?
questions.e: The lecture lists 'Stomach pH = 1' among the three key body compartments relevant to medicine absorption.

questions.q: What approximate pH range is given for the intestine?
questions.e: The lecture lists 'Intestine pH = 6 - 8' among the three key body compartments relevant to medicine absorption.

questions.q: What approximate pH is given for blood plasma?
questions.e: The lecture lists 'Plasma pH = 7.4' among the three key body compartments relevant to medicine absorption.

questions.q: A drug's acid-base properties chiefly influence which two pharmacological characteristics, according to the lecture?
o: Its melting point alone, unrelated to absorption
Its color and odor, not its pharmacological action
Its atomic mass, not its ionization behavior
questions.e: The lecture states: 'A DRUG'S ACID – BASE PROPERTIES CAN INFLUENCE GREATLY ITS BIO-DISTRIBUTION AND PARTITION CHARACTERISTICS.'

questions.q: According to the lecture, the extent of ionization of a weak acid or base drug in the body is determined by:
o: The pKa of the drug and the pH of the medium
Body temperature alone, independent of chemistry
The drug's molecular weight alone, not its ionization
The color of the solution, an unrelated physical property
questions.e: The lecture states: 'THE EXTENT OF IONIZATION IS DETERMINED BY THE PKA OF THE DRUG AND THE PH OF THE MEDIUM.'

questions.q: Why does the unionized form of a drug diffuse through cell membranes more easily than the ionized form?
o: The ionized form is smaller in size and crosses membranes faster
There is no difference between the two forms in permeability
Cell membranes actively transport only ionized drugs across the bilayer
The unionized form is lipid-soluble, while the ionized form has low lipid solubility
questions.e: The lecture explains: 'THE IONIZED FORM PENETRATES CELL MEMBRANES WITH DIFFICULTY BECAUSE OF THEIR LOW LIPID SOLUBILITY, WHEREAS THE UNIONIZED FORM, BEING LIPID SOLUBLE, DIFFUSES THROUGH CELL MEMBRANES WITH EASE.'

questions.q: Why are weakly basic drugs with pKa values generally above 7.4 well absorbed in the small intestine?
o: Because such drugs cannot dissolve at all in any aqueous medium, unlike their salts
Because plasma at pH 7.4 destroys the drug entirely before absorption can ever occur
Because stomach acid at pH 1 fully ionizes them, preventing any absorption there instead
At intestinal pH they exist mostly in the unionized, lipid-soluble form that penetrates cell walls easily
questions.e: The lecture explains that 'WEAKLY BASIC DRUGS WITH PKA VALUES GENERALLY ABOVE 7.4 ARE ABSORBED WELL IN THE SMALL INTESTINES... THE WEAKLY BASIC DRUGS ARE MOSTLY AVAILABLE IN THE UNIONIZED FORM AND THUS ABLE TO PENETRATE THE CELL WALLS EASILY.'

questions.q: In their important organic reactions, amines behave chemically as:
o: Neither nucleophiles nor electrophiles at all
Oxidizing agents only, never reducing agents
questions.e: The lecture's overview states: 'THE IMPORTANT ORGANIC REACTIONS OF AMINES (NUCLEOPHILES) ARE WITH THE COMMON ELECTROPHILES.'

questions.q: When an amine reacts with an alkyl halide, what type of mechanism operates?
questions.e: The lecture lists 'ALKYL HALIDES VIA NUCLEOPHILIC SUBSTITUTION' as one of the three key reaction types of amines.

questions.q: When an amine reacts with an aldehyde or ketone, what type of mechanism operates?
questions.e: The lecture lists 'ALDEHYDES OR KETONES VIA NUCLEOPHILIC ADDITION' as one of the three key reaction types of amines.

questions.q: When an amine reacts with a carboxylic acid derivative such as an acid chloride or anhydride, what type of mechanism operates?
o: Nucleophilic substitution at an sp3 carbon
questions.e: The lecture lists 'CARBOXYLIC ACID DERIVATIVES, ESPECIALLY ACID CHLORIDES OR ANHYDRIDES, VIA NUCLEOPHILIC ACYL SUBSTITUTION' as one of the three key reaction types of amines.

questions.q: Acid chlorides and anhydrides are grouped together in the lecture's reaction overview as examples of:
o: Aldehydes, which never react with amines under any conditions at all
Carboxylic acid derivatives that react with amines via nucleophilic acyl substitution
Alkyl halides, which react by nucleophilic substitution mechanisms only
Simple alcohols, which do not react with amines under normal conditions
questions.e: The lecture groups 'CARBOXYLIC ACID DERIVATIVES, ESPECIALLY ACID CHLORIDES OR ANHYDRIDES' together as the electrophiles that react with amines via nucleophilic acyl substitution.

questions.q: In all three of the amine reaction types outlined in the lecture (with alkyl halides, with aldehydes/ketones, and with carboxylic acid derivatives), what role do the electrophilic partners play?
o: They are always solvents, not reactants in the mechanism
They convert the amine into ammonia during the reaction
They act as bases toward the nucleophilic amine reagent
They are the common electrophiles that the nucleophilic amine reacts with
questions.e: The lecture frames amines as nucleophiles reacting with 'THE COMMON ELECTROPHILES': alkyl halides, aldehydes/ketones, and carboxylic acid derivatives — three distinct mechanisms, one common role for amines.

questions.q: Why does the lecture describe heterocyclic compounds as important organic compounds?
o: Because they never occur anywhere in nature
Because they are intimately connected with the processes of life
Because they are always toxic to living cells
Because they are found only in synthetic plastics
questions.e: The lecture states: 'HETEROCYCLIC COMPOUNDS ARE IMPORTANT ORGANIC COMPOUNDS WHICH ARE INTIMATELY CONNECTED WITH THE PROCESSES OF LIFE.'

questions.q: Which of the following is listed in the lecture as an example of a biologically important heterocyclic compound?
questions.e: The lecture's list of heterocyclic-compound examples includes 'THIAMINE, FOLIC ACID, NUCLEIC ACIDS, HAEMOGLOBIN, CHLOROPHYLL'.

questions.q: Folic acid, nucleic acids, haemoglobin and chlorophyll are all cited by the lecture as examples of:
o: Simple aliphatic amines with no ring system
Inorganic mineral salts found in rock
Carboxylic acids with no nitrogen atom
Heterocyclic compounds important to the processes of life
questions.e: These four compounds appear together in the lecture's list of heterocyclic compounds 'intimately connected with the processes of life', alongside thiamine.

questions.q: Besides carbon and nitrogen, which other atoms may be present in the ring of a heterocyclic compound, per the lecture?
questions.e: The lecture states: 'IN ADDITION TO CARBON, ONE OR MORE ATOMS OF O, N, S MAY BE PRESENT' in a heterocyclic ring.

questions.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed among the lecture's stated learning objectives?
o: Identify amine drugs and their basicity
questions.e: The learning objectives include: 'IDENTIFY AMINE DRUGS', alongside recognizing the -NH2 group, classifying and naming amines, explaining basicity's effect on biological activity, and outlining preparation/reactions of amines.

questions.q: How are alkyl halides defined and designated in general formula?
o: R-OH, where R is an alkyl group, defines an alcohol
R-X, where R is an alkyl group and X = F, Cl, Br or I
R-NH2, an amine, not a halogen-containing compound
R2C=O, a carbonyl compound such as an aldehyde or ketone
questions.e: Alkyl halides are compounds with a halogen substituent (fluoro, chloro, bromo, iodo) bonded to an alkyl group, designated R-X where R is alkyl and X is the halogen.

questions.q: What is the classification basis for primary, secondary and tertiary alkyl halides?
o: The number of halogens present in the molecule overall
The number of other carbons attached to the carbon bearing the halogen
The total molecular weight of the compound, unrelated to structure
The boiling point of the compound relative to its isomers
questions.e: Classification is based on the carbon atom to which the halogen is directly attached: how many OTHER carbon atoms that carbon is bonded to (one=primary, two=secondary, three=tertiary).

questions.q: If the carbon bearing the halogen is attached to no other carbon atoms, what is the compound called?
questions.e: If the carbon bonded to the halogen has no other carbon attached, the compound is a methyl halide (e.g. CH3Cl), distinct from the primary/secondary/tertiary classes.

questions.q: In (CH3)3C-Br, how is the carbon bearing the bromine classified?
o: Secondary, since it is attached to two other carbons
Tertiary, since it is attached to three other carbons
Methyl, since it is attached to no other carbons
Primary, since it is attached to one other carbon
questions.e: The central carbon of (CH3)3C-Br is bonded to three methyl carbons, so it is a tertiary alkyl halide.

questions.q: Halogen derivatives of alkenes (e.g. CH2=CHCl) are known by what name?
questions.e: The lecture distinguishes alkyl halides (from alkanes), alkenyl halides/haloalkenes (from alkenes), alkynyl halides/haloalkynes (from alkynes), and aryl halides/halobenzenes (from arenes).

questions.q: In IUPAC nomenclature of a haloalkane, how is the longest chain numbered when there is a choice?
o: Always starting from the left as drawn on the page
In the direction giving the substituted carbon the lowest number
In the direction giving the highest total locant sum
Alphabetically regardless of position on the chain
questions.e: The carbon chain is numbered in the direction that gives the substituted carbon (bearing the halogen) the lowest possible number, and if there's a tie, the substituent that is first alphabetically gets the lower number.

questions.q: When naming a haloalkane with multiple different halogen substituents, in what order are they listed in the name?
o: Order of position on the chain regardless of letter
Order of molecular weight, heaviest first
Order of atomic number of the halogen
Alphabetical order of the substituent names
questions.e: The lecture specifies that substituents are numbered and listed in alphabetical order (e.g. bromo before chloro before fluoro before iodo).

questions.q: CH3-CH2-Br is named using the IUPAC system as:
questions.e: The lecture's example designates CH3-CH2-Br as ethyl bromide (common name) or bromoethane (IUPAC name) — the halogen is a substituent on the parent ethane chain.

questions.q: In common nomenclature of alkyl halides, how is the name constructed?
o: Only numbers are used, no words at all in the name
The molecular formula alone is used, with no substituent name
The halide is named first followed by 'yl' then the alkyl group
The alkyl group name is followed by the word 'halide'
questions.e: Common names treat the alkyl group as a substituent on the halide: e.g. methyl fluoride, pentyl chloride, cyclohexyl iodide. This system is useful only for small alkyl groups.

questions.q: What is CHCl3 commonly called, using the 'haloform' naming pattern?
questions.e: CHX3-type compounds are called haloforms; CHCl3 specifically is chloroform. CH2X2 compounds are methylene halides (e.g. CH2Cl2 = methylene chloride) and CX4 compounds are carbon tetrahalides (e.g. CCl4 = carbon tetrachloride).

questions.q: Which named chloroalkane solvents are noted in the lecture as having cumulative toxicity and carcinogenic potential requiring fume-hood use?
questions.e: The lecture explicitly warns that many chloroalkanes, including CH2Cl2, CHCl3, and CCl4, have cumulative toxicity and are carcinogenic, so they should be used only in fume hoods with great care.

questions.q: For the IUPAC name 3-bromo-3-ethylpentane, what is the parent chain and where is the bromine located?
o: A 5-carbon pentane chain, with bromo at C1
A 3-carbon propane chain, with bromo at C1
A 5-carbon pentane chain, with bromo at C3
A 6-carbon hexane chain, with bromo at C3
questions.e: The parent chain named is pentane (5 carbons); the locants '3-bromo-3-ethyl' place both the bromo and ethyl substituents on C3, making that carbon tertiary (bonded to three other carbons).

questions.q: Why do alkyl halides have higher boiling points than alkanes with the same number of carbons?
o: Greater molecular weight and greater polarity
They form hydrogen bonds with each other
Lower molecular weight and reduced polarity
They are ionic compounds with no covalent character
questions.e: The lecture states alkyl halides have higher boiling points than alkanes of the same carbon number because of greater molecular weight and greater polarity (not hydrogen bonding, which alkyl halides cannot do with themselves).

questions.q: For isomeric alkyl halides, how does boiling point change as branching increases?
o: Boiling point decreases with increased branching
Boiling point increases with increased branching
Boiling point is unaffected by branching
questions.e: The lecture states that for isomeric halides, boiling point decreases as branching increases — a trend also seen in alkanes, due to reduced surface area for intermolecular (van der Waals) contact.

questions.q: Why are alkyl halides insoluble in water despite being polar molecules?
o: They have no dipole moment at all
Water is nonpolar and cannot form hydrogen bonds
They cannot form hydrogen bonds with water molecules
questions.e: Although alkyl halides are polar, they are insoluble in water because they are unable to form hydrogen bonds with water molecules; they are, however, soluble in typical organic solvents.

questions.q: Which alkyl halides are typically LESS dense than water (1.00 g/mL)?
o: All alkyl iodides, regardless of chain length
All alkyl bromides, regardless of chain length
Alkyl chlorides with two or more chlorine atoms
Alkyl fluorides and alkyl chlorides with just one chlorine atom
questions.e: Alkyl fluorides and mono-chloro alkyl chlorides are less dense than water; chlorides with two or more Cl atoms, and all bromides and iodides, are denser than water because of the heavy halogen atoms.

questions.q: Comparing RX to its parent alkane RH, which statement is correct regarding density?
o: RX is less dense than RH because halogens are somewhat lighter than hydrogen atoms
RX and RH always have identical densities regardless of the specific halogen substituent involved
RX is always less dense than RH regardless of which specific halogen atom is present
RX is more dense than RH, since it carries a heavy halogen atom, with density order RI > RBr > RCl > RF
questions.e: The lecture's worked exercise states RX is more dense than RH because of the heavy X atom, with density decreasing in the order RI > RBr > RCl > RF, paralleling the atomic mass of the halogens.

questions.q: What happens to carbon-halogen bond length and bond strength going down the halogen group of the periodic table (F to I)?
o: Both bond length and strength increase
Bond length increases and bond strength decreases
Both bond length and strength decrease
Bond length decreases and bond strength increases
questions.e: As halogen atomic size increases down the group, the carbon-halogen bond length increases while bond strength decreases, which is why fluoroalkanes (shortest, strongest C-X bond) are the least reactive.

questions.q: What is the correct order of reactivity among the hydrogen halides (HX)?
o: All hydrogen halides react at the same rate
questions.e: The lecture states the order of reactivity among HX is HI > HBr > HCl >> HF, consistent with C-X (and H-X) bond strength decreasing down the halogen group.

questions.q: Why does the C-X bond in an alkyl halide become polarized, giving carbon a partial positive charge?
o: Halogens are more electronegative than carbon
Carbon is more electronegative than halogens
The bond is purely ionic, not covalent
questions.e: Halogens are more electronegative than carbon, so they pull electron density toward themselves; carbon acquires a partial positive charge (delta+) and the halogen a partial negative charge (delta-), making carbon an electrophilic site.

questions.q: Which of the following is described as the major method for synthesizing alkyl halides?
o: Direct fluorination with F2 gas only
Preparation from alcohols reacting with HX reagents
Electrolysis of alkanes in aqueous solution
Reaction of alkanes with sodium halide salts
questions.e: The lecture explicitly states that the major method for synthesizing alkyl halides is preparation from alcohols, which react with a variety of reagents (HX, SOCl2, PX3) to yield alkyl halides.

questions.q: Among the classes of alcohols reacting with hydrogen halides to give alkyl halides, which is the MOST reactive?
questions.e: The lecture states that among the classes of alcohols, tertiary alcohols are observed to be the most reactive toward hydrogen halides, and primary alcohols the least reactive (consistent with the SN1 mechanism favouring stable tertiary carbocations).

questions.q: In the reaction (CH3)3COH + HCl -> (CH3)3C-Cl + H-OH, what mechanism operates and why?
o: SN1, because a stable tertiary carbocation intermediate forms
E2, because a strong bulky base is present
SN2, because the substrate is primary
Free-radical halogenation, because UV light is required
questions.e: The lecture states this reaction of a tertiary alcohol with HCl occurs by an SN1 mechanism and involves a carbocation intermediate, consistent with tertiary substrates favouring SN1/carbocation chemistry.

questions.q: What are the products of the reaction R-OH + SOCl2 -> ?
questions.e: Thionyl chloride reacts with alcohols to give the alkyl chloride plus sulfur dioxide and hydrogen chloride as by-products: R-OH + SOCl2 -> R-Cl + SO2 + HCl.

questions.q: Besides reaction with alcohols, which two other synthesis routes to alkyl halides are listed in the lecture?
o: Reduction of carboxylic acids and Grignard reactions
Oxidation of ethers and hydrolysis of esters
Halogenation of alkanes and addition of HX to alkenes
questions.e: Alongside preparation from alcohols, the lecture lists halogenation of alkanes with Cl2 or Br2 under UV radiation, and addition of HX (or X2, giving vic-dihalides) to alkenes, as synthesis routes.

questions.q: What does the '1' in SN1 refer to?
o: The rate-determining step involves only one molecule
Only one product forms regardless of conditions
Only primary substrates react via this pathway
The reaction has only one mechanistic step
questions.e: In SN1, 'S' = substitution, 'N' = nucleophilic, and '1' = unimolecular, meaning the rate-determining step entails only one species, R-X.

questions.q: What does the '2' in SN2 refer to?
o: The rate-determining step involves two species
The reaction takes two steps to complete
questions.e: In SN2, '2' = bimolecular, meaning the rate-determining (and only) step entails two species: the substrate R-X and the nucleophile Nu-.

questions.q: In an SN1 reaction, what happens in Step 1?
o: Two separate molecules of R-X react directly with each other in a single step
The alkene is formed directly and immediately by simultaneous loss of H and X from the substrate
R-X dissociates, forming a carbocation and the leaving group, in a slow rate-determining step
The nucleophile attacks the carbon directly in a single fast concerted step
questions.e: Step 1 of SN1 is the slow, rate-determining ionization of R-X: the C-X bond breaks as the substrate dissociates into a carbocation (R+) and the leaving group (X-), involving only one species.

questions.q: In an SN1 reaction, what happens in Step 2, and how fast is it relative to Step 1?
o: A second molecule of substrate attacks the carbocation; it proceeds at the same rate as Step 1
The carbocation slowly decomposes back to starting material; it is slower than Step 1 and unfavorable
The carbocation combines rapidly with a nucleophile to give the product; it is fast relative to the slow Step 1
The leaving group re-attaches to the carbocation immediately to reform the original starting R-X
questions.e: Step 2 is a rapid reaction in which the highly reactive carbocation (only 6 electrons around the positive carbon) combines with a nucleophile to give the product, R-Nu; this step is fast compared to the slow ionization in Step 1.

questions.q: What is the correct rate law for an SN1 reaction?
questions.e: Because the rate-determining step of SN1 (ionization) involves only R-X, the rate law is Rate = k[R-X], independent of nucleophile concentration.

questions.q: What is the correct rate law for an SN2 reaction?
o: Rate = k[R-X] only, independent of nucleophile concentration
Rate = k[R-X][Nu-], depending on both concentrations
Rate = k[Nu-] only, independent of substrate concentration
Rate = k, independent of concentration of either species
questions.e: Because the rate-determining (and only) step of SN2 involves collision between R-X and the nucleophile, the rate law is Rate = k[R-X][Nu-], dependent on both species' concentrations.

questions.q: Why do primary (1 degree) alkyl halides generally NOT undergo SN1 reactions?
o: Primary carbocations are too unstable to form readily
Primary halides are insoluble in all common solvents
Primary halides have no leaving group at all
SN1 requires two nucleophile molecules, which primary halides lack
questions.e: Carbocation stability increases with the number of attached R groups (3 degree > 2 degree > 1 degree); primary carbocations are unstable, so primary alkyl halides generally proceed via SN2 rather than SN1.

questions.q: What is the stereochemical outcome at a chiral center in an SN1 reaction, and why?
o: Complete inversion, because the nucleophile attacks from the backside only
No stereochemical change is possible since SN1 cannot occur at a chiral center
Complete retention, because the nucleophile attacks only from the front side directly
Racemization, because the nucleophile can attack either face of the planar carbocation intermediate
questions.e: Because the carbocation intermediate is planar, the nucleophile can attack from either face with roughly equal probability, converting an R-enantiomer into a near 50:50 mixture of R and S products — racemization.

questions.q: What is the stereochemical outcome at a chiral center in an SN2 reaction?
o: Racemization, a 50:50 mixture of both enantiomers formed
Inversion of configuration — an R-enantiomer becomes the S-enantiomer
Retention of configuration at the chiral center
The chiral center is destroyed and becomes achiral
questions.e: SN2 proceeds through backside attack in a single concerted step, leading to inversion of configuration at the chiral center — an R-enantiomer is converted into an S-enantiomer.

questions.q: At what angle does the nucleophile approach the C-X bond in an SN2 reaction?
questions.e: The nucleophile in SN2 approaches the C-X bond at 180 degrees, attacking from the side directly opposite the leaving group (backside attack), which is what produces inversion of configuration.

questions.q: What is the correct reactivity order of alkyl halides in SN2 reactions, and why?
o: 3 degree > 2 degree > 1 degree, because tertiary carbocations are by far the most stable
2 degree > 3 degree > 1 degree, with no clear or consistent steric trend observed experimentally at all
All classes of alkyl halide react at exactly the same rate in SN2 reactions regardless of structure
1 degree > 2 degree > 3 degree, because bulky substituents sterically hinder backside nucleophilic attack
questions.e: SN2 reactivity follows 1 degree > 2 degree > 3 degree because steric hindrance from bulky R groups blocks the nucleophile's backside approach; tertiary halides essentially do not undergo SN2 at all.

questions.q: Why does the SN2 transition state make sterically hindered alkyl halides unreactive via this pathway?
o: Sterically hindered halides have no leaving group at all present in the molecule
The transition state has no carbon atom involved in it at all during the process
The transition state involves a pentacoordinate carbon, which bulky groups block from forming
The transition state requires two entirely separate carbocation intermediates to form
questions.e: The SN2 transition state involves a pentacoordinate (5-bonded) carbon as the nucleophile partially bonds while the leaving group partially departs; bulky substituents prevent the nucleophile from reaching this geometry.

questions.q: In an elimination (dehydrohalogenation) reaction of an alkyl halide, what is eliminated and what product typically forms?
o: CO2 is eliminated from the molecule, forming an alcohol product
Only hydrogen is eliminated, forming an unusual carbocation salt
Only the halogen is eliminated, forming a reactive carbanion
The elements of H-X are eliminated from adjacent carbons, typically forming an alkene
questions.e: In elimination reactions of alkyl halides, the elements of H-X are eliminated from adjacent (alpha and beta) carbons; the product is very often an unsaturated compound (alkene), via dehydrohalogenation.

questions.q: What is the key mechanistic similarity between the E1 mechanism and the SN1 mechanism?
o: Both proceed in a single concerted step with no intermediate species forming at all
Both share the same first step: slow, rate-determining ionization of the substrate to form a carbocation
Both mechanisms always give exclusively retention of configuration at the reacting carbon
Both mechanisms require a pentacoordinate transition state to form at the reacting carbon
questions.e: The E1 mechanism is a two-step process whose first step is identical to SN1's: the slow ionization of R-X to form a carbocation intermediate, followed (in E1) by base removal of a beta-proton to yield the alkene.

questions.q: How does the E2 mechanism compare structurally to the E1 mechanism?
o: E2 is a one-step process where C-H and C-X bonds break simultaneously, unlike the two-step E1
E2 is a two-step process just like E1, forming a carbocation intermediate first
E2 requires a discrete carbocation intermediate to form first, exactly as in E1
E2 and E1 are essentially identical mechanisms, simply given two different names
questions.e: Like SN2, the E2 mechanism is a single concerted step: the base removes the beta-hydrogen while the leaving group departs simultaneously, giving the alkene directly without any intermediate — unlike the two-step, carbocation-forming E1.

questions.q: Why does a strong, bulky base (e.g. potassium tert-butoxide) favor E2 over SN2?
o: Bulky bases supposedly cannot act as bases at all in this type of reaction, only ever as nucleophiles toward the substrate
A bulky base has difficulty reaching the backside of the alpha-carbon for inline attack, but can still easily pluck off a nearby beta-hydrogen
Bulky bases actually increase the rate of SN2 far more than they increase the rate of E2 in this particular case overall
Bulky bases only work efficiently with primary alkyl substrates, never with secondary or tertiary alkyl halides at all
questions.e: A bulky base struggles to approach the crowded alpha-carbon from the backside required for SN2 attack, but can readily abstract a more accessible beta-hydrogen, so elimination (E2) is favored over substitution.

questions.q: An acyl halide is defined by which structural feature?
o: A halogen bonded to an alkene carbon
A halogen bonded to a saturated sp3 carbon only
A halogen directly bonded to a carbonyl group carbon
A halogen bonded to a benzene ring carbon
questions.e: Acyl halides have the halogen directly bonded to the carbonyl carbon, distinguishing them from vinyl halides (halogen on an alkene carbon) and aryl halides (halogen on an aromatic ring carbon).

questions.q: Vinyl chloride (H2C=CHCl) is chiefly used industrially to produce which polymer?
questions.e: Vinyl chloride monomer (VCM), an organochloride with formula H2C=CHCl, is an important industrial chemical chiefly used to produce the polymer polyvinyl chloride (PVC), which comes in rigid and flexible forms.

questions.q: What distinguishes rigid PVC from soft/flexible PVC?
o: The molecular formula of the monomer
The amount of plasticizers in the polymer
Whether chlorine or fluorine is used
The temperature at which it is stored
questions.e: PVC has two forms depending on the amount of plasticizers (usually phthalates) present: rigid PVC (pipes, doors, windows, bottles, cards) and soft PVC (plumbing, cable insulation, imitation leather, rubber substitute).

questions.q: DDT (dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane) is formed by condensation of which two reagents?
o: Phosphorus trichloride and benzene under heat
Chlorobenzene and chloral in concentrated H2SO4
Vinyl chloride and ethanol under acid catalysis
questions.e: The lecture states DDT is formed by condensation of chlorobenzene and chloral (trichloroacetaldehyde) in concentrated sulfuric acid, producing a highly toxic synthetic insecticide.

questions.q: How does DDT act as an insecticide, according to the lecture?
o: By dehydrating the insect exoskeleton completely
By acting as a fungal antibiotic in the soil
As a contact poison that disorganizes the nervous system of insects
By blocking photosynthesis in target plant cells
questions.e: DDT is described as a synthetic insecticide, highly toxic to a wide variety of insects, acting as a contact poison that disorganizes the nervous system.

questions.q: Chloramphenicol is described in the lecture as what kind of pharmaceutical agent?
o: An antitumor Grignard reagent used in synthesis
questions.e: Chloramphenicol is a broad-spectrum bacteriostatic antibiotic, useful for treating a number of bacterial infections and effective against most Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and anaerobic organisms.

questions.q: Why have chlorofluorocarbon (CFC) refrigerants like Freons fallen out of favor since the 20th century?
o: They are too expensive to manufacture
They cannot absorb or release heat effectively
questions.e: Chlorofluorocarbons such as trichlorofluoromethane (CCl3F) and dichlorodifluoromethane (CCl2F2) were widely used as refrigerants but have limited use today because of their ozone-depletion effects; alternatives include ammonia, sulfur dioxide, and non-halogenated hydrocarbons like propane.

questions.q: Ranking carbocation stability for a primary (A), tertiary (B), and secondary (C) carbocation, what is the correct order of INCREASING stability?
o: A = B = C, all equally stable
questions.e: Carbocation stability increases with the number of attached alkyl groups: primary (A) is least stable, secondary (C) is intermediate, and tertiary (B) is most stable, giving the order A < C < B.

questions.q: What is the general formula and defining functional group of an alcohol?
o: R-CHO, defined by an aldehyde group
R-NH2, defined by an amine group
R-OH, defined by the hydroxyl group
R-X, defined by a halogen substituent
questions.e: Alcohols are organic compounds that contain the hydroxyl group (-OH) as their functional group, with the general formula R-OH.

questions.q: How are alcohols classified as primary, secondary, or tertiary?
o: By whether the -OH is attached to a primary, secondary, or tertiary carbon, exactly as alkyl halides are classified
By the boiling point of the alcohol relative to its structural isomers and molecular weight
By the total number of carbons present in the entire molecular structure overall, ignoring functional groups
By whether the molecule is aromatic or aliphatic in its overall carbon skeleton structure entirely
questions.e: The lecture states alcohols are classified as primary, secondary, or tertiary depending on whether the OH group is attached to a primary, secondary, or tertiary carbon — the same classification scheme used for alkyl halides.

questions.q: C4H9OH can exist as three different alcohols with the same molecular formula. What distinguishes 1-butanol, 2-butanol, and 2-methyl-2-propanol?
o: Their molecular formulas, which are actually all different
The type of halogen present in each functional group
The number of carbons attached to the carbon bearing the -OH group
Only their boiling points, with identical structures otherwise
questions.e: All three share the formula C4H9OH but differ in classification: 1-butanol is primary (1 carbon attached to the C-OH), 2-butanol is secondary (2 carbons attached), and 2-methyl-2-propanol (tert-butyl alcohol) is tertiary (3 carbons attached).

questions.q: In IUPAC nomenclature, how is the systematic name of an alcohol derived from its parent hydrocarbon?
o: Add the prefix 'hydroxy-' to the front of the alkane name only
Replace the final 'e' of the parent hydrocarbon name with 'ol'
Add 'ene' to the parent hydrocarbon name
questions.e: The lecture states the systematic name of an alcohol is obtained by replacing the 'e' at the end of the parent hydrocarbon name with 'ol' (e.g. propane -> propanol).

questions.q: When an alcohol has two hydroxyl groups, what suffix is added to the parent hydrocarbon name?
questions.e: If there are two OH groups, 'diol' is added to the name of the parent hydrocarbon, as in the example '7-methyl-3,5-octanediol' from the lecture's exercise.

questions.q: How is the parent hydrocarbon chain numbered when naming an alcohol?
o: Numbering is not required at all for naming any alcohol compound
Alphabetically by substituent name only, ignoring position
In the direction that gives the -OH functional group the lowest possible number
Always starting from the carbon farthest from the -OH group itself
questions.e: As with alkyl halides, the parent hydrocarbon is numbered in the direction that gives the functional group (here, -OH) the lowest possible locant.

questions.q: What is the common (functional class) name for CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3, and what is its classification?
questions.e: CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3 has the OH on a carbon attached to two other carbons, making it secondary; its common name is sec-butyl alcohol (also 2-butanol), classified as 2 degree in the lecture's exercise.

questions.q: How is a common (functional class) name for a simple alcohol constructed?
o: Use only the molecular formula with no substituent name mentioned at all
Replace the alkane's final 'e' ending with the suffix 'ol' instead of anything else
Name the alkyl group bearing the hydroxyl substituent, then add 'alcohol' as a separate word
Add 'oic acid' onto the very end of the alkyl group's own name instead of anything else
questions.e: The lecture describes common names as naming the alkyl group that bears the hydroxyl substituent and then adding 'alcohol' as a separate word — e.g. isopropyl alcohol, benzyl alcohol.

questions.q: What is the common name and classification of t-butyl alcohol, (CH3)3COH?
questions.e: (CH3)3COH has the -OH carbon attached to three other carbons, making it tertiary; its common name is t-butyl (tert-butyl) alcohol, classified 3 degree in the lecture's exercise list.

questions.q: What is the common name and classification of benzyl alcohol (C6H5CH2OH)?
questions.e: Benzyl alcohol has its -OH carbon (the CH2) attached to only one other carbon (the aromatic ring carbon counts as the attachment point), so it is classified as primary (1 degree) in the lecture's exercise.

questions.q: If there is more than one substituent in an alcohol's IUPAC name, in what order are they listed?
o: Order of molecular weight, heaviest substituent first
Order of appearance in the structure, left to right
Reverse alphabetical order of the substituents
Alphabetical order of the substituent names
questions.e: The lecture specifies that if there is more than one substituent, the substituents are listed in alphabetical order — the same rule used for naming alkyl halides.

questions.q: Why are the boiling points of alcohols much higher than those of alkanes or alkyl halides of similar molecular weight?
o: Alcohols have a much higher molecular weight than alkyl halides
Alcohols form intermolecular hydrogen bonds through the O-H group
Alcohols cannot exist as liquids at room temperature
Alcohols are ionic compounds with charged bonds
questions.e: The lecture explains that the ability of alcohol molecules to associate with each other through intermolecular hydrogen bonding is responsible for their much higher boiling points compared with alkanes and alkyl halides of similar molecular weight.

questions.q: What determines whether an alcohol is soluble in water, according to the lecture?
o: The color of the alcohol as it is observed in solution under normal everyday lighting conditions
The size of the alkyl group — fewer than 4 carbons tend to be soluble, more than 4 carbons tend to be insoluble
Only the presence of a benzene ring somewhere within the entire molecular structure itself
Whether the alcohol is primary, secondary, or tertiary in its overall classification
questions.e: Solubility in water depends on the size of the alkyl group: alcohols with fewer than four carbons are generally soluble in water, while those with more than four carbons are increasingly insoluble as the hydrocarbon character dominates.

questions.q: Why is tert-butyl alcohol more soluble in water than n-butyl alcohol, despite having the same number of carbons?
o: tert-Butyl alcohol is fully ionic while n-butyl alcohol remains covalent
n-Butyl alcohol reacts destructively with water instead of simply dissolving
tert-Butyl alcohol has an extra oxygen atom compared to n-butyl alcohol
Branching minimizes the contact surface of the nonpolar portion of the molecule with water
questions.e: Branched alkyl groups minimize the nonpolar surface area exposed to water, so branched alcohols (like tert-butyl alcohol) are more water-soluble than their unbranched isomers (like n-butyl alcohol) with the same carbon count.

questions.q: What is the approximate density of liquid alcohols, and how does it compare to water?
o: About 0.8 g/mL — less dense than water
About 2.0 g/mL — much denser than water
questions.e: The lecture states that all liquid alcohols have densities of approximately 0.8 g/mL, making them less dense than water (1.00 g/mL) — this is why alcohol floats on water.

questions.q: Why can propanol dissolve in water while propane cannot?
o: Propane is denser than liquid water at ordinary room temperature and pressure
Propanol has more carbon atoms than propane, which fully explains the difference
Propanol can hydrogen-bond with water via its -OH group, while propane has no polar group to do so
Propane is a gas and propanol is a solid at ordinary room temperature conditions
questions.e: The lecture's worked exercise explains that propanol, unlike propane or butane, is soluble in water because it can hydrogen-bond with water through its hydroxyl group; propane has no such polar functional group.

questions.q: Why does n-hexanol fail to dissolve appreciably in water, even though it has an -OH group?
o: Hexanol is supposedly a solid at ordinary room temperature, quite unlike propanol
Hexanol has no oxygen atom anywhere at all in its molecular structure, apparently
As the alkyl group becomes larger, ROH resembles the hydrocarbon more closely, reducing water solubility
Hexanol reacts destructively and immediately with water on any contact with it at all
questions.e: The lecture states that as the R group becomes larger, the ROH molecule increasingly resembles the nonpolar hydrocarbon, so the influence of the single -OH group on solubility diminishes and n-hexanol is not soluble in water.

questions.q: Alcohols can be synthesized by hydration of alkenes. What does 'hydration' mean in this context?
o: Addition of the elements of water across the alkene's double bond
Reaction of the alkene with a hydrogen halide reagent
Removal of water from the alkene to form a diene
Addition of hydrogen gas only, with no oxygen involved
questions.e: Hydration of alkenes adds the elements of water across the double-bonded carbons, which can occur in either a Markovnikov's or anti-Markovnikov's manner, producing an alcohol.

questions.q: Which reducing agent is described as 'a very strong reducing agent that will reduce many functional groups in addition to aldehydes and ketones'?
o: Hydrogen gas with a platinum catalyst
Lithium aluminum hydride, commonly abbreviated LiAlH4
Sodium borohydride, a much milder reagent
questions.e: The lecture contrasts LiAlH4, a very strong reducing agent that reduces many functional groups besides aldehydes/ketones, with the milder NaBH4, which basically reduces only aldehydes and ketones to alcohols.

questions.q: What alcohol classification results from reduction of a carboxylic acid, and what reagent is standard for this reduction?
o: A secondary alcohol; hydrogen gas with nickel is standard
No alcohol forms; carboxylic acids cannot be reduced
A primary alcohol; lithium aluminum hydride is the standard choice
A tertiary alcohol; sodium borohydride is standard
questions.e: Reduction of a carboxylic acid leads to formation of a primary alcohol; this reduction requires a very strong reducing agent, and lithium aluminum hydride is the standard choice, since NaBH4 is too weak.

questions.q: When an ester such as methyl benzoate is reduced with LiAlH4, what products form?
o: One alcohol and one carboxylic acid
A single alcohol only, with no other product
One aldehyde and one ketone forming together
Two alcohols — benzyl alcohol and methanol
questions.e: The lecture gives the specific example that esters, like carboxylic acids, are normally reduced with LiAlH4, and in these reactions two alcohols are formed — reduction of methyl benzoate gives benzyl alcohol and methanol.

questions.q: When a Grignard reagent reacts with formaldehyde (HCHO), what class of alcohol is produced?
o: No alcohol forms; an ether forms instead
questions.e: The lecture specifies that a Grignard reagent reacting with formaldehyde produces a primary alcohol, because formaldehyde contributes only one carbon substituent beyond the Grignard's R group.

questions.q: When a Grignard reagent reacts with a ketone, what class of alcohol is produced?
questions.e: Per the lecture, a Grignard reagent reacting with a ketone (which already has two carbon substituents on the carbonyl carbon) produces a tertiary alcohol, since the Grignard's R group adds a third.

questions.q: When a Grignard reagent reacts with an aldehyde other than formaldehyde, what class of alcohol is produced?
questions.e: The lecture states that a Grignard reagent reacting with any other aldehyde (besides formaldehyde) produces a secondary alcohol, since the aldehyde already carries one carbon substituent and the Grignard's R group adds a second.

questions.q: How does the oxygen atom of an alcohol affect the C-O and O-H bonds, and what consequence does this have for the O-H bond?
o: It converts the alcohol molecule entirely into a fully ionic salt compound of some rather unusual kind
It makes the C-O bond completely nonpolar and entirely unreactive toward any nucleophiles whatsoever
It has no significant effect on either bond at all, leaving both entirely unchanged and unaffected by the oxygen
It polarizes both bonds; polarization of the O-H bond makes the hydrogen partially positive, so alcohols behave as weak acids
questions.e: The lecture states the oxygen atom of an alcohol polarizes both the C-O and O-H bonds; polarization of the O-H bond makes the hydrogen partially positive, which is why alcohols act as weak acids.

questions.q: Why is OH- described as a 'very poor leaving group' in reactions of alcohols?
o: OH- reacts instantly with any nucleophile that happens to be present nearby
OH- carries no charge at all in solution, unlike any typical leaving group would
OH- is a strong base, due to the electron pairs on oxygen, and strong bases make poor leaving groups
OH- is too small in physical size to ever properly leave the molecule at all
questions.e: The lecture explains that OH- is a strong base because of the electron pairs on oxygen, and strong bases are poor leaving groups — this is why alcohols often need activation (e.g. protonation, or conversion to a better leaving group) before substitution.

questions.q: What is the correct order of decreasing acid strength among alcohols, as given in the lecture?
o: All classes of alcohol have identical acid strength
Secondary alcohol is the strongest acid of all classes
Methyl alcohol > 1 degree alcohol > 2 degree alcohol > 3 degree alcohol
questions.e: The lecture states the acid strength of alcohols follows the order: methyl alcohol > 1 degree alcohol > 2 degree alcohol > 3 degree alcohol, reflecting decreasing stabilization of the alkoxide as branching (electron donation) increases.

questions.q: When ethanol reacts with sodium metal (2 C2H5OH + 2 Na), what are the products?
questions.e: The lecture's equation shows 2 C2H5OH + 2 Na -> 2 C2H5O-Na+ + H2: the alcohol acts as a weak acid, losing H+ to sodium to form the alkoxide (sodium ethoxide) and releasing hydrogen gas.

questions.q: What synthetic application does the reaction of an alkoxide with a primary alkyl halide serve?
questions.e: The lecture notes that alkoxides formed from alcohols and sodium can react with primary alkyl halides to form ethers — this is the Williamson synthesis of ethers (e.g. C2H5O-Na+ + CH3-Cl -> C2H5O-CH3 + NaCl).

questions.q: Oxidation of a primary alcohol can give which two classes of products, depending on conditions?
o: An aldehyde or a carboxylic acid
Only a ketone, regardless of conditions
questions.e: The lecture states primary alcohols can be oxidized to aldehydes (isolated cleanly using Cr(VI) reagents like PCC or PDC in anhydrous media) and to carboxylic acids (using stronger oxidants).

questions.q: What are pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) and pyridinium dichromate (PDC) used for, and why are they favored for this purpose?
o: Forming Grignard reagents from alkyl halides and magnesium metal in anhydrous dry ether solvent
Dehydrating alcohols to alkenes under strong acid conditions and quite considerable applied heat
Oxidizing primary alcohols cleanly to aldehydes, because they are anhydrous Cr reagents that stop oxidation at the aldehyde stage
Reducing ketones to secondary alcohols using strong metal hydride reducing reagents
questions.e: The lecture describes PCC and PDC as Cr(VI) oxidants used in anhydrous media (dichloromethane) that permit easy isolation of aldehydes in good yield from primary alcohols, avoiding over-oxidation to the carboxylic acid that aqueous oxidants would cause.

questions.q: What happens when a secondary alcohol is oxidized, and why does the reaction typically stop there?
o: It cannot be oxidized under any ordinary laboratory conditions at all, not ever, under any circumstances
It is oxidized to an ether only under unusually strong, forcing, and rather extreme reaction conditions
It is oxidized all the way through, eventually, to a fully formed carboxylic acid end product
It is oxidized to a ketone, and the reaction usually stops at the ketone stage because ketones resist further oxidation under the same conditions
questions.e: The lecture states 2 degree alcohols can be oxidized to ketones, and the reaction usually stops at the ketone stage, unlike primary alcohols which can proceed further to carboxylic acids.

questions.q: Why do tertiary alcohols not undergo oxidation readily?
o: They have too many hydrogens present on the hydroxyl-bearing carbon
They are always completely insoluble in whatever oxidizing solvent happens to be used
They have no hydrogen atom on the hydroxyl-bearing carbon needed for the oxidation mechanism
Tertiary alcohols are actually already fully oxidized compounds by nature
questions.e: The lecture explains that tertiary alcohols have no hydrogen on their hydroxyl-bearing carbon, and since oxidation of an alcohol requires removing that C-H hydrogen along with the O-H hydrogen, tertiary alcohols do not undergo this oxidation readily.

questions.q: In the dehydration of alcohols with strong acid and heat, what elements are removed and from where?
o: H and OH are removed from adjacent carbons, forming an alkene
Only a hydrogen is removed, forming an unstable radical
CO2 is removed from the molecule, forming an ether
Only the OH group is removed, forming a carbocation salt
questions.e: Heating most alcohols with a strong acid causes loss of H and OH from adjacent carbons to form an alkene — directly analogous to dehydrohalogenation of alkyl halides.

questions.q: Which class of alcohol is the MOST difficult to dehydrate, and which is dehydrated under the mildest conditions?
o: All classes of alcohol dehydrate equally easily under the very same conditions
Secondary alcohols are hardest to dehydrate; primary alcohols dehydrate the mildest
Tertiary alcohols are hardest to dehydrate; primary alcohols dehydrate under the mildest conditions
Primary alcohols are hardest to dehydrate; tertiary alcohols dehydrate under the mildest conditions
questions.e: The lecture states primary alcohols are the most difficult to dehydrate, secondary alcohols dehydrate under milder conditions, and tertiary alcohols dehydrate under extremely mild conditions — paralleling the stability trend of the intermediate carbocation.

questions.q: What functional group class results from reacting an alcohol with a carboxylic acid, acid anhydride, or acid chloride?
questions.e: The lecture states that alcohols react with carboxylic acids, acid anhydrides, or acid chlorides to form esters — the esterification reaction.

questions.q: When an alcohol reacts with a hydrohalic acid (HCl, HBr, or HI), what type of reaction occurs and what is formed?
o: Reduction, forming an alkane product directly from the alcohol
Oxidation, forming a carboxylic acid as the final product
Elimination, forming an alkene as the major reaction product
Substitution, forming an alkyl halide by excision of the carbon-hydroxyl bond
questions.e: The lecture states alcohols react with hydrohalic acids to form alkyl halides by excision (breaking) of the carbon-hydroxyl bond; since halide ions are good nucleophiles, substitution products predominate. Inorganic halides such as PCl5 and PCl3 can also be used.

questions.q: What defines 'absolute alcohol' as described in the lecture?
o: Any alcohol with fewer than 4 carbons
Alcohol that has been denatured with methanol
Alcohol containing no water — i.e. 100% C2H5OH
questions.e: The lecture defines absolute alcohol as alcohol containing no water, i.e. 100% C2H5OH, distinguishing it from rectified spirit (95.5% ethanol + water) and other diluted forms.

questions.q: Why are ethanol and isopropyl alcohol widely used as disinfectants?
o: They evaporate quickly and dissolve lipids, denaturing the proteins of infecting organisms
They are inexpensive food additives used quite widely in preservation
They form a permanent protective waterproof coating on the skin surface
They react with oxygen in the air to form ozone gas rather rapidly indeed
questions.e: The lecture explains that alcoholic disinfectants such as ethanol and isopropyl alcohol are effective because of their ability to evaporate quickly and dissolve lipids, which denatures the proteins of infecting organisms.

questions.q: What is the composition of 'rectified spirit' as given in the lecture?
questions.e: The lecture defines rectified spirit as containing 95.5% ethyl alcohol and 4.5% water, distinct from absolute alcohol (100% ethanol).

questions.q: How is 'methylated spirit' (denatured alcohol) produced, and why?
o: By simply diluting absolute alcohol with ordinary distilled water only, with nothing else ever added at all
By adding sugar and yeast to rectified spirit in order to referment it fully and then carefully redistill it again
Rectified spirit is rendered poisonous by addition of 4-10% methyl alcohol plus traces of pyridine and copper sulphate, to prevent it being consumed as a beverage
By carefully distilling rectified spirit a second time in order to increase its purity even further still
questions.e: The lecture states methylated spirit is rectified spirit rendered poisonous by adding 4-10% methyl alcohol, along with traces of pyridine and copper sulphate — deliberately making it unfit for drinking while remaining useful as a solvent.

questions.q: What is the typical alcohol (ethanol) content range for alcoholic beverages, as stated in the lecture?
questions.e: The lecture states that alcoholic beverages typically contain 2% to 50% alcohol (ethanol) by volume, spanning the range from light beers to strong spirits.

questions.q: How is a carboxylic acid defined structurally?
o: An organic acid with a ketone group linked to an amine
An organic acid with an acyl group linked to a hydroxyl group
An ester in which the alkoxy group has been removed
A hydrocarbon with a single hydroxyl substituent
questions.e: The lecture defines a carboxylic acid as an organic acid that has an acyl group (RCO) linked to a hydroxyl group (OH), condensed as RCO2H or RCOOH.

questions.q: What distinguishes an 'aliphatic acid' from an 'aromatic acid'?
o: Aliphatic acids supposedly cannot form salts at all, but aromatic acids readily and easily can
An aliphatic acid always and necessarily contains nitrogen; an aromatic acid never does at all
Aromatic acids are always fully dicarboxylic; aliphatic acids are always purely monocarboxylic
An aliphatic acid has an alkyl group bonded to the carboxyl group; an aromatic acid has an aryl group bonded to it
questions.e: The lecture's structure slide classifies carboxylic acids as aliphatic (alkyl group bonded to the carboxyl group) or aromatic (aryl group bonded to the carboxyl group).

questions.q: Carboxylic acids are described in the lecture as the starting materials for which class of compounds?
questions.e: The lecture states carboxylic acids (RCO2H) are starting materials for acyl derivatives such as esters, amides, and acid chlorides.

questions.q: According to the lecture, carboxylic acids are abundant in nature largely because they arise from what metabolic process?
o: Reduction of amino acids in the liver
Oxidation of aldehydes and alcohols in metabolism
Hydrolysis of nucleic acids in the cell
questions.e: The lecture notes that carboxylic acids are abundant in nature from the oxidation of aldehydes and alcohols in metabolism, giving examples such as acetic acid (vinegar) and butanoic acid (rancid butter).

questions.q: Which carboxylic acid is responsible for the characteristic smell of vinegar?
questions.e: The lecture lists acetic acid, CH3CO2H, as the carboxylic acid responsible for vinegar's characteristic sourness/smell.

questions.q: Butanoic acid (CH3CH2CH2CO2H) is specifically associated with which characteristic odor in the lecture?
questions.e: The lecture lists butanoic acid, CH3CH2CH2CO2H, as giving the smell of rancid butter.

questions.q: Long-chain aliphatic carboxylic acids commonly arise in the body from the breakdown of which biomolecule?
questions.e: The lecture states that long-chain aliphatic acids are produced from the breakdown of fats, alongside acetic acid (from vinegar) and butanoic acid (from rancid butter) as everyday examples of naturally occurring carboxylic acids.

questions.q: Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) and ibuprofen, both shown in the lecture as drugs containing a carboxylic acid group, share what common functional feature relevant to this topic?
o: Both retain a free -COOH group in their structure
Both are salts of hydrochloric acid
Both are amides, not carboxylic acids
questions.e: The lecture's 'Drugs with carboxylic acid group' slide shows salicylic acid, acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin), ibuprofen, and diclofenac sodium all retaining the -COOH (or its sodium salt) functional group, which is central to their chemistry and formulation.

questions.q: What is salicylic acid, structurally, based on the lecture's drug examples?
questions.e: Salicylic acid, shown alongside acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) and NSAIDs in the 'Drugs with carboxylic acid group' slide, is benzoic acid bearing a hydroxyl group at the ortho position (o-hydroxybenzoic acid).

questions.q: What is the Latin origin of the name 'formic acid' (HCO2H)?
questions.e: The lecture's common-names table shows formic acid (HCO2H) derives its name from the Latin formica ('ant'), since it was first isolated from ants.

questions.q: The common name 'acetic acid' (CH3CO2H) derives from which Latin word, and what does it mean?
questions.e: The common-names table shows acetic acid derives from the Latin acetum, meaning vinegar.

questions.q: 'Butyric acid' (CH3CH2CH2CO2H) takes its common name from which Latin word?
questions.e: The common-names table lists butyric acid as deriving from the Latin butyrum, meaning butter.

questions.q: In the Greek-letter labeling system for carboxylic acid substituent positions, which carbon is designated the 'alpha' (α) carbon?
o: The terminal carbon at the very end of the chain
The carbon directly adjacent to the carboxyl carbon
The carboxyl carbon itself, not an adjacent one
Any carbon bearing a halogen substituent atom
questions.e: The lecture's Greek-letter diagram labels the carbon adjacent to the carboxyl group as α, the next as β, then γ, δ, ε, and so on along the chain — used in names like α-chloropropionic acid and γ-aminobutyric acid.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC rule for choosing the 'parent chain' when naming a carboxylic acid?
o: The chain containing the most double bonds overall, regardless of the carboxyl group's position
Any chain of exactly six carbons only, regardless of any substituents present at all
The shortest possible chain that deliberately avoids the carboxyl group entirely
The longest continuous carbon chain that contains the carboxyl group, with the alkane name's -e dropped and -oic acid added
questions.e: The lecture states the parent chain is the longest, continuous carbon chain that contains the carboxyl group; the alkane name has its terminal -e dropped and -oic acid added.

questions.q: In IUPAC nomenclature of a carboxylic acid, which carbon is always numbered C-1?
o: The carbon at the far end of the chain from the carboxyl group
There is no fixed numbering rule at all for these acids
Whichever carbon happens to bear the largest substituent
The carbon of the carboxyl group itself, by convention
questions.e: The lecture explicitly states that the carbon of the carboxyl group is numbered C-1 in IUPAC nomenclature of carboxylic acids.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of HCOOH?
questions.e: HCOOH (formic acid) is named methanoic acid under IUPAC rules, following the alkane-stem-plus-'oic acid' pattern shown in the lecture.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH3CO2H?
questions.e: CH3CO2H (acetic acid) is named ethanoic acid under IUPAC rules, as shown directly in the lecture's nomenclature slide.

questions.q: CH3CH(CH3)COOH is named, under IUPAC rules, as:
questions.e: The lecture shows this exact structure (a methyl branch on the carbon adjacent to -COOH of a 3-carbon acid chain) named 2-methylpropanoic acid.

questions.q: What is the simplest aromatic carboxylic acid, consisting of a benzene ring with one -COOH group?
questions.e: The lecture's 'Special names' slide identifies the benzene ring bearing a single -COOH group as benzoic acid, the parent name used for naming other aromatic acids.

questions.q: o-Toluic acid, m-toluic acid, and p-toluic acid all share which structural feature?
o: A hydroxyl group replacing the carboxyl group
An additional carboxyl group at a second ring position
A chlorine substituent on a benzoic acid ring
A methyl group on a benzoic acid ring, differing only in ring position
questions.e: The lecture's 'Special names' slide shows o-, m-, and p-toluic acid as benzoic acid with a methyl (CH3) substituent at the ortho, meta, or para ring position, respectively.

questions.q: How are aliphatic dicarboxylic acids named under IUPAC rules?
o: By adding the prefix di- to the common name of the corresponding monocarboxylic acid
By using the suffix -diol acid attached directly onto the root chain's name
By adding the suffix -dioic acid to the root name of the longest chain containing both carboxyl groups
By naming them exclusively using informal, non-systematic common names only, never systematically
questions.e: The lecture states that aliphatic dicarboxylic acids are named by adding the suffix -dioic acid to the root name from the longest carbon chain containing both carboxyl groups, with numbering starting at the end closest to a substituent.

questions.q: HOOC-COOH is the simplest dicarboxylic acid and is commonly known as:
questions.e: The lecture's dicarboxylic acids table lists HOOC-COOH as oxalic acid, the two-carbon dicarboxylic acid.

questions.q: HO2C-CH2CH2-CO2H (4 carbons) is the dicarboxylic acid commonly known as:
questions.e: The lecture's table lists HO2C-CH2CH2-CO2H as succinic acid, distinguishing it from malonic acid (3 carbons, HO2C-CH2-CO2H) and glutaric acid (5 carbons).

questions.q: A cycloalkane ring directly bonded to a -COOH group (where the ring carbon does not itself become part of the 'carboxylic acid' carbon count) is named as a:
questions.e: The lecture's 'Naming Cyclic Acids' slide states that cycloalkanes bonded to -COOH are named as cycloalkanecarboxylic acids, e.g. 2-isopropylcyclopentanecarboxylic acid — distinct from aromatic acids, which are named as benzoic acids.

questions.q: Cinnamic acid, Ph-CH=CH-COOH (trans isomer), is given what full IUPAC-style name in the lecture?
questions.e: The lecture's IUPAC Names slide gives cinnamic acid the systematic name trans-3-phenyl-2-propenoic acid: C-1 is the carboxyl carbon, the C2=C3 double bond gives '2-propenoic acid', and the phenyl group is at C-3.

questions.q: Why do carboxylic acids generally have higher boiling points than alcohols of similar molecular weight?
o: Alcohols cannot form any hydrogen bonds whatsoever with each other, under any circumstances at all
Carboxylic acids are always considerably heavier in molecular weight than similar alcohols
Carboxylic acids reportedly contain fully ionic bonds throughout, quite unlike ordinary alcohols entirely
Two carboxylic acid molecules form a cyclic, hydrogen-bonded dimer, effectively doubling the intermolecular attraction that must be broken
questions.e: The lecture's Boiling Points slide shows that carboxylic acids form a hydrogen-bonded acid dimer (two O-H...O hydrogen bonds linking two -COOH groups), giving them higher boiling points than similar alcohols.

questions.q: What is the boiling point of acetic acid given in the lecture, and to what is it attributed?
o: 0°C, attributed to weak van der Waals forces only
questions.e: The lecture states acetic acid has a boiling point of 118°C, attributed to the hydrogen-bonded acid dimer it forms in the liquid and vapor phase.

questions.q: According to the lecture, aliphatic carboxylic acids with how many carbons or more are typically solids at room temperature?
o: They are always liquids regardless of chain length
More than 8 carbons in the chain
More than 20 carbons in the chain
More than 2 carbons in the chain
questions.e: The Melting Points slide states that aliphatic acids with more than 8 carbons are solids at room temperature.

questions.q: How do double bonds, especially cis double bonds, affect the melting point of a fatty (carboxylic) acid?
o: They raise the melting point of the fatty acid
They lower the melting point of the fatty acid
They convert the acid into a gas at room temperature
They have no effect on the melting point at all
questions.e: The lecture states that double bonds (especially cis) lower the melting point, illustrated by the three 18-carbon acids given.

questions.q: Among the three 18-carbon acids compared in the lecture, which has the highest melting point and why?
o: Oleic acid, because it contains just a single cis double bond in its chain
Stearic acid, because it is fully saturated with no double bonds to disrupt chain packing
Linoleic acid, because it contains two separate cis double bonds
All three have exactly identical melting points overall, with no variation
questions.e: The lecture lists stearic acid (saturated) at 72°C, oleic acid (one cis double bond) at 16°C, and linoleic acid (two cis double bonds) at -5°C — melting point falls as cis-unsaturation increases and disrupts orderly packing.

questions.q: How does the water solubility of carboxylic acids change with increasing carbon-chain length?
o: It remains completely constant regardless of chain length changes
It decreases steadily as the carbon chain gets longer
It increases steadily as the carbon chain gets longer
Solubility is unrelated to chain length; it depends only on molecular weight
questions.e: The Solubility slide states that water solubility decreases with the length of the carbon chain, as the hydrophobic hydrocarbon portion increasingly dominates over the polar carboxyl group.

questions.q: Up to how many carbons is a carboxylic acid typically miscible (fully soluble) in water?
o: Up to 1 carbon in the chain only
Up to 20 carbons in the chain
Up to 4 carbons in the chain
questions.e: The lecture states that up to 4 carbons, a carboxylic acid is miscible in water, after which solubility falls off with increasing chain length.

questions.q: Why are carboxylic acids also soluble in relatively nonpolar solvents such as chloroform?
o: Because chloroform is actually far more polar than plain water itself is
Because carboxylic acids are fully ionic compounds by their very nature
Because nonpolar solvents react directly and quite chemically with the -COOH group
Because they dissolve as a hydrogen-bonded dimer, which is less polar overall than the monomer
questions.e: The lecture explains that carboxylic acids are also soluble in relatively nonpolar solvents like chloroform because they dissolve as a dimer, whose cyclic, hydrogen-bonded structure masks much of the polarity of the individual -OH and C=O groups.

questions.q: Besides water, in what other solvent are carboxylic acids described as being 'more soluble'?
questions.e: The Solubility slide states that carboxylic acids are 'more soluble in alcohol' in addition to their water solubility (which decreases with chain length).

questions.q: In the hydrogen-bonded carboxylic acid dimer shown in the lecture, how many hydrogen bonds link the two molecules together?
o: Zero — dimers are held together by covalent bonds
questions.e: The lecture's dimer diagram shows each -COOH group of one molecule hydrogen-bonding to the -COOH group of a second molecule at both the C=O and O-H positions, giving two hydrogen bonds total in the cyclic dimer.

questions.q: Linoleic acid, an 18-carbon fatty acid with two cis double bonds, has a melting point of approximately:
questions.e: The Melting Points slide lists linoleic acid (two cis double bonds) at -5°C, the lowest of the three 18-carbon acids compared, reflecting the greater disruption to packing caused by two cis kinks.

questions.q: How does the acidity of carboxylic acids compare to that of alcohols and acetylene, according to the lecture?
o: Carboxylic acids are less acidic than alcohols and acetylene
Carboxylic acids have identical acidity to alcohols
Carboxylic acids are more acidic than alcohols and acetylene
Acidity cannot be compared between these classes
questions.e: The 'Acidity of CAs' slide states directly that carboxylic acids are more acidic than alcohols and acetylene, consistent with the overall acid-strength ordering given later in the lecture.

questions.q: What happens when a strong aqueous base reacts with a carboxylic acid?
o: It completely deprotonates the acid, forming a carboxylate salt
It reduces the carboxyl group to a primary alcohol
It has no effect on the carboxylic acid
It converts the acid into an acid chloride
