questions.e: The lecture states that strong aqueous bases can completely deprotonate carboxylic acids, forming salts of carboxylic acids (carboxylates).

questions.q: What happens when a strong aqueous mineral acid (like HCl) is added to a carboxylate salt?
o: It readily converts the salt back to the carboxylic acid
It has no effect, since the salt is already the more stable form
It causes the carboxylate to decompose into CO2 and an alkane
It converts the salt into an amide under these conditions
questions.e: The lecture states that strong aqueous mineral acids readily convert the carboxylate salt back to the carboxylic acid — the reverse of the base-mediated salt formation, and a reversible acid-base equilibrium.

questions.q: Carboxylate salts (e.g. sodium acetate) are generally soluble in water but behave how in nonpolar solvents such as hexane or dichloromethane?
o: They become gaseous in nonpolar solvents
They react violently with nonpolar solvents
They are insoluble in nonpolar solvents
They are equally soluble in nonpolar solvents as in water
questions.e: The lecture states that carboxylate salts are soluble in water but insoluble in nonpolar solvents such as hexane or dichloromethane, reflecting their ionic character.

questions.q: Which equation correctly represents the dissociation of a carboxylic acid (e.g. acetic acid) in water?
questions.e: Carboxylic acid dissociation in water is correctly represented as CH3COOH + H2O ⇌ CH3COO- + H3O+: the acid transfers a proton to water, forming the carboxylate anion and hydronium ion, matching the mechanism diagram in the 'Acidity of CAs' slide.

questions.q: According to the overall acid-strength order given in the lecture (CH4 < NH3 < HC≡CH < ROH < HOH < H2CO3 < RCO2H < HF), where do carboxylic acids rank relative to water and carbonic acid?
o: Carboxylic acids are the least acidic species in the entire series
Carboxylic acids are less acidic than water but more acidic than methane
Carboxylic acids are exactly as acidic as water itself, no more and no less
Carboxylic acids are more acidic than both water and carbonic acid, but less acidic than HF
questions.e: In the lecture's ordering, RCO2H sits above H2CO3 and HOH (water) but below HF, meaning carboxylic acids are more acidic than water and carbonic acid, but less acidic than hydrofluoric acid.

questions.q: What is the general rule for naming a carboxylic acid salt (e.g. converting acetic acid to its sodium salt)?
o: The acid's common name is always kept exactly the same throughout
Name of the cation alone, with no reference to the acid at all
Name of the cation + name of the acid with the ending changed from -ic acid to -ate
Name of the acid left completely unchanged, with 'salt of' prefixed
questions.e: The lecture states the salt-naming rule as: name of cation + name of acid, dropping -ic acid and adding -ate — e.g. CH3CO2Na is named sodium acetate (or sodium ethanoate).

questions.q: What is the correct name for CH3CO2Na, based on the lecture's salt-naming convention?
questions.e: Following the cation + '-ate' rule, CH3CO2Na (from acetic/ethanoic acid) is named sodium acetate or, using the IUPAC acid name, sodium ethanoate, exactly as given in the lecture.

questions.q: What are two general physical properties of carboxylic acid salts, according to the lecture?
o: Usually gases with a strong odor
questions.e: The 'Properties of Acid Salts' slide states that carboxylate salts are usually solids with no odor, unlike the often pungent, volatile parent carboxylic acids.

questions.q: What is soap, chemically, according to the lecture?
o: A primary amide of a short-chain acid
An acid anhydride of acetic acid
The soluble sodium salt of a long-chain fatty acid
questions.e: The lecture defines soap as the soluble sodium salt of a long-chain fatty acid, one of the practical properties listed for carboxylic acid salts.

questions.q: What happens when a carboxylic acid reacts with sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3)?
o: An ester is formed as the sole product
The acid is reduced to an alcohol
No reaction occurs because NaHCO3 is not basic enough
A salt is formed and CO2 gas is released
questions.e: The lecture states that salts can be formed by the reaction of an acid with NaHCO3, releasing CO2 — a classic qualitative test that distinguishes carboxylic acids (which effervesce with bicarbonate) from weaker acids like phenols.

questions.q: Looking at the Ka values given for substituted benzoic acids (p-amino 1.4×10⁻⁵, p-hydroxy 2.6×10⁻⁵, p-methoxy 3.3×10⁻⁵, p-toluic 4.2×10⁻⁵, benzoic 6.3×10⁻⁵, p-chloro 10.3×10⁻⁵, p-nitro 36.0×10⁻⁵), which substituent produces the STRONGEST acid, and why is this consistent with general substituent-effect principles?
o: The methoxy group, because the -OCH3 substituent stabilizes negative charge through electron donation
The amino group, because the -NH2 substituent is apparently strongly electron-withdrawing by induction here too
The nitro group, because -NO2 is strongly electron-withdrawing and stabilizes the carboxylate anion by pulling electron density away from it
The methyl group, because alkyl substituent groups always increase acidity quite substantially every time
questions.e: p-Nitrobenzoic acid has by far the largest Ka (36.0×10⁻⁵), because the electron-withdrawing nitro group stabilizes the negatively charged carboxylate conjugate base through induction/resonance, making the acid more willing to lose its proton; electron-donating groups like -NH2 and -OCH3 do the opposite and give smaller Ka values.

questions.q: Per a review question in the lecture, the water solubility of compounds containing a carboxylic acid group can be increased by reaction with which reagent?
questions.e: Reacting a carboxylic acid with sodium hydroxide converts the poorly water-soluble neutral acid into its ionic, water-soluble sodium carboxylate salt, increasing overall aqueous solubility — the basis of this lecture review question.

questions.q: What type of reagent is used to oxidize a primary alcohol directly to a carboxylic acid, per the lecture's synthesis examples?
o: A halogenating agent such as Cl2
A dehydrating agent such as H2SO4 alone
An oxidizing agent such as CrO3 or KMnO4
A reducing agent such as LiAlH4
questions.e: The lecture's synthesis slides show n-butyl alcohol oxidized by CrO3 to butyric acid, and isobutyl alcohol oxidized by KMnO4 to isobutyric acid — both using strong oxidizing agents to convert a 1° alcohol fully to a carboxylic acid.

questions.q: Oxidation of n-butyl alcohol (1-butanol, CH3CH2CH2CH2-OH) with CrO3 produces which carboxylic acid?
questions.e: The lecture's Synthesis slide shows CH3CH2CH2CH2-OH + CrO3 → CH3CH2CH2CO2H, i.e. 1-butanol oxidized to butyric acid (butanoic acid).

questions.q: What class of carboxylic acid is produced when an alkylbenzene (e.g. toluene, p-xylene, or ethylbenzene) is oxidized with hot KMnO4?
o: A mixture of aldehydes and ketones only, never a carboxylic acid at all
Aliphatic acids only, since the entire aromatic ring is destroyed
Aromatic acids only — the alkyl side chain is oxidized all the way down to a ring-attached -COOH
Only acid anhydrides ever form here, never any free carboxylic acids at all
questions.e: The lecture explicitly notes 'aromatic acids only!' next to the oxidation-of-arenes examples: hot KMnO4 oxidizes an alkyl side chain on a benzene ring all the way to a -COOH group directly attached to the ring, regardless of the original side-chain length.

questions.q: Oxidizing p-xylene (1,4-dimethylbenzene) with hot KMnO4 produces which dicarboxylic aromatic acid?
questions.e: The lecture's arene-oxidation slide shows p-xylene, with methyl groups at the 1 and 4 positions, oxidized by hot KMnO4 to terephthalic acid (benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid).

questions.q: When ethylbenzene is oxidized by hot KMnO4, what two products form?
questions.e: The lecture's diagram shows ethylbenzene oxidized by hot KMnO4 to give benzoic acid plus CO2 — the two-carbon ethyl side chain is cleaved, with the ring-attached carbon becoming -COOH and the terminal carbon lost as CO2.

questions.q: Per the Synthesis Review slide, cleavage of an alkene with hot KMnO4 produces a carboxylic acid under what specific structural condition?
o: Only if there is a hydrogen on the double-bonded carbon being cleaved
Only if the alkene is part of an aromatic ring
Regardless of substitution — a carboxylic acid always forms
Only if the alkene has no substituents at all
questions.e: The Synthesis Review slide states that cleavage of an alkene with hot KMnO4 produces a carboxylic acid specifically if there is a hydrogen on the double-bonded carbon; a fully substituted alkene carbon instead gives a ketone upon cleavage.

questions.q: Which functional derivatives, when hydrolyzed with H2O, react FAST to regenerate the parent carboxylic acid, per the 'Preparation cont'd' slide?
o: Primary amides only, and nothing else
None — all derivatives hydrolyze at the same rate
Esters only, and no other derivative
questions.e: The lecture's diagram shows acid chlorides (R-COCl) and acid anhydrides (R-CO-O-CO-R) reacting fast with H2O alone to give the carboxylic acid, in contrast to primary amides.

questions.q: How does a primary amide (R-CONH2) get hydrolyzed back to a carboxylic acid, and how does this compare in rate to acid chloride/anhydride hydrolysis?
o: It cannot be hydrolyzed under any conditions
It requires NaOH and heat, and proceeds slowly
It requires LiAlH4 and proceeds fast
It requires only cold water, and proceeds instantly
questions.e: The Preparation slide shows that a primary amide requires NaOH plus heat to hydrolyze to the carboxylic acid, and this reaction is explicitly marked as 'slow', in contrast to the fast hydrolysis of acid chlorides and anhydrides with plain water.

questions.q: What is the molecular formula of pentanoic acid, a saturated straight-chain monocarboxylic acid?
questions.e: A saturated monocarboxylic acid follows the general formula CnH2nO2. For n = 5 (pentanoic acid), this gives C5H10O2.

questions.q: Oxidizing isobutyl alcohol (2-methyl-1-propanol) with KMnO4 produces which carboxylic acid?
questions.e: The lecture's synthesis slide shows CH3CH(CH3)CH2-OH (isobutyl alcohol, 2-methyl-1-propanol) oxidized by KMnO4 to CH3CH(CH3)COOH — isobutyric acid, systematically 2-methylpropanoic acid.

questions.q: Which THREE routes for producing carboxylic acids does the 'Synthesis Review' slide list?
o: Only hydrolysis of nitriles under strongly acidic, quite hot aqueous reaction conditions
Fischer esterification, Friedel-Crafts acylation, and simple saponification reactions
Reduction with LiAlH4, simple esterification, and quite direct amide formation reactions
Oxidation of 1° alcohols/aldehydes, alkene cleavage with hot KMnO4, and oxidation of alkylbenzenes with hot KMnO4/chromic acid
questions.e: The Synthesis Review slide lists oxidation of primary alcohols and aldehydes, cleavage of an alkene with hot KMnO4 (provided there is a hydrogen on the double-bonded carbon), and oxidation of an alkylbenzene to benzoic acid with hot KMnO4 or hot chromic acid, plus synthesis from derivatives.

questions.q: What are the three general categories of reaction that carboxylic acids undergo, as outlined in the lecture?
o: Only nucleophilic substitution at the carbon chain
Only acid-base reactions of any kind whatsoever
Acting as acids, reduction, and conversion into functional derivatives
questions.e: The 'Carboxylic acids_Reactions' slide lists three categories: (1) as acids, (2) reduction, and (3) conversion into functional derivatives (acid chlorides, esters, amides).

questions.q: What is the product when a carboxylic acid (RCO2H) reacts with an active metal such as sodium?
questions.e: The lecture's equation shows RCO2H + Na → RCO2⁻Na⁺ + H2(g): the acidic proton is displaced by the active metal, releasing hydrogen gas and forming the sodium carboxylate salt.

questions.q: What is the product when a carboxylic acid (RCO2H) reacts with a base such as NaOH?
questions.e: The lecture's equation shows RCO2H + NaOH → RCO2⁻Na⁺ + H2O: a standard acid-base neutralization producing the sodium carboxylate salt and water.

questions.q: What reagent combination is used to reduce a carboxylic acid all the way to a primary alcohol?
o: NaBH4 alone, without any acid workup
questions.e: The lecture's Reduction slide shows RCO2H + LiAlH4; then H+ → RCH2OH: lithium aluminum hydride is a strong enough reducing agent to fully reduce the carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol after an aqueous acidic workup.

questions.q: Reduction of octanoic acid (caprylic acid) with LiAlH4, followed by H+ workup, produces which product?
questions.e: The lecture's Reduction slide shows CH3(CH2)6COOH (octanoic/caprylic acid) reduced by LiAlH4, then H+, to CH3(CH2)7OH, i.e. 1-octanol — a primary alcohol, not an intermediate aldehyde.

questions.q: Why is LiAlH4 an effective reagent for reducing a carboxylic acid, compared to weaker hydride reagents?
o: It selectively stops the reduction right at the aldehyde stage only, every time
It converts the acid into an acid chloride first, without any actual reduction occurring
It only ever works effectively on aromatic carboxylic acids specifically, never aliphatic ones
It is a strong enough hydride donor to reduce the less electrophilic carboxylic acid carbonyl all the way to a primary alcohol
questions.e: Carboxylic acids are less electrophilic than aldehydes/ketones due to resonance donation from the -OH oxygen, so a strong hydride source like LiAlH4 (rather than a milder reagent) is needed to fully reduce them to the primary alcohol.

questions.q: When benzoic acid reacts with NaOH, what is the resulting product?
questions.e: Benzoic acid + NaOH undergoes simple acid-base neutralization to give sodium benzoate (plus water), following the same RCO2H + NaOH → RCO2⁻Na⁺ + H2O pattern shown generally in the lecture.

questions.q: Which three functional derivatives does the lecture identify as the products of 'conversion into functional derivatives' from a carboxylic acid?
questions.e: The Reactions overview slide lists conversion into functional derivatives as: (a) acid chlorides, (b) esters, (c) amides — the three transformations detailed in later slides (with acid anhydrides covered as an additional derivative class).

questions.q: Why does a carboxylic acid effervesce (release gas) when treated with sodium bicarbonate, while a simple alcohol does not?
o: A carboxylic acid is acidic enough to protonate bicarbonate, releasing CO2 gas; an alcohol is not acidic enough to do this
Bicarbonate only ever reacts chemically with alkenes under strongly acidic conditions
Carbon dioxide is released only from aromatic carboxylic compounds specifically
Alcohols always react much faster with bicarbonate than carboxylic acids ever do, according to this claim
questions.e: Carboxylic acids are acidic enough (pKa roughly 4-5) to protonate the bicarbonate ion, forming carbonic acid which decomposes to CO2 and water — alcohols (pKa roughly 16-18) are far too weakly acidic to do this, which is why the NaHCO3 fizz test distinguishes carboxylic acids.

questions.q: In the relative acid-strength comparison RCO2H vs. HOH (water), which is the stronger acid, and what does this mean for carboxylate salt formation?
o: HOH is supposedly the stronger acid, so carboxylic acids cannot form any salts in water
Neither is acidic at all; both are simply classified as fully neutral species here instead
They are equally acidic, so essentially no net reaction ever occurs with NaOH
RCO2H is the stronger acid, so it readily transfers its proton to hydroxide/water-based bases to form stable carboxylate salts
questions.e: In the lecture's acid-strength order, RCO2H sits above HOH, confirming carboxylic acids are more acidic than water and will be readily and essentially completely deprotonated by aqueous hydroxide bases to form carboxylate salts.

questions.q: What determines the class of acyl (carboxylic acid derivative) compound formed, according to the 'Acid Derivatives' slide?
o: The color of the compound in solution
Whether the compound is aromatic or aliphatic
The number of carbons in the R group
The group bonded to the acyl carbon
questions.e: The lecture states that the group bonded to the acyl carbon determines the class of compound: -OH gives a carboxylic acid, -Cl an acid chloride, -OR' an ester, and -NH2 an amide.

questions.q: An acyl carbon bonded to -Cl defines which class of compound?
questions.e: Per the Acid Derivatives slide, -Cl bonded to the acyl carbon defines an acid chloride (also called an acyl chloride).

questions.q: An acyl carbon bonded to -OR' defines which class of compound?
questions.e: Per the Acid Derivatives slide, -OR' bonded to the acyl carbon defines an ester.

questions.q: Why are acid chlorides described as an 'activated form' of the carboxylic acid?
o: Chloride is a good leaving group, so acid chlorides undergo acyl substitution easily
Acid chlorides cannot react with any nucleophiles at all, ever
Acid chlorides are always more stable thermodynamically than carboxylic acids
Acid chlorides are less reactive than the parent carboxylic acid
questions.e: The Acid Chlorides slide states that chloride is a good leaving group, so acid chlorides readily undergo acyl substitution — this is why they are considered an 'activated' derivative, useful for making esters, amides, and anhydrides.

questions.q: Which reagents are used to synthesize an acid chloride directly from a carboxylic acid?
o: Excess NaOH and heat applied together
Thionyl chloride, or alternatively PCl3 or PCl5
questions.e: The lecture states that acid chlorides are synthesized using thionyl chloride (SOCl2) with the acid, and also shows PCl3 (or PCl5) as alternative reagents for the same conversion.

questions.q: When acid chlorides react with alcohols, what products form, and what is the reaction mechanism?
o: Esters form via nucleophilic addition of the alcohol to the carbonyl, chloride ion leaving, followed by deprotonation
Ethers form via the complete loss of the entire carbonyl group from the whole molecule
Amides form via direct substitution of chlorine by the alcohol's oxygen without any addition step
Carboxylic acids simply re-form entirely, releasing the alcohol completely unreacted
questions.e: The 'Esters from Acid Chlorides' slide states that acid chlorides react with alcohols to give esters in good yield; mechanistically, the alcohol's oxygen adds to the carbonyl carbon (nucleophilic addition), the chloride ion then leaves, and the resulting oxocarbenium is deprotonated to give the neutral ester.

questions.q: What is Fischer esterification, and what type of catalyst does it require?
o: A base-catalyzed reaction between an acid chloride and a fairly simple alcohol
The acid-catalyzed, reversible reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol to give an ester plus water
A reaction between two separate carboxylic acid molecules to form an anhydride
An irreversible reaction requiring absolutely no catalyst of any kind at all
questions.e: The Fischer Esterification slide states that acid plus alcohol yields ester plus water, that the reaction is acid-catalyzed (because the alcohol is a comparatively weak nucleophile), and that all steps are reversible, reaching equilibrium.

questions.q: Why is Fischer (direct) esterification often described as not favoring the ester product, and how can the equilibrium be shifted toward the ester?
o: Because esters spontaneously decompose back to acid and alcohol at room temperature regardless of conditions
Because the reaction only ever proceeds under strict vacuum conditions and cannot otherwise occur at all
Because Fischer esterification always requires the acid to first be converted into an acid chloride reagent
Because the reaction is reversible and reaches equilibrium; using an excess of alcohol or acid, or removing the products, shifts the equilibrium toward the ester
questions.e: The lecture notes that direct ('Fischer') esterification is reversible and often does not favor the ester; using an excess of the alcohol or acid, or removing the products (e.g. water) as they form, shifts the equilibrium toward completion.

questions.q: What is the key advantage of 'indirect' esterification (converting the acid to an acid chloride first, then reacting with the alcohol) over direct Fischer esterification?
o: It requires absolutely no catalyst of any kind whatsoever in this particular method
The acid-chloride-to-ester step is not reversible, so it avoids the unfavorable equilibrium of the direct method
It works only with aromatic alcohols specifically, never with aliphatic ones at all
It produces water as a byproduct instead, quite unlike the direct method used
questions.e: The lecture states that in indirect esterification, the acid is converted into the acid chloride first (via PCl3, for example), and the subsequent acid-chloride-plus-alcohol step to form the ester is not reversible — avoiding the equilibrium limitations of direct Fischer esterification.

questions.q: How is an amide formed directly from a carboxylic acid and an amine, according to the 'Amides from Acids' slide?
o: No direct reaction is ever possible at all here; only acid chlorides can readily form amides
The amine directly substitutes for the -OH group at room temperature with no intermediate
The carboxylic acid must first be fully reduced to an aldehyde before ever reacting with the amine
The amine first removes a proton from the acid to form a salt; heating the salt above 100°C then drives off water/steam to form the amide
questions.e: The lecture shows that the amine (a base) first removes a proton from the -COOH group, forming an ammonium carboxylate salt; heating this salt above 100°C then drives off water as steam, forming the amide.

questions.q: What happens if ammonia is simply mixed with a carboxylic acid at room temperature, without further heating?
o: An acid chloride forms immediately at room temperature
An ester forms immediately at room temperature
The amide forms immediately and irreversibly
Only an ammonium carboxylate salt forms — not the amide
questions.e: The lecture explicitly notes that directly reacting ammonia with a carboxylic acid results in an ammonium salt (RCOOH + NH3 → RCOO⁻NH4⁺, acid + base), not the amide; forming the amide requires the additional heating step to drive off water.

questions.q: When acid chlorides react with ammonia or amines to form amides, what additional reagent is typically added, and why?
o: A reducing agent, to prevent over-oxidation
An excess of water, to hydrolyze the acid chloride first
A base such as NaOH or pyridine, to remove the HCl byproduct
A strong oxidizing agent, to activate the amine
questions.e: The 'Amides from Acid Chlorides' slide states that a base (NaOH or pyridine) is added to remove the HCl byproduct generated when the acid chloride reacts with ammonia or an amine, driving the reaction toward the amide product.

questions.q: What is the 'indirect only' route to synthesizing an amide starting from a carboxylic acid, as emphasized in the lecture?
o: RCOOH + SOCl2 → RCOCl, then RCOCl + NH3 → RCONH2
RCOOH + NH3 directly gives RCONH2 with no intermediate
questions.e: The lecture's 'amides — indirect only!' slide shows the sequence RCOOH + SOCl2 → RCOCl + NH3 → RCONH2: the acid is first converted to the acid chloride, which then reacts with ammonia to give the amide — because direct reaction of the acid with ammonia gives only the ammonium salt.

questions.q: How is an acid anhydride prepared directly from a carboxylic acid such as acetic acid, per the lecture's example?
o: Reacting the acid with NaOH under carefully controlled cold conditions
Reacting the acid with LiAlH4 at ordinary room temperature only
Simply mixing two acid molecules at room temperature with no catalyst or heat
Heating the acid with an H+ catalyst at about 200°C drives off water to give the anhydride
questions.e: The lecture's 'Preparation of Acid Anhydrides Directly from Acids' slide shows acetic acid, with an H+ catalyst at about 200°C, losing water to form acetic anhydride (CH3CO-O-COCH3).

questions.q: Phthalic acid (a benzene ring with two adjacent -CO2H groups), when heated with an H+ catalyst at about 200°C, forms which product?
o: Benzoic acid, with loss of CO2 gas
A cyclic phthalic anhydride, with loss of water
questions.e: The lecture's slide shows phthalic acid (ortho-dicarboxylic benzoic acid) heated with H+ at ~200°C forming a cyclic (5-membered ring) phthalic anhydride, releasing water — the two adjacent -COOH groups condense intramolecularly.

questions.q: According to the lecture, direct high-temperature acid-to-anhydride conversion (H+, ~200°C) is described as being especially good for which cases?
o: Anhydrides of tertiary alcohols only, never primary ones
Acetic anhydride, and 5- and 6-membered ring anhydrides
Only long-chain aliphatic anhydrides above 12 carbons
Only anhydrides of aromatic monocarboxylic acids with no ring strain concerns
questions.e: The lecture explicitly states that the direct H+/200°C method is 'good for acetic and 5- and 6-membered ring anhydrides', reflecting that intramolecular anhydride formation from a dicarboxylic acid is favorable only when it produces a low-strain 5- or 6-membered ring.

questions.q: Ranking the four acyl derivatives by increasing reactivity, what order does the 'Structure and Reactivity of Carboxylic Acid Derivatives' slide give?
o: Ester < amide < acid chloride < acid anhydride
Amide < ester < acid anhydride < acid chloride
Acid chloride < acid anhydride < ester < amide
All four derivatives have identical reactivity
questions.e: The lecture's reactivity diagram explicitly orders the derivatives by increasing reactivity as: amide < ester < acid anhydride < acid chloride.

questions.q: Why is the acid chloride the most reactive of the four carboxylic acid derivatives toward nucleophilic acyl substitution?
o: Chloride is a poor leaving group but a fairly strong nucleophile
Chloride ion is the best leaving group among Cl-, carboxylate, alkoxide, and amide ion
Acid chlorides contain no carbonyl group whatsoever in their structure
Acid chlorides are the least electrophilic at the carbonyl carbon
questions.e: Reactivity in nucleophilic acyl substitution correlates with how good a leaving group the substituent is; chloride ion is a much better (more stable, weaker-base) leaving group than a carboxylate, alkoxide, or amide ion, which is why acid chlorides sit at the top of the reactivity ranking shown in the lecture.

questions.q: According to the lecture's reactivity/preparation diagram, can all four acyl derivatives be prepared directly from the parent carboxylic acid?
o: Yes — all acyl derivatives can be prepared directly from the carboxylic acid
No — only the simple amide can be made directly from the parent acid itself
No — none of the derivatives can be made directly from the acid; all require multi-step synthesis
No — only the acid chloride can be made directly from the parent acid itself
questions.e: The lecture's diagram explicitly states 'All acyl derivatives can be prepared directly from the carboxylic acid,' shown by arrows from 'carboxylic acid' to each of acid chloride, acid anhydride, ester, and amide.

questions.q: Per the lecture's reactivity/preparation diagram, why are the less reactive derivatives (esters and amides) more readily prepared FROM the more reactive derivatives (acid chlorides and anhydrides) than the reverse?
o: Less reactive derivatives are always synthesized first industrially, purely for cost reasons only
Amides can supposedly be converted into acid chlorides just as easily as the reverse process
A more reactive acyl derivative undergoes substitution easily to generate a less reactive one, whereas converting a less reactive derivative into a more reactive one is generally not favorable
There is no preferred direction at all here; both reaction directions are considered entirely equally easy
questions.e: Nucleophilic acyl substitution proceeds most readily from a good leaving group to a worse one — so a highly reactive acid chloride is readily converted into an anhydride, ester, or amide, while going the other direction (e.g. amide to acid chloride) is not a simple, favorable substitution.

questions.q: Which derivative sits directly between 'ester' and 'acid chloride' in the lecture's reactivity ordering, and is prepared directly from an acid chloride but can itself be converted into esters and amides?
questions.e: In the reactivity order amide < ester < acid anhydride < acid chloride, the acid anhydride sits between ester and acid chloride; the preparation diagram shows an acid chloride converts to an acid anhydride, which can in turn be converted to an ester or an amide.

questions.q: An acyl carbon bonded to -NH2 defines which class of compound?
questions.e: Per the Acid Derivatives slide, -NH2 bonded to the acyl carbon defines an amide, the least reactive of the four acyl derivative classes covered in the lecture.

questions.q: Why is knowledge of aromatic chemistry emphasised for pharmacy/medical students, per the lecture's opening slide?
o: Many drugs are aromatic compounds, and this chemistry explains their nature, stability, pharmacological action and toxicity
Aromaticity has absolutely no relevance to pharmacology or drug design whatsoever, at all, ever
Aromatic compounds are supposedly the only class of molecules found anywhere in the body
Aromatic rings supposedly prevent all drugs from ever being toxic to any patients at all
questions.e: The lecture opens by stating that many drugs are aromatic compounds, and that knowledge of aromatic chemistry helps to understand the chemical nature, physical properties, stability, pharmacological actions and toxicities of a majority of drug molecules.

questions.q: Who is credited with first isolating benzene, and from what source, according to the lecture?
o: Michael Faraday, isolated from coal gas in 1825
August Kekulé, isolated from coal tar in 1865
Justus von Liebig, isolated from vinegar in 1830
Friedrich Wöhler, isolated from urea in 1828
questions.e: The lecture states that benzene (C6H6), the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon (arene), was isolated from coal gas in 1825 by Michael Faraday.

questions.q: Which everyday-life application is NOT listed among the six applications of aromatic compounds in the lecture?
questions.e: The lecture lists six applications: perfumes and fragrances, pharmaceuticals, food flavorings, dyes and pigments, polymers, and solvents — nuclear fuel rods are not an application of aromatic compounds mentioned.

questions.q: Benzene is described in the lecture as a 'highly unsaturated hydrocarbon.' What distinguishes its chemical behaviour from that of alkenes, alkynes and dienes?
o: Benzene has no double bonds at all present, unlike typical alkenes
Benzene reacts explosively with all reagents unlike alkenes
Benzene readily undergoes addition reactions just like alkenes
Whereas alkenes/alkynes/dienes readily undergo addition reactions, benzene does not
questions.e: The lecture explicitly contrasts benzene with other unsaturated hydrocarbons: although highly unsaturated, benzene does not readily undergo the addition reactions typical of alkenes, alkynes and dienes.

questions.q: In the lecture's comparison, what happens when Br2 is added to ethylene (an alkene) versus benzene (an arene)?
o: Ethylene gives no reaction; benzene gives an addition product
Ethylene gives an addition product; benzene gives no reaction
Both compounds explode on contact with Br2
Both ethylene and benzene give the same addition product
questions.e: The lecture's diagram shows ethylene + Br2 forming a 1,2-dibromide addition product, while benzene (C6H6) + Br2 gives 'No reaction' under the same simple conditions — demonstrating benzene's unusual stability.

questions.q: According to the lecture's 'Revision' slide, what colour and character does the flame of burning aromatic hydrocarbons typically display?
o: No visible flame at all when burned
A strong and sooty yellow flame
A green flame with no soot at all
A clean blue flame with no soot
questions.e: The revision slide notes that when burnt, aromatic hydrocarbons display a strong and sooty flame which is yellow — a consequence of their relatively high carbon-to-hydrogen ratio.

questions.q: What does the revision slide say about the ratio of carbon atoms to hydrogen atoms in aromatic hydrocarbons?
o: It is relatively high compared to other hydrocarbon classes
It is lower than in typical alkanes
It cannot be determined for aromatic compounds
It is always exactly 1:1 in every case
questions.e: The lecture states that the ratio of carbon atoms to hydrogen atoms is relatively high in aromatic-type molecules, which is also why they burn with a sooty flame.

questions.q: What general type of reaction do aromatic compounds generally undergo, as summarised on the revision slide?
questions.e: The revision slide states that aromatic compounds generally undergo substitution reactions (rather than the addition reactions typical of alkenes), preserving the stable aromatic ring.

questions.q: How many structural criteria must a compound satisfy to be classified as aromatic, according to the lecture?
questions.e: The lecture states that four structural criteria must be satisfied for a compound to be aromatic: it must be cyclic, planar, completely conjugated, and satisfy Hückel's rule.

questions.q: What is criterion [1] for aromaticity given in the lecture?
o: A molecule must be cyclic, forming a closed ring
A molecule must be planar, lying in a flat plane
A molecule must have an even number of carbons
questions.e: Criterion [1] states that a molecule must be cyclic. The lecture contrasts benzene (cyclic, aromatic) with 1,3,5-hexatriene (acyclic — its terminal p orbitals cannot overlap, so it is not aromatic).

questions.q: Why is 1,3,5-hexatriene not aromatic, even though it has three alternating double bonds like benzene?
o: It contains a nitrogen atom that breaks conjugation entirely
It contains far too many hydrogen atoms overall for its carbon count
Its double bonds are not conjugated with each other at all
It is acyclic — there is no overlap possible between the p orbitals of the two terminal carbons
questions.e: Hexatriene is not aromatic because it is not cyclic; there can be no p-orbital overlap between the two terminal carbons of an open chain, unlike the continuous ring overlap in benzene.

questions.q: What is criterion [2] for aromaticity, and why is cyclooctatetraene an example of a compound that fails it?
o: The molecule must be strictly cyclic; cyclooctatetraene is actually entirely acyclic in shape
The molecule must satisfy Hückel's rule; cyclooctatetraene has 6 pi electrons
The molecule must be fully conjugated; cyclooctatetraene supposedly has no double bonds at all
The molecule must be planar; cyclooctatetraene adopts a non-planar, tub-shaped conformation so its p orbitals cannot align to delocalize
questions.e: Criterion [2] requires planarity so that all adjacent p orbitals can align for delocalization. Cyclooctatetraene is a non-planar, tub-shaped, eight-membered ring, so adjacent p orbitals cannot overlap, and it is not aromatic — it reacts with Br2 to give an addition product, just like other alkenes.

questions.q: What is criterion [3] for aromaticity, and which two compounds does the lecture cite as failing it despite being cyclic?
o: Complete saturation; benzene and naphthalene fail it
An odd number of ring atoms; pyridine and furan fail it
Presence of a heteroatom; benzene and naphthalene fail it
questions.e: Criterion [3] requires the ring to be completely conjugated, with a p orbital on every atom. 1,3-Cyclohexadiene has an sp3 carbon with no p orbital, and 1,3,5-cycloheptatriene likewise has one sp3 (CH2) carbon that breaks conjugation, so neither is aromatic.

questions.q: What does Hückel's rule (criterion [4]) state about the number of pi electrons required for aromaticity?
o: An aromatic compound must contain exactly 6 pi electrons and no other number
An aromatic compound must contain exactly 4n pi electrons total
An aromatic compound must contain exactly 4n + 2 pi electrons total
An aromatic compound must contain an odd number of pi electrons
questions.e: Hückel's rule states that a cyclic, planar, completely conjugated compound is aromatic only if it contains 4n + 2 pi electrons, where n = 0, 1, 2, and so forth (giving 2, 6, 10, 14 … electrons).

questions.q: What term describes cyclic, planar, completely conjugated compounds that contain 4n pi electrons, and why are they especially unstable?
o: Heteroaromatic — they always contain at least one heteroatom
Aromatic — they are supposedly the most stable of all known ring systems
Antiaromatic — they are especially unstable, unlike the special stability of aromatic 4n+2 systems
Nonaromatic — they behave exactly like ordinary alkenes with no special character
questions.e: The lecture defines such 4n-pi-electron systems as antiaromatic, and states they are especially unstable, in contrast to 4n+2 aromatic systems, which are especially stable.

questions.q: How many pi electrons does benzene have, and how does applying Hückel's rule (4n+2) with n=1 confirm this?
o: 4 pi electrons; 4 = 4, so benzene is antiaromatic
6 pi electrons; 4+2 = 6, so benzene is aromatic
2 pi electrons only; calculated from n=0
8 pi electrons; it does not fit the 4n+2 formula
questions.e: Benzene has 6 pi electrons (one from each of its 6 p orbitals), and 4n+2 with n=1 gives 4(1)+2 = 6, confirming benzene is aromatic and especially stable.

questions.q: Why is cyclobutadiene classified as antiaromatic in the lecture?
o: It has 4 pi electrons, fitting the 4n pattern, making it especially unstable
It has exactly 6 pi electrons total, just like benzene does
It contains no double bonds anywhere in the ring
It is entirely acyclic, so Hückel's rule does not apply at all
questions.e: Cyclobutadiene has 4 pi electrons; using 4n with n=1 gives 4n = 4, matching the antiaromatic pattern, so cyclobutadiene is especially unstable rather than especially stable.

questions.q: Naphthalene is aromatic according to the lecture. How many pi electrons does it have, and why does this matter for Hückel's rule?
o: 12 pi electrons, which does not fit any Hückel pattern
6 pi electrons, the same count as benzene
8 pi electrons, fitting the 4n antiaromatic pattern
questions.e: The lecture states naphthalene is aromatic because every carbon is sp2 and it has 10 pi electrons (not 8 or 12) — 4n+2 with n=2 gives 4(2)+2=10, satisfying Hückel's rule.

questions.q: Why is cyclooctatetraene, despite having alternating double bonds, not aromatic according to the pi-electron count discussed in the lecture?
o: It has no pi electrons in the ring at all, which is unusual
It has 10 pi electrons total, satisfying Hückel's rule perfectly well
It has 8 pi electrons, which does not satisfy 4n+2 — and it is also non-planar
It has exactly 6 pi electrons like benzene but is still unstable for unrelated reasons
questions.e: Cyclooctatetraene has 8 pi electrons rather than 6 or 10, so it fails Hückel's rule (4n+2); it is also non-planar (tub-shaped), failing the planarity criterion as well, so it is non-aromatic.

questions.q: The cyclopentadienyl anion and the cycloheptatrienyl (tropylium) cation are both listed in the lecture as 6-pi-electron aromatic systems. What do they have in common structurally with benzene?
o: Each is cyclic, planar, completely conjugated, and has 6 delocalized pi electrons satisfying Hückel's rule
Each is non-planar in overall shape, much like cyclooctatetraene is
Each has only 4 pi electrons total, just like cyclobutadiene does
Each contains a heteroatom somewhere in the ring, like pyridine does
questions.e: Like benzene, the cyclopentadienyl anion (cyclopentadienide ion) and the cycloheptatrienyl (tropylium) cation are cyclic, planar, completely conjugated ring systems bearing 6 pi electrons, satisfying all four aromaticity criteria.

questions.q: Pentalene, an 8-pi-electron bicyclic system shown in the lecture, is described as:
o: A heterocyclic aromatic compound with a ring nitrogen
Antiaromatic if it adopts a planar conformation
questions.e: The lecture groups pentalene among the '8 pi electron systems (antiaromatic if planar)' alongside cyclooctatetraene, the cycloheptatrienyl anion, and the cyclononatetraenyl cation.

questions.q: What is the molecular formula of benzene, the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon (arene)?
questions.e: Benzene, C6H6, is introduced in the lecture as the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon (or arene).

questions.q: According to the resonance description of benzene, how are the C–C bonds best described?
o: Alternating triple and single bonds throughout the ring
Purely single bonds throughout the entire ring structure
Neither purely double nor purely single, but something in between — like a '1½' bond
Purely double bonds throughout the entire ring structure
questions.e: The lecture describes benzene as a hybrid of two equivalent Kekulé structures, each contributing equally, so that the C–C bonds are neither double nor single but something in between (a '1½' bond).

questions.q: How many equivalent Kekulé structures does the lecture use to represent benzene as a resonance hybrid?
questions.e: The lecture depicts benzene as a hybrid of two equivalent Kekulé contributing structures, connected by a double-headed resonance arrow, each making an equal contribution to the true structure.

questions.q: What shape is the carbon skeleton of benzene, and what are the C–C–C and H–C–C bond angles?
o: A regular hexagon, with all bond angles at 120°
A triangle shape, with all bond angles equal to 60°
An irregular pentagon, with angles varying between 100° and 140°
A square shape, with all bond angles equal to 90°
questions.e: The lecture's structural diagram states the carbon skeleton is a regular hexagon, with all C–C–C and H–C–C bond angles equal to 120°, consistent with sp2 hybridization at every carbon.

questions.q: According to the bond-length data shown for benzene's structure, what are the approximate C–H and C–C bond lengths?
questions.e: The structure-of-benzene slide gives a C–H bond length of 1.09 Å and a uniform C–C bond length of 1.39 Å around the ring — intermediate between a typical single (1.54 Å) and double (1.34 Å) C–C bond, consistent with delocalization.

questions.q: What hybridization does each ring carbon of benzene adopt, and what kind of bonds does this create with the neighbouring ring carbon and with hydrogen?
o: sp2 hybridized; forming sp2–sp2 bonds to adjacent ring carbons and an sp2–1s bond to hydrogen
sp3d hybridized; forming five separate bonds per carbon
sp hybridized; forming sp–sp triple bonds only, exclusively
sp3 hybridized; forming sp3–sp3 single bonds only, exclusively
questions.e: The structure-of-benzene diagram labels the ring-carbon bonds as sp2–sp2 (to the neighbouring ring carbon) and sp2–1s (to the attached hydrogen), consistent with each carbon being sp2 hybridized.

questions.q: According to the hybridization-of-carbon slide, which excited-state configuration of carbon leads to sp3 hybridization?
o: Three electrons promoted directly into empty 3d orbitals
One electron promoted from 2s into the empty 2pz orbital, giving four singly occupied orbitals
Two electrons remaining paired in 2s with only two half-filled 2p orbitals
All electrons remaining paired in the 1s orbital only, unchanged
questions.e: The hybridization slide shows carbon's excited state promoting one 2s electron into the previously empty 2pz orbital, giving four unpaired electrons (2s, 2px, 2py, 2pz) that mix to form four equivalent sp3 orbitals.

questions.q: Which hybridization state is relevant to the ring carbons of benzene, based on the carbon-hybridization slide's three excited-state configurations (sp3, sp2, sp)?
o: sp3 — arising from mixing the 2s orbital with all three of the 2p orbitals
No hybridization occurs at all in any of benzene's ring carbons whatsoever
sp2 — arising from mixing the 2s orbital with two of the three 2p orbitals, leaving one unhybridized p orbital for the pi system
sp — arising from mixing the 2s orbital with only one single 2p orbital present
questions.e: Benzene's ring carbons are sp2 hybridized: the 2s orbital mixes with two of the three 2p orbitals (leaving one 2pz unhybridized), which is exactly the configuration the slide shows leading to the sp2 label, and the remaining p orbital forms the delocalized pi system.

questions.q: What happens to each unhybridized p orbital on a benzene ring carbon, and why is this essential to aromaticity?
o: It points directly at the centre of the ring and forms a sigma bond to the opposite carbon
It overlaps with the p orbitals on the two neighbouring carbons, allowing continuous delocalization of the pi electrons around the ring
It somehow becomes the hydrogen 1s orbital instead, entirely replacing it completely
It remains completely isolated and does not interact with any other orbital
questions.e: Aromaticity criterion [1]/[3] material explains that in benzene every p orbital overlaps with two neighbouring p orbitals, allowing pi electron density to delocalize continuously around the ring, which is the structural basis of aromatic stabilization.

questions.q: Which four compounds are given in the lecture as examples of 'benzene and its monocyclic derivatives'?
o: Toluene, xylene, styrene, and cumene only
questions.e: The classification-of-aromatics slide lists benzene, toluene (with a CH3 group), phenol (with an OH group), and aniline (with an NH2 group) as monocyclic benzenoid derivatives.

questions.q: Naphthalene and anthracene are given as examples of which classification of aromatic compounds?
questions.e: Naphthalene (two fused rings) and anthracene (three linearly fused rings) are shown under 'Polycyclic benzenoids' in the classification-of-aromatics slide.

questions.q: Azulene is given in the lecture as an example of which category of aromatic compound?
questions.e: Azulene, a fused five- and seven-membered ring system, is listed under 'Nonbenzenoids' — an aromatic compound that is not built from benzenoid (six-membered) rings alone.

questions.q: [14]Annulene is given in the lecture as an example of which category of aromatic compound?
questions.e: [14]Annulene, a large 14-membered fully conjugated monocyclic ring, is listed under 'Macrocyclic' aromatics in the classification slide.

questions.q: What defines a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH), and what health concern is associated with many of them?
o: A compound containing a heteroatom in every ring; PAHs are used only as solvents
A compound with two or more fused aromatic rings; many PAHs are carcinogenic
A compound with only one aromatic ring; PAHs are generally harmless
A compound with no double bonds at all present; PAHs are entirely inert
questions.e: The lecture defines PAHs as containing two or more fused aromatic rings, notes they have multiple resonance structures, and states that many PAHs are carcinogenic.

questions.q: Which four PAHs are shown together in the lecture's PAH slide (naphthalene, anthracene, and two others)?
questions.e: The PAH slide shows naphthalene, anthracene, phenanthrene, and benzo[a]pyrene as examples of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons with fused aromatic rings.

questions.q: What is a heterocyclic compound, as defined in the lecture?
o: A compound that contains one or more atoms other than carbon in its ring
A compound containing only carbon and hydrogen in a ring
A compound with absolutely no rings present at all
A compound that cannot be aromatic under any circumstances
questions.e: The lecture defines a heterocyclic compound as one that contains one or more atoms other than carbon (heteroatoms) in its ring — nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur, etc.

questions.q: Pyridine and pyrimidine are described in the lecture as heterocyclic analogs of which parent aromatic compound?
questions.e: The lecture states that pyridine and pyrimidine are heterocyclic analogs of benzene, in which one or two ring CH units are replaced by nitrogen; each is aromatic.

questions.q: Which two ring sizes recur across the 'other heterocyclic aromatic compounds' shown in the lecture (pyridine, pyrrole, imidazole, furan)?
questions.e: Pyridine is a six-membered heterocycle (one N replacing CH), while pyrrole, imidazole, and furan are five-membered heterocycles containing N, N/N, and O respectively.

questions.q: In pyridine (C5H5N), what hybridization does the ring nitrogen adopt?
questions.e: The lecture states that the nitrogen atom of pyridine is sp2 hybridized, matching the sp2 hybridization of the five ring carbons.

questions.q: Where does pyridine's nitrogen lone pair reside, and is it part of the aromatic sextet?
o: It lies in a 2p orbital and IS indeed fully part of the aromatic sextet system
It lies in an sp2 hybrid orbital, perpendicular to the six 2p orbitals of the pi system, and is NOT part of the aromatic sextet
It is delocalized equally over all five ring carbons and the nitrogen atom
It lies in the 1s orbital and is entirely and completely irrelevant to aromaticity
questions.e: The lecture explains that pyridine's unshared electron pair occupies an sp2 hybrid orbital that is perpendicular to the six 2p orbitals of the pi system, so this electron pair is not part of the six pi electrons making up the aromatic sextet.

questions.q: In pyrrole, where does the nitrogen's lone pair reside, and is it part of the aromatic sextet?
o: It is shared equally between two entirely separate rings
It is in a p orbital and IS part of the aromatic sextet
It is in an sp2 orbital and is NOT part of the aromatic sextet, just like in pyridine
It does not exist — pyrrole nitrogen has no lone pair at all
questions.e: Unlike pyridine, pyrrole's nitrogen lone pair sits in a p orbital and is part of the aromatic sextet (contributing 2 of the 6 pi electrons), which is why pyrrole nitrogen is a much weaker base than pyridine nitrogen.

questions.q: In furan, one of oxygen's two lone pairs is part of the aromatic sextet and the other is not. Where does the non-aromatic lone pair reside?
o: In a p orbital, fully part of the aromatic sextet
On a separate oxygen atom entirely
In an sp2 orbital, not part of the aromatic sextet
There is no non-aromatic lone pair on furan's oxygen
questions.e: The lecture's furan diagram shows that one oxygen lone pair sits in a p orbital and is part of the aromatic sextet, while the other lone pair is in an sp2 orbital and is not part of the aromatic sextet — furan's oxygen is analogous to pyrrole's nitrogen in this respect.

questions.q: Which two heterocyclic aromatics does the lecture specifically list as 'other examples of aromatic heterocyclic compounds' beyond pyridine, alongside a discussion of their lone-pair placement?
questions.e: The lecture states 'Other examples of aromatic heterocyclic compounds are furan and pyrrole,' and details how each heteroatom contributes one lone pair to the aromatic pi system while retaining a second, non-aromatic lone pair (or none, for pyrrole's single lone pair).

questions.q: Imidazole, shown among the heterocyclic aromatics, contains how many nitrogen atoms in its five-membered ring?
questions.e: Imidazole's structure (H–N and a second, doubly-bonded N in the ring) shows two nitrogen atoms in its five-membered aromatic ring, distinguishing it from pyrrole (one N) and furan (one O).

questions.q: Which heterocyclic 6-pi aromatic system pairs with pyridine, pyrrole, and furan in the lecture's overview of aromatic ring-electron-count systems?
o: They are grouped as 8 pi electron systems
These three are grouped together as 'Heterocyclic 6 pi systems'
They are grouped as 4 pi electron antiaromatic systems
They are not grouped with any electron-count category
questions.e: The lecture's pi-electron-count overview slide places pyridine, pyrrole and furan together under the heading 'Heterocyclic 6 pi systems (aromatic),' parallel to the all-carbon 6-pi aromatic systems (benzene, cyclopentadienyl anion, tropylium cation).

questions.q: Why is a heteroatom's lone pair placement (p orbital vs. sp2/sp3 orbital) chemically important for determining aromaticity?
o: Only a lone pair in a p orbital, aligned with the ring's pi system, can be delocalized and counted toward the Hückel 4n+2 pi-electron total
Lone pair placement supposedly has no effect whatsoever on aromaticity in any heterocycle at all
All heteroatom lone pairs automatically count toward the aromatic sextet regardless of orbital
Aromaticity is determined only by overall ring size, never by lone pair placement at all
questions.e: Only lone pairs residing in a p orbital that is parallel to (and part of) the ring's continuous pi system can be delocalized and thus contribute to the Hückel pi-electron count; a lone pair in an sp2 (in-plane) orbital, as in pyridine, is excluded from the aromatic sextet.

questions.q: Given that pyrrole's nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the aromatic ring while pyridine's is not, which nitrogen would you expect to be the weaker base (less available lone pair for protonation)?
o: Pyrrole's nitrogen, because its lone pair is tied up in the aromatic pi system
Both are equally basic since both are aromatic amines
Pyridine's nitrogen, because its lone pair is delocalized into the ring
Neither nitrogen can act as a base at all under any conditions
questions.e: Because pyrrole's nitrogen lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet (in a p orbital), it is much less available to accept a proton than pyridine's lone pair, which sits in an sp2 orbital outside the pi system — making pyrrole nitrogen far less basic than pyridine nitrogen.

questions.q: In monosubstituted benzenes such as fluorobenzene, chlorobenzene, bromobenzene and nitrobenzene, what serves as the parent name?
o: The substituent name alone, without any reference to benzene
Benzene, with the substituent indicated by a prefix
A Greek-letter locant with no parent name
The substituent itself, with 'benzo' as a suffix
questions.e: The lecture states that in many simple compounds, benzene is the parent name and the substituent is simply indicated by a prefix, e.g. fluorobenzene, chlorobenzene, bromobenzene, nitrobenzene.

questions.q: Which of the following is the retained common name for C6H5CH3 (rather than 'methylbenzene')?
questions.e: The lecture lists toluene as the common/retained parent name for the benzene ring bearing a methyl group, alongside other accepted names such as ethylbenzene, cumene, styrene, phenol, aniline, benzaldehyde, benzoic acid, and anisole.

questions.q: Which accepted common name corresponds to benzene substituted with an isopropyl group (CH(CH3)2)?
questions.e: The monosubstituted-benzenes slide lists cumene as the accepted name for isopropylbenzene.

questions.q: Which accepted common name corresponds to benzene substituted with a vinyl group (CH=CH2)?
questions.e: Styrene is the retained name for vinylbenzene (C6H5CH=CH2), as shown among the accepted common parent names in the lecture.

questions.q: Which accepted common name corresponds to benzene substituted with a methoxy group (OCH3)?
questions.e: Anisole is the retained name for methoxybenzene (C6H5OCH3), listed alongside phenol (OH), aniline (NH2), benzaldehyde (CHO), and benzoic acid (COOH) as accepted parent names.

questions.q: For disubstituted benzenes, what do the locants 'ortho,' 'meta,' and 'para' correspond to in numerical terms?
questions.e: The lecture defines the classical locators for disubstituted benzenes as ortho (1,2-), meta (1,3-), and para (1,4-).

questions.q: What is the correct IUPAC/common name for the compound with NH2 at position 1 and F at position 3 on a benzene ring?
questions.e: Because the NH2 group imparts the special parent name 'aniline,' the compound is named as a derivative of aniline: 3-fluoroaniline, also written m-fluoroaniline — one of the lecture's worked practice questions.

questions.q: When naming a disubstituted or polysubstituted benzene where one group imparts a special retained name (e.g. phenol, aniline, toluene), what rule does the lecture give?
o: Use the special name only if there are absolutely no other substituents at all
Alphabetize all substituents and ignore which one gives a special name
Always ignore the special name and use only numerical locants instead
Name the compound as a derivative of that special parent name, with the special group's carbon numbered as C-1
questions.e: The lecture states that where one group imparts a special name, the compound should be named as a derivative of that molecule (e.g., a substituted 'phenol' or 'aniline'), with that carbon assigned position 1.

questions.q: For polysubstituted benzenes (three or more substituents) where NO group imparts a special retained name, what numbering/naming rule applies?
o: Always start numbering from the substituent that comes last alphabetically
Number the ring to give the lowest set of locants, and list the substituents alphabetically
Number substituents completely randomly since no rule applies
Use Roman numerals instead of ordinary Arabic numbers entirely
questions.e: The lecture's polysubstituted-benzenes rule states that if no group imparts a special name, one should number the ring to give the smallest set of numbers, and list the substituents alphabetically in the name.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name for the trisubstituted benzene bearing OH at C-1 and Br at C-2, C-4, and C-6?
questions.e: Since OH imparts the special parent name 'phenol' (assigned C-1), and bromines occupy C-2, C-4 and C-6, the compound is named 2,4,6-tribromophenol, as shown in the lecture's polysubstituted-benzene example.

questions.q: As a substituent branch, what is a benzene ring (C6H5–) called?
questions.e: The lecture states that as a branch, the benzene ring itself is known as a phenyl group, abbreviated Ph.

questions.q: What distinguishes a 'benzyl' group from a 'phenyl' group?
o: Benzyl is a benzene ring with an additional CH2 carbon as the branch point, while phenyl is the ring itself attached directly
Benzyl refers only and exclusively to naphthalene-based ring systems entirely
Benzyl and phenyl are simply two different names for the exact same group
Phenyl always contains a nitrogen atom somewhere, while benzyl never does
questions.e: The lecture explains that the term benzyl is reserved for a benzene ring with an additional carbon (CH2) as a branch point (e.g. PhCH2Cl = benzyl chloride), distinct from the phenyl group, which is the ring attached directly.

questions.q: What is the accepted name for PhCH2Cl, based on the lecture's phenyl/benzyl distinction?
questions.e: PhCH2Cl (a benzene ring attached via an extra CH2 carbon to a chlorine) is named benzyl chloride, illustrating the benzyl (Bn) group as distinct from a phenyl (Ph) substituent.

questions.q: What is described as 'the most characteristic reaction of aromatic compounds'?
o: Addition across a ring double bond
Reduction of the aromatic ring to cyclohexane
Ring-opening to form a straight-chain alkane
questions.e: The 'Reactions of Benzene' slide states that the most characteristic reaction of aromatic compounds is substitution at a ring carbon, preserving the aromatic system rather than destroying it (as addition would).

questions.q: Which six reaction types are shown branching from the 'aromatic ring' hub in the lecture's overview diagram?
o: Halogenation, acylation, nitration, alkylation, sulfonation, and hydroxylation
Halogenation and nitration only, with no other reaction types
Oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis, esterification, amination, and dehydration
Addition, elimination, substitution, polymerization, fermentation, and combustion only
questions.e: The overview diagram shows six substitution reaction types radiating from the aromatic ring: halogenation, acylation, nitration, alkylation, sulfonation, and hydroxylation.

questions.q: What is Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS), as defined in the lecture?
o: A reaction in which the entire aromatic ring is reduced to a cyclohexane ring
A reaction in which a nucleophile substitutes for an H on an aromatic ring
A reaction in which an electrophile, E+, substitutes for an H on an aromatic ring
A radical chain reaction that adds two substituents across a double bond
questions.e: The lecture defines EAS as a reaction in which an electrophile, E+, substitutes for a hydrogen on an aromatic ring, giving the overall equation ArH + E+ → ArE + H+.

questions.q: In the general EAS equation ArH + E+ → ArE + H+, what is released as a byproduct?
questions.e: The lecture's EAS diagram shows benzene + E+ yielding the substituted arene (ArE) plus H+, released as the aromatic ring re-establishes its full pi system after substitution.

questions.q: What reagent converts benzene into benzenesulfonic acid, and what byproduct forms?
o: Cl2/FeCl3, with HCl released as a byproduct
H2SO4, with H2O released as a byproduct
HNO3, with H2O released as a byproduct
RX/AlCl3, with HX released as a byproduct
questions.e: The lecture's sulfonation equation shows benzene + H2SO4 → benzenesulfonic acid (C6H5SO3H) + H2O.

questions.q: In the lecture's alkylation equation, benzene + RX in the presence of AlCl3 gives an alkylbenzene plus which byproduct?
questions.e: The alkylation equation shows benzene + RX, catalysed by AlCl3, producing an alkylbenzene (Ar–R) and HX as the byproduct.

questions.q: In the lecture's acylation equation, benzene reacts with an acyl halide (R–C(=O)–X) in the presence of AlCl3 to give which product?
questions.e: The acylation equation shows benzene + an acyl halide, catalysed by AlCl3, forming an acylbenzene (a ketone with the carbonyl attached directly to the ring) plus HX.

questions.q: Besides halogen, acyl and alkyl groups, which other functional group is specifically named in the lecture as substitutable onto the benzene ring via EAS-type reactions?
questions.e: The lecture states that other functional groups that can be substituted on the benzene ring include the sulfonyl group (sulfonation), the alkyl group (alkylation), and the acyl group (acylation).

questions.q: A wisecrack quoted in the lecture states, 'Every interesting drug molecule contains ______ somewhere.' What phrase completes this quote?
questions.e: The lecture quotes 'some wise dude' as saying 'Every interesting drug molecule contains a substituted benzene ring somewhere,' underscoring the medicinal-chemistry relevance of aromatic substitution chemistry.

questions.q: What new type of bond does Friedel-Crafts alkylation form, and between what two components?
o: A new C=C double bond within the ring itself
A new C–O bond, between an aromatic ring and an alcohol
A new C–C bond, between an aromatic ring and an alkyl group
A new C–N bond, between an aromatic ring and an amine
questions.e: The lecture defines Friedel-Crafts alkylation as forming a new C–C bond between an aromatic ring and an alkyl group, using an alkyl halide and a Lewis acid catalyst such as AlCl3.

questions.q: In the lecture's worked example, benzene + 2-chloropropane (isopropyl chloride), catalysed by AlCl3, gives which product?
questions.e: The Friedel-Crafts alkylation example shows benzene + 2-chloropropane/AlCl3 → isopropylbenzene (also known as cumene) + HCl.

questions.q: In Friedel-Crafts acylation, what type of product results, and where is the aromatic ring positioned relative to the carbonyl group?
o: The product is a carboxylic acid, with the ring replacing the OH
The product is an amide, with the ring bonded to nitrogen
The product is a ketone, with the aromatic ring on one side of the carbonyl group
The product is an alcohol, with the ring bonded to the oxygen
questions.e: The lecture states that treating an aromatic ring with an acid (acyl) chloride in the presence of AlCl3 gives a ketone as the product, with the aromatic ring on one side of the carbonyl carbon.

questions.q: In the lecture's worked Friedel-Crafts acylation example, benzene + acetyl chloride (CH3COCl), catalysed by AlCl3, gives which product?
questions.e: The Friedel-Crafts acylation example shows benzene + acetyl chloride/AlCl3 → acetophenone (a ketone) + HCl.

questions.q: How does the lecture define an acid (acyl) chloride?
o: A derivative of an amine in which –NH2 is replaced by chlorine
A derivative of a carboxylic acid in which the –OH group is replaced by a chlorine
A derivative of an alcohol in which the –OH is replaced by chlorine
A derivative of benzene in which one hydrogen is replaced by chlorine
questions.e: The lecture defines an acid (acyl) chloride as a derivative of a carboxylic acid in which the hydroxyl (–OH) group has been replaced by a chlorine atom, e.g. CH3COCl (acetyl chloride) from acetic acid.

questions.q: What role does AlCl3 play in both Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation?
o: It acts as a simple reducing agent that converts the ring to cyclohexane
It acts as the electrophile itself, becoming incorporated into the final product
It acts as a simple proton source only, protonating the ring directly itself
It acts as a Lewis acid catalyst, activating the alkyl or acyl halide toward reaction with the aromatic ring
questions.e: In both Friedel-Crafts reactions shown in the lecture, AlCl3 is written above the reaction arrow as the catalyst — a Lewis acid that activates the alkyl halide or acyl halide toward reaction with the aromatic ring.

questions.q: Why can Friedel-Crafts acylation be a more reliable synthetic strategy than Friedel-Crafts alkylation for introducing a single substituent onto benzene (a point implicit in the ketone vs. alkylbenzene products)?
o: The acylium/ketone product is deactivated toward further EAS, limiting over-substitution, unlike the activated alkylbenzene product
Acylation never uses a catalyst at all, making it far simpler
Alkylation simply and entirely cannot ever use AlCl3 as a catalyst at all here whatsoever
Acylation always produces multiple rings, unlike alkylation
questions.e: Although the lecture presents both reactions in parallel, a key downstream consequence (built on the directing-effects material) is that the ketone carbonyl product of acylation is a deactivating group, which limits further substitution — whereas the alkyl product of alkylation is activating and prone to polysubstitution.

questions.q: How do existing substituents on a benzene ring influence further electrophilic aromatic substitution, according to the lecture?
o: They influence both the orientation and the rate of further substitution
They only ever affect rate, never the orientation
They only ever affect orientation, never the rate
They have no effect on either orientation or rate
questions.e: The lecture states that existing groups on a benzene ring influence further substitution in both orientation (directing to ortho-para or meta) and rate (activating or deactivating).

questions.q: What defines an 'ortho-para director' in terms of relative attack positions and cation stability?
o: Ortho-para directors always slow down the reaction regardless of cation stability
Meta attack forms a more stable carbocation intermediate, so ortho-para products form faster
Ortho-para directors form no carbocation intermediate whatsoever at all, ever
Ortho-para attack forms a more stable carbocation intermediate than meta attack, so ortho-para products form faster
questions.e: The lecture states that for ortho-para directors, ortho-para attack forms a more stable cation than meta attack, and as a result ortho-para products are formed faster than meta products.

questions.q: What defines a 'meta director' in terms of relative attack positions and cation stability?
o: Meta directors simply cannot ever participate in EAS reactions at all
Meta attack forms a more stable carbocation intermediate than ortho-para attack, so meta products form faster
Ortho-para attack forms a more stable carbocation intermediate, so meta products form faster
Meta directors always form the least stable possible cation intermediate
questions.e: The lecture states that for meta directors, meta attack forms a more stable cation than ortho-para attack, so meta products are formed faster than ortho-para products.

questions.q: In the lecture's worked example, bromination of anisole (C6H5OCH3) gives which product distribution, and why is –OCH3 described as strongly activating?
o: 96% meta-bromoanisole, requiring a particularly strong Lewis acid catalyst here
50% ortho and 50% para exactly, with no observable rate difference from plain benzene at all
96% para-bromoanisole and 4% ortho-bromoanisole; the reaction proceeds many times faster than bromination of benzene, and no catalyst is required
100% meta-bromoanisole; the reaction proceeds far slower than bromination of benzene
questions.e: The lecture shows anisole + Br2/CH3COOH giving 96% p-bromoanisole and 4% o-bromoanisole, and notes that bromination of anisole proceeds many times faster than bromination of benzene — in fact –OCH3 is so activating that no catalyst is necessary.

questions.q: In the lecture's worked example, nitration of nitrobenzene gives which product distribution, and why is –NO2 described as deactivating?
o: 100% o-dinitrobenzene only, with absolutely and completely no meta product formed at all
93% p-dinitrobenzene, with the reaction proceeding faster than nitration of benzene
93% m-dinitrobenzene, but the reaction proceeds at exactly the same rate as plain benzene
93% m-dinitrobenzene, with less than 7% combined ortho/para product; nitration of nitrobenzene proceeds many times slower than nitration of benzene
questions.e: The lecture shows nitrobenzene + HNO3/H2SO4 at 100°C giving 93% m-dinitrobenzene, with less than 7% combined ortho and para product, and notes that nitration of nitrobenzene proceeds many times slower than nitration of benzene, consistent with –NO2 being a deactivating, meta-directing group.

questions.q: What structural feature of activating groups such as –NH2, –OH, and –OR allows them to activate the ring and direct ortho/para, per the lecture's 'Activating Directors' slide?
o: A permanent and fixed negative formal charge placed directly on the ring carbon
The complete and total absence of any lone pairs on the substituent atom
An inductive electron-withdrawing effect that raises the activation energy
A resonance effect that delocalizes the positive charge on the cation intermediate, lowering the activation energy for its formation
questions.e: The lecture explains that the resonance effect of electron-donating groups like –NH2, –OH and –OR delocalizes the positive charge on the arenium (cation) intermediate, lowering the activation energy for its formation and thus activating the ring toward further EAS, directing to ortho and para.

questions.q: According to the 'Deactivating Directors' slide, which list of groups is given as examples of deactivating, meta-directing substituents?
questions.e: The Deactivating Directors slide lists –NO2, –C=O, –SO3H, –NR3+, –CCl3, and –CF3 as electron-withdrawing groups (by resonance or induction) that decrease ring electron density, deactivate the ring, and direct meta.

questions.q: According to Table 9.1 in the lecture, are alkyl groups (–R) and the phenyl group classified as ortho-para directing or meta directing, and how strongly do they activate?
o: Ortho-para directing, and only weakly activating
questions.e: Table 9.1 places –R (alkyl) groups in the 'weakly activating' / ortho-para directing row, along with the phenyl-substituted ring itself, distinguishing them from the strongly activating –NH2/–OH/–OR groups.

questions.q: According to Table 9.1, where do the halogens (–F, –Cl, –Br, –I) fall in the activation/directing scheme — and why are they an important exception?
o: Strongly activating and ortho-para directing, just like the –OH group is
Non-directing — halogens supposedly have no influence on EAS regioselectivity at all
Weakly deactivating, yet still ortho-para directing — an exception to the rule that all o,p-directors are activating
Strongly deactivating and meta directing overall, just like the –NO2 group is
questions.e: Table 9.1 classifies halogens as weakly deactivating, yet they are still ortho-para directing (because their lone pairs can still stabilize the ortho/para cation by resonance, even though their strong electronegativity withdraws electron density inductively) — the lecture's Generalizations slide explicitly calls halogens the exception to 'all ortho-para directors are activating.'

questions.q: Per the lecture's four 'Generalizations,' which three types of substituents are ortho-para directing?
o: Alkyl groups, phenyl groups, and substituents where the atom bonded to the ring has an unshared pair of electrons
Only groups with absolutely no lone pairs at all and no alkyl character present
Only halogens and nitro groups specifically, absolutely nothing else at all
Only groups bearing a full positive charge on the ring-bonded atom
questions.e: Generalization 1 lists three classes of ortho-para directors: (a) alkyl groups, (b) phenyl groups, and (c) substituents in which the atom bonded to the ring has an unshared pair of electrons (e.g. N, O, halogens).

questions.q: Per Generalization 2, are all ortho-para directing groups activating toward further substitution, and what is the stated exception?
o: Yes, all are activating with absolutely no exceptions
No, all ortho-para directors are actually deactivating
Yes, all are activating, except the halogens, which are weakly deactivating
No, only alkyl groups among ortho-para directors are activating
questions.e: Generalization 2 states that all ortho-para directing groups are activating toward further substitution, except the halogens, which are weakly deactivating despite still being ortho-para directors.

questions.q: Per Generalization 3 in the lecture, what is true of all substituents that are NOT ortho-para directors?
o: They are meta directing in every single case
They can only ever be halogens specifically, nothing but that
They are non-directing and give a statistical mixture of all three positions
They always deactivate the ring only inductively, never by resonance
questions.e: Generalization 3 states simply: 'All other substituents are meta directing' — i.e., any group that is not an alkyl group, a phenyl group, or a lone-pair-bearing substituent directs new substitution to the meta position.

questions.q: Per Generalization 4, what common structural feature do all meta-directing groups share on the atom directly bonded to the ring?
o: They are all halogens specifically, nothing else at all whatsoever
They all contain a lone pair available for resonance donation
They all carry either a partial or a full positive charge on the atom bonded to the ring
They all carry a full negative charge on the atom bonded to the ring
questions.e: Generalization 4 states that all meta directing groups carry either a partial or full positive charge on the atom bonded to the ring (e.g. the carbonyl carbon of –C=O, –COR, the S of –SO3H, or the fully positive N of –NR3+/–NH3+), which withdraws electron density and disfavors the more electron-poor ortho/para cation intermediates.

questions.q: With excess reagent, what does the lecture note is likely for ortho-para directing (activating) rings, per Generalization 2?
o: The ring becomes completely unreactive after the first substitution
Disubstituted and trisubstituted rings are likely to form, since the activated ring reacts further at additional ortho/para positions
The ring is completely and utterly destroyed by over-oxidation reactions entirely
Only meta products ever form at all with excess reagent used here
questions.e: The lecture notes under Generalization 2 that because ortho-para directing groups (other than halogens) are activating, disubstituted and trisubstituted rings are likely to form when excess electrophilic reagent is used, since the ring remains more reactive than benzene after the first substitution.

questions.q: What is the valence shell electron configuration of a ground-state carbon atom?
questions.e: Carbon's ground-state valence configuration is 2s2, 2px1, 2py1, 2pz0. Promotion of one 2s electron into the empty 2pz orbital, followed by hybridization, explains carbon's four equivalent bonds in methane.

questions.q: How many hybrid orbitals does an sp3 carbon (e.g. in an alkane) have, and what is their geometry?
questions.e: Mixing the 2s orbital with all three 2p orbitals produces four equivalent sp3 hybrid orbitals, oriented tetrahedrally at 109.5° — the geometry of methane and every sp3 carbon.

questions.q: Why does a carbon involved in a C=C double bond use only sp2 (not sp3) hybridization?
o: Double bonds always use d orbitals for bonding
sp2 carbons supposedly cannot ever form pi bonds at all here
It has only three sigma-bonding partners, so it needs only three hybrid orbitals
It has five separate bonding partners overall
questions.e: A carbon in a double bond has three sigma-bonding partners (two substituents plus the other alkene carbon), so only three hybrid orbitals (sp2) are needed; the remaining, unhybridized p orbital is used for the pi bond.

questions.q: An sp2 hybrid orbital is formed by mixing the 2s orbital with how many 2p orbitals, and how many p orbitals are left unhybridized?
o: Two 2p orbitals mixed in; one p orbital left over
One 2p orbital mixed in; two left over
No 2p orbitals mixed in; three left over
Three 2p orbitals mixed in; none left over
questions.e: sp2 hybridization mixes the 2s orbital with two of the three 2p orbitals, giving three sp2 orbitals (120° apart) and leaving one p orbital unhybridized, perpendicular to the sp2 plane, to form the pi bond.

questions.q: In ethylene (H2C=CH2), the C=C double bond consists of which combination of bonds?
o: One sigma bond and two pi bonds
Two sigma bonds only, with no pi bond
One sigma bond plus one pi bond
Two pi bonds only, with no sigma bond
questions.e: Two sp2 carbons join through a sigma bond (head-on overlap of sp2 hybrid orbitals) plus a pi bond (sideways overlap of the two unhybridized p orbitals, above and below the molecular plane).

questions.q: A carbon with only two sigma-bonding partners (as in an alkyne) is hybridized as:
o: sp, giving linear geometry with a 180° bond angle
questions.e: With only two sigma-bonding partners, carbon needs only two hybrid orbitals: the 2s orbital mixes with one 2p orbital to give two sp orbitals, directed 180° apart (linear geometry) — as in the H–C≡C–H skeleton of acetylene.

questions.q: How many pi bonds make up a carbon–carbon triple bond, and where do the electrons for them come from?
o: One pi bond, from a single leftover p orbital
Three pi bonds, from three leftover p orbitals
Zero pi bonds — a triple bond is three sigma bonds
Two pi bonds, from the two unhybridized p orbitals on each sp carbon
questions.e: Each sp-hybridized carbon in a triple bond has two unused, mutually perpendicular p orbitals. These overlap sideways in pairs to give two pi bonds, in addition to the sp–sp sigma bond, totaling a triple bond (1 sigma + 2 pi).

questions.q: Why is the C–H bond of a terminal alkyne (sp carbon) more polar than the C–H bond of an alkane (sp3 carbon)?
o: Alkyne hydrogens are supposedly attached to oxygen instead of carbon entirely
sp carbons supposedly have a full negative formal charge on them entirely
sp3 carbons are actually more electronegative than sp carbons
The sp orbital has more s character, holding electrons closer to the nucleus and making the sp carbon more electronegative
