questions.e: An sp orbital has 50% s character versus 25% for sp3, and s orbitals hold electron density closer to the nucleus. This makes the sp carbon more electronegative, polarizing the terminal alkynyl C–H bond more than an alkane or alkene C–H bond.

questions.q: Geometric (cis/trans) isomerism, which arises from restricted pi-bond rotation, is possible for alkenes but NOT possible for:
questions.e: Restricted rotation around a C=C pi bond is what makes cis/trans isomerism possible in alkenes. This kind of isomerism is not possible for simple alkanes (free rotation around C–C single bonds) or for alkynes (linear geometry has no distinguishable 'sides').

questions.q: What is the general IUPAC naming rule for converting an alkane name into the corresponding alkene name?
o: Add the prefix cyclo– to the name
questions.e: Alkenes are named by replacing the alkane suffix –ane with –ene (e.g. ethane → ethene, propane → propene), with a locant number indicating the position of the double bond where needed.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH2=CH–CH=CH2?
questions.e: CH2=CH–CH=CH2 has two double bonds starting at carbons 1 and 3 of a four-carbon chain, giving the name 1,3-butadiene — a simple conjugated diene.

questions.q: What functional group does the trivial name 'vinyl' refer to, and what is vinyl chloride?
o: The CH2=CH–CH2– group; vinyl chloride is CH2=CH–CH2Cl
The CH2=CH– group; vinyl chloride is CH2=CHCl
The =CH2 group; vinyl chloride is a cyclic compound
A five-carbon chain; vinyl chloride has no chlorine
questions.e: 'Vinyl' is the trivial name for the CH2=CH– group. Vinyl chloride, CH2=CHCl, is the monomer used to manufacture PVC.

questions.q: What functional group does the trivial name 'allyl' refer to, as in allyl bromide (CH2=CH–CH2Br)?
o: The =CH2 group attached directly to a ring
questions.e: 'Allyl' refers to the CH2=CH–CH2– group; allyl bromide is CH2=CH–CH2Br, where the bromine is on the carbon adjacent to (not part of) the double bond.

questions.q: Why are alkenes slightly more soluble in water than the corresponding alkanes, even though both are considered nonpolar overall?
o: Alkenes supposedly contain oxygen atoms that hydrogen-bond directly with water
The exposed pi electrons of the double bond have some slight interaction with water molecules, an interaction absent in alkanes
Alkanes repel water more strongly due to their triple bonds
Alkenes are supposedly fully ionic compounds throughout their entire structure
questions.e: Because of the exposed pi electrons in alkenes, there is some slight interaction with water molecules that is absent in alkanes, making alkenes marginally more water-soluble — although alkenes are still considered nonpolar overall.

questions.q: How does the boiling point of a typical alkene compare with that of its alkane parent (same carbon skeleton)?
o: Essentially identical in almost every case
Always much higher in every case
Alkenes have no measurable boiling point
Always much lower in every case
questions.e: The lecture notes that physical properties such as boiling point are essentially identical between an alkene and its alkane parent, despite the alkene's slightly greater water solubility.

questions.q: Elimination reactions used to prepare alkenes from alkyl halides or alcohols typically produce:
o: No reaction occurs at all under any conditions
A single pure alkene product with 100% selectivity every time
Mixtures of alkene products, regardless of whether the substrate is 1°, 2°, or 3°
Only aromatic products form here, never any alkenes at all
questions.e: The lecture states that whether the substrate is a 1°, 2°, or 3° halide or alcohol, elimination reactions generally give mixtures of alkene products (e.g. 2-bromopentane with base gives a mixture of trans-2-pentene, cis-2-pentene, and 1-pentene).

questions.q: Why can't a cis and a trans isomer of an alkene interconvert at room temperature?
o: The C=C double bond cannot rotate without breaking the pi bond
Single bonds are rigid, but double bonds rotate freely
Rotation around C=C requires only a small amount of thermal energy
cis and trans isomers are actually identical molecules
questions.e: Unlike a C–C single bond, the C=C double bond cannot rotate freely because rotation would require breaking the pi bond; this restricted rotation is exactly what allows distinct, stable cis and trans isomers to exist.

questions.q: What does it mean for double bonds to be 'conjugated', as in CH2=CH–CH=CH–CH3?
o: Conjugation supposedly only ever applies to triple bonds specifically here
The double bonds are on adjacent carbons with no single bond between them
The compound supposedly contains no single bonds anywhere at all
The double bonds alternate with single bonds in a sequential pattern, increasing the molecule's stability
questions.e: Sequential double-bond/single-bond patterns are described as 'conjugated'; the lecture states that this arrangement increases the stability of the molecule compared with an isolated (non-conjugated) diene of the same formula.

questions.q: What happens when a six-membered ring contains three alternating (conjugated) double bonds?
o: The ring converts into an alkyne
The ring becomes unstable and spontaneously decomposes
The compound is benzene, stabilised by aromaticity
The compound becomes a simple, unconjugated triene
questions.e: Three sequential double bonds within a six-membered ring gives benzene, a compound stabilised by aromaticity — fundamentally more stable and less reactive toward addition than an ordinary, non-aromatic alkene or triene.

questions.q: When benzene reacts with Br2 in the presence of a FeBr3 catalyst, what type of reaction occurs, and why is this significant?
o: Reduction, giving cyclohexane directly as the final product
No reaction occurs at all even with a catalyst present
Addition, giving a simple vicinal dibromide, just like an ordinary alkene
Substitution — because addition would destroy benzene's aromatic stabilisation
questions.e: C6H6 + Br2 (FeBr3 catalyst) gives C6H5Br + HBr — a substitution reaction, not an addition. This is highlighted because it distinguishes aromatic compounds like benzene from ordinary alkenes, which undergo addition readily; benzene 'protects' its aromatic pi system by substituting instead.

questions.q: What term describes non-aromatic compounds, in contrast to 'aromatic' compounds like benzene?
questions.e: The lecture states that non-aromatics were historically called 'aliphatic' — a term contrasted with 'aromatic', which originally referred to the pleasant smell of many early-studied benzene derivatives.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH3)2C=CH–CH2–CH3?
questions.e: The longest chain bearing the double bond is a 5-carbon (pentene) chain, with a methyl branch at C-2 and the double bond starting at C-2, giving 2-methyl-2-pentene (also describable as a pent-2-ene).

questions.q: What is the general form of an addition reaction to a C=C double bond?
o: –C=C– + A–B → –C≡C– + AB2, with loss of a hydrogen
–C=C– + A–B always forms an aromatic ring product
–C=C– is unreactive toward all reagents A–B
–C=C– + A–B → –C–C–, with rehybridization and no loss of atoms
questions.e: Addition reactions have the general form: the reagent A–B adds across the double bond, the carbons rehybridize from sp2 to sp3, and no atoms are lost from the starting materials — this is the defining reactivity pattern of alkenes.

questions.q: Why do alkenes act as nucleophiles toward electrophiles such as H+ or Br2?
o: Alkenes have no electrons at all available for bonding
Alkenes carry a full negative formal charge on every carbon
Electrophiles are repelled by all carbon atoms equally
The exposed, loosely-held pi electron density is attacked by electron-poor species
questions.e: The pi bond represents a region of relatively exposed, loosely-held electron density, which is attractive to electron-poor electrophiles — this is the basis of essentially all alkene addition chemistry.

questions.q: What catalyst(s) are used for the catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene to an alkane?
questions.e: Hydrogenation of alkenes requires a metal catalyst — Pt, Pd, or Ni are most common (also PtO2, and occasionally Ru, Rh, or Re) — to activate H2 at the metal surface.

questions.q: Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene delivers both hydrogen atoms to the same face of the double bond. What is this stereochemical outcome called?
questions.e: Because both H atoms are delivered from the same catalyst surface, catalytic hydrogenation is a syn-addition and is stereospecific — this is the basis of industrial hydrogenation of fats/oils to margarine.

questions.q: What reactive intermediate forms when Br2 adds to an alkene, and how does it control the reaction's stereochemistry?
o: A carbanion intermediate; giving simple syn-addition
A free radical intermediate; giving no stereochemical preference at all
An aromatic ring intermediate forms instead of any ion
A cyclic bromonium ion; the bromide nucleophile attacks from the opposite face, giving anti-addition
questions.e: The alkene's pi electrons attack Br2 to form a bridged, cyclic bromonium ion (with Br+ bonded to both carbons), releasing Br-. The bromide ion is then forced to attack from the face opposite the bromonium ion (backside attack), giving stereospecific anti-addition.

questions.q: When HBr adds to 2-methylpropene, (CH3)2C=CH2, what is the major product and why?
o: A 50:50 mixture of products, because there is no preference at all here
No reaction occurs at all because the alkene is too sterically hindered
3C–Br, because H adds to the carbon with more hydrogens, forming the more stable tertiary carbocation
2CH–CH2Br, because Br always adds to the terminal carbon
questions.e: Protonation occurs to give the more stable (tertiary) carbocation at the more substituted carbon; bromide then attacks that carbocation, so the major product is (CH3)3C–Br — the halide ends up on the more highly substituted carbon, per Markovnikov's rule.

questions.q: State Markovnikov's rule for the addition of an acid H–X to an unsymmetrical alkene.
o: Markovnikov's rule only ever applies to perfectly symmetric alkenes
The hydrogen of the acid always attaches to the least substituted carbon regardless of hydrogen count
The halide always attaches instead to the least substituted carbon
The hydrogen of the acid attaches to the carbon atom that already holds the greater number of hydrogens
questions.e: Markovnikov's original 1870 statement: in the ionic addition of an acid to a C=C double bond, the hydrogen of the acid attaches to the carbon atom which already holds the greater number of hydrogens ('them that has, gets').

questions.q: What is the key difference between a 'regioselective' and a 'regiospecific' reaction?
o: Regiospecific reactions supposedly never occur at all in alkene chemistry, ever
A regioselective reaction forms one product in larger amount than another possible one; a regiospecific reaction forms only one possible product
These two terms are exact synonyms with completely identical meaning in every context
A regioselective reaction always gives 100% of one product; a regiospecific reaction gives a random mixture
questions.e: The lecture distinguishes: a regioselective reaction is one where one of the possible products forms in larger amounts than the other; a regiospecific reaction is one where only one of the possible products forms at all (100%).

questions.q: In the two-step mechanism for Markovnikov addition of HBr to an alkene, what happens in step 1 (the slow step)?
o: The alkene is oxidised to a carboxylic acid
The alkene attacks H+, forming a carbocation intermediate
Br– attacks the alkene directly to form the product
Two alkene molecules simply dimerize together
questions.e: Step 1 (slow): the pi electrons of the alkene act as the nucleophile and attack H+, generating a carbocation (protonation occurs so as to give the more stable, more substituted carbocation).

questions.q: In the two-step Markovnikov mechanism, what happens in step 2, and why is it fast?
o: A second equivalent of HBr is required to complete the reaction
Water attacks the carbocation instead of bromide ion
Br– attacks the carbocation, which is a high-energy, very reactive species
The carbocation is reduced back to the starting alkene
questions.e: Step 2 (fast): the bromide nucleophile attacks the electrophilic (and highly reactive) carbocation intermediate, forming the C–Br bond of the major product almost as soon as the carbocation forms.

questions.q: Rank the general stability order of carbocations from most to least stable.
questions.e: Alkyl groups stabilise an adjacent positive charge through induction and hyperconjugation, so more substituted carbocations are more stable: tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl. This ordering explains why Markovnikov addition favours formation of the more substituted carbocation.

questions.q: In a carbocation rearrangement (e.g. addition of HCl to 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene), what drives the 1,2-hydride or 1,2-methyl shift?
o: Rearrangement supposedly never affects which product ends up major at all
The shift converts the carbocation into a stable radical
Rearrangement only ever occurs with alkynes, never with alkenes at all
Migration occurs to convert a less stable carbocation into a more stable one, giving a rearranged major product
questions.e: If the initially formed carbocation can rearrange (via hydride or methyl shift) to a more stable carbocation, it will — and because the more stable cation forms faster/reacts more, the rearranged skeleton usually dominates as the major product, even though it is not the 'obvious' connectivity from the starting alkene.

questions.q: Under radical conditions (e.g. HBr with peroxides present), addition of HBr to an alkene proceeds anti-Markovnikov. Why?
o: A bromine radical mechanism operates, forming the more stable radical, which places Br on the less-substituted carbon
Peroxides act as strong reducing agents that fully block cationic pathways
Anti-Markovnikov addition occurs with HCl and HI just as often as with HBr itself
Markovnikov's rule is simply reversed for all halogens under any conditions
questions.e: Under radical-initiating conditions, HBr adds via a bromine-radical chain mechanism rather than a carbocation mechanism; the bromine radical adds first to give the more stable (more substituted) carbon radical, which places the H on that carbon and Br on the less-substituted carbon — the anti-Markovnikov (peroxide) effect. This is specific to HBr; HCl and HI do not undergo this radical pathway efficiently.

questions.q: What product results from adding cold, concentrated H2SO4 to an alkene?
questions.e: Cold, concentrated H2SO4 adds across the double bond by the same Markovnikov (carbocation) mechanism as HX addition, producing an alkyl hydrogen sulfate — a classic intermediate en route to alcohols on hydrolysis.

questions.q: Acid-catalysed hydration of an alkene (H2O, H+) follows which regiochemical pattern, and why?
o: Markovnikov orientation, because it proceeds through the same carbocation mechanism as HX addition
No regiochemical preference at all is ever observed in this case
Anti-Markovnikov orientation, because water is a weak nucleophile
It always gives a racemic mixture regardless of the substitution pattern
questions.e: Acid-catalysed hydration proceeds through protonation to the more stable carbocation, then attack by water — the same carbocation mechanism as HX addition — so the OH group ends up on the more substituted carbon, per Markovnikov's rule.

questions.q: Treating an alkene with cold, dilute KMnO4/OH– gives which product, and with what stereochemistry?
o: Complete cleavage to two separate carboxylic acids
An alkyl halide product forms instead of anything else
No reaction — KMnO4 does not react with alkenes under mild conditions
A 1,2-diol, with both new OH groups added to the same face
questions.e: Cold, dilute KMnO4/OH– performs a mild syn-dihydroxylation via a cyclic intermediate (analogous to an epoxide/manganate ester), adding both new hydroxyl groups to the same face of the former double bond to give a 1,2-diol (glycol).

questions.q: What happens when an alkene is treated with hot, concentrated KMnO4, in contrast to the cold/dilute conditions?
o: The reaction stops at the diol stage, exactly as with cold KMnO4
The alkene is somehow converted directly into an alkyne instead entirely
The C=C bond is oxidatively cleaved entirely, giving aldehydes, ketones, or carboxylic acids depending on substitution
The double bond is simply reduced entirely to a single bond instead
questions.e: Hot, concentrated KMnO4 is a harsher oxidant that cleaves the C=C bond completely; depending on the substitution pattern at each alkene carbon, the products are aldehydes, ketones, or carboxylic acids (a terminal =CH2 carbon is oxidised all the way to CO2).

questions.q: What is the general molecular formula for an acyclic alkyne with one triple bond?
questions.e: Alkynes follow the general formula CnH2n-2 — the same formula as a molecule with two degrees of unsaturation, consistent with a triple bond (one sigma + two pi bonds, i.e. two degrees of unsaturation).

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of H–C≡C–H, and what is its common name?
questions.e: H–C≡C–H is named ethyne by IUPAC rules (alkane 'ethane' → drop –ane, add –yne), and is universally known by its common name, acetylene.

questions.q: Under IUPAC rules, how is an alkyne's parent chain selected, and how is the suffix formed?
o: The parent chain is the longest continuous chain that contains the triple bond; drop –ane and add –yne with the lowest possible locant
The parent chain must always and entirely exclude the triple bond completely
The suffix is always formed by adding –ene instead, never –yne
The parent chain is always exactly 5 carbons long, without exception
questions.e: IUPAC alkyne nomenclature: the parent chain is the longest continuous carbon chain that contains the triple bond; the alkane suffix –ane is dropped and –yne added, with the locant chosen to give the triple bond the lowest possible number.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name for CH3CH2C≡CCH3?
questions.e: Numbering the 5-carbon chain from the end nearest the triple bond, the triple bond starts at C-2, giving 2-pentyne (common name: ethylmethylacetylene).

questions.q: What defines a 'terminal' alkyne, as opposed to an 'internal' alkyne?
o: The triple bond is located at the very end of the carbon chain
The molecule contains no hydrogens present at all
The triple bond is located exactly in the middle of the chain
The molecule must be entirely cyclic in shape
questions.e: Terminal alkynes have the triple bond at the end of the chain, so one triple-bond carbon bears a hydrogen directly attached (≡C–H), as in 1-butyne (CH3CH2C≡CH), distinguishing them from internal alkynes like 2-butyne.

questions.q: How do the general physical properties of alkynes (polarity, hydrogen bonding, boiling point, water solubility) compare with those of alkanes and alkenes?
o: Alkynes have unusually high melting and boiling points due to ionic bonding
Alkynes form unusually strong hydrogen bonds specifically due to the triple bond
Alkynes are strongly polar and highly water-soluble, unlike alkanes and alkenes
Broadly similar — weakly/non-polar, no hydrogen bonding, relatively low mp/bp, and water-insoluble
questions.e: The lecture states that alkynes, like alkanes and alkenes, are weakly or non-polar, cannot hydrogen-bond, have relatively low melting/boiling points, and are insoluble in water.

questions.q: Which pair of relative acid strengths, as presented in the lecture, is correct?
o: All of these compounds are equally acidic
HF < H2O < ROH < HC≡CH < NH3 < CH4
HC≡CH < CH4 < NH3 < HF < H2O < ROH
CH4 < NH3 < HC≡CH < ROH < H2O < HF
questions.e: The lecture's acid-strength scale (weakest to strongest) is: CH4 < NH3 < HC≡CH < ROH < H2O < HF — terminal alkynes are weak acids, weaker than water, but stronger than ammonia or methane.

questions.q: Why does HC≡CH + NaOH give NO REACTION (NR), even though hydroxide is a base?
o: Sodium hydroxide cannot dissolve at all in the presence of alkynes
Water is a stronger acid than the terminal alkyne, so hydroxide is too weak a base to deprotonate it
Hydroxide only ever reacts with alkenes, never at all with alkynes
Acetylene supposedly has no acidic hydrogens at all present anywhere
questions.e: Because H2O is a stronger acid than the terminal alkyne (per the acid-strength order CH4 < NH3 < HC≡CH < ROH < H2O < HF), the hydroxide ion (OH–, the conjugate base of the stronger acid H2O) is too weak a base to remove the alkyne's proton — the equilibrium lies overwhelmingly on the starting-material side, so effectively NR.

questions.q: Why can sodium amide (NaNH2) successfully deprotonate a terminal alkyne to form an acetylide, when NaOH cannot?
o: Sodium amide only ever works on internal alkynes specifically
NaNH2 is not actually considered to be a real base at all here whatsoever
NH3 is a much weaker acid than the terminal alkyne, making NH2– a strong enough base to remove the proton
NaOH reacts faster but gives an entirely different product
questions.e: Since NH3 is a much weaker acid than HC≡CH (per the acid-strength order), its conjugate base, amide ion (NH2–), is a much stronger base than hydroxide — strong enough to deprotonate a terminal alkyne (a weak acid), driving the reaction: RC≡CH + NaNH2 → RC≡C–Na+ + NH3.

questions.q: What natural compound class, described in the lecture as having powerful antibiotic and anticancer properties, contains a nine- or ten-membered ring with two triple bonds separated by a double bond?
questions.e: Enediynes are a class of naturally occurring compounds with powerful antibiotic and anticancer properties; they contain a nine- or ten-membered ring with two triple bonds separated by a double bond. Calicheamicin and esperamicin (antitumour agents derived from bacteria) are examples, and some enediynes are in clinical trials.

questions.q: Ichthyothereol, a naturally occurring alkyne mentioned in the lecture, was traditionally used by Amazon Indians for what purpose?
o: As a convulsant applied to poisoned arrowheads
questions.e: The lecture describes ichthyothereol as a naturally occurring alkyne that is a convulsant, traditionally used by Amazon Indians for poisoned arrowheads; capillin, another natural alkyne mentioned, has fungicidal activity instead.

questions.q: Which of the following is a synthetic (not naturally occurring) alkyne-containing drug used as an antihypertensive, per the lecture?
questions.e: Pargyline (trade names Eudatin, Supirdyl) is a synthetic antihypertensive drug containing an alkyne group. Capillin, calicheamicin, and ichthyothereol are all naturally occurring alkyne-containing compounds, not synthetic drugs.

questions.q: Mestranol, an alkyne-containing synthetic drug named in the lecture, is used as:
questions.e: Mestranol (trade names Norquen, Ovastol) is listed in the lecture as a synthetic alkyne drug that serves as a component in oral contraceptives; parsalmide is the listed analgesic, and pargyline is the listed antihypertensive.

questions.q: How is an alkyne prepared from an alkene via dehydrohalogenation?
o: React the alkene directly with plain AgNO3 reagent instead
Hydrogenate the alkene, then oxidise it with KMnO4
Halogenate the alkene to a vicinal dihalide, then remove two equivalents of HX with base
Directly treat the alkene with NaNH2 in just one single step
questions.e: The two-step route is: (1) add X2 to the alkene to form a vicinal dihalide, then (2) remove two equivalents of HX by double elimination, typically with KOH followed by NaNH2 (or 2 equivalents of KOH with heat), to give the alkyne.

questions.q: In the acetylide-alkylation route (R–C≡C–Na+ + R'X → R–C≡C–R' + NaX), what mechanism operates, and what restriction applies to R'X?
o: No mechanism restriction applies — any alkyl halide works equally well
SN2 mechanism; R'X must be a primary or methyl halide
SN1 mechanism; R'X can be any halide, including tertiary
E1 mechanism; R'X must be a secondary alkyl halide only
questions.e: The acetylide ion is a strong nucleophile that performs an SN2 displacement on the alkyl halide; this only works cleanly when R'X is primary or methyl. A hindered, backside-blocked tertiary halide cannot undergo SN2.

questions.q: What happens if a metal acetylide (R–C≡C–Na+) is combined with a tertiary (3°) alkyl halide, instead of a primary one?
o: E2 elimination occurs instead of substitution, because the acetylide is too basic/hindered for SN2 on a 3° substrate
The reaction proceeds normally via SN2 to give the coupled alkyne
The tertiary halide is simply and directly reduced to an alkane instead
No reaction ever occurs at all, under any circumstances whatsoever here
questions.e: Acetylide ions are strong, bulky bases as well as nucleophiles. With a tertiary alkyl halide, SN2 substitution is blocked sterically, so the acetylide instead acts as a base and promotes E2 elimination, regenerating an alkene and reforming the neutral starting alkyne.

questions.q: Full catalytic hydrogenation of an alkyne (2 equivalents H2, Ni/Pt/Pd catalyst) gives which product?
o: No reaction — alkynes cannot be hydrogenated
questions.e: With excess H2 over a standard hydrogenation catalyst (Ni, Pt, or Pd), an alkyne is fully reduced through the alkene stage all the way to the saturated alkane.

questions.q: Which reagent/conditions selectively reduce an internal alkyne to the CIS-alkene?
o: Na or Li in liquid NH3
questions.e: H2 over the Lindlar catalyst (palladium poisoned to reduce its activity, deposited on CaCO3 with lead/quinoline) delivers syn-addition of hydrogen to the alkyne, stopping cleanly at the alkene stage to give the cis-alkene.

questions.q: Which reagent/conditions selectively reduce an internal alkyne to the TRANS-alkene?
o: Na in liquid NH3, giving anti-addition
Cold, dilute KMnO4/OH–, giving a diol
H2 with Lindlar catalyst, giving syn-addition
Aqueous AgNO3 solution, giving a precipitate
questions.e: Dissolving-metal reduction with Na or Li in liquid ammonia proceeds by a radical-anion mechanism that delivers anti-addition of hydrogen across the triple bond, giving the trans-alkene selectively.

questions.q: What happens when an internal alkyne is treated with two full equivalents of Br2?
o: Br2 has no reaction at all whatsoever with alkynes
The triple bond is completely destroyed with no new bonds formed
Addition occurs twice, first giving a dihaloalkene, then a tetrahalide
Only one equivalent can ever add to an alkyne
questions.e: Analogous to alkene halogenation but occurring twice: the first equivalent of Br2 adds across the triple bond to give a dihaloalkene (still containing a C=C), and a second equivalent adds across that new double bond to give the fully saturated tetrahalide.

questions.q: What is the final product when propyne (CH3C≡CH) reacts with two full equivalents of HCl, following Markovnikov orientation at each step?
o: Propyne does not react with HCl
questions.e: The first HCl adds with Markovnikov orientation to give 2-chloropropene (CH3CCl=CH2); the second HCl again adds with Markovnikov orientation to the same carbon, giving the geminal dihalide 2,2-dichloropropane (CH3CCl2CH3).

questions.q: Acid-catalysed hydration of an alkyne (H2O, H+, HgO catalyst) initially gives an unstable enol. What happens to the enol next, and what is the final product?
o: It spontaneously loses all of its oxygen atoms entirely
It undergoes keto-enol tautomerization to the more stable carbonyl compound
The enol is the stable final product and undergoes no further change
It reacts further with even more water to form a diol
questions.e: The initial hydration product is an enol (–CH=C(OH)–), which is unstable relative to its carbonyl tautomer; keto-enol tautomerization rapidly converts it to the far more stable ketone, e.g. 1-butyne + H2O/H2SO4/HgO gives 2-butanone.

questions.q: A terminal alkyne reacting with an active metal such as sodium (CH3C≡CH + Na → CH3C≡C–Na+ + ½H2) illustrates which type of alkyne reactivity?
o: The alkyne acting as an electrophile toward the metal
A simple addition reaction across the triple bond
The alkyne acting as an acid, being deprotonated by the metal
An oxidation reaction occurring at the triple bond
questions.e: This reaction is grouped under 'alkynes as acids' — the terminal alkyne's mildly acidic C–H bond is deprotonated by the reactive metal, releasing hydrogen gas and forming the sodium acetylide salt. Only terminal alkynes undergo this reaction.

questions.q: What is the significance of a terminal alkyne forming a precipitate when treated with AgNO3 (Tollens'-type silver test)?
o: It is a qualitative test that identifies terminal alkynes specifically, since internal alkynes give no reaction
It merely shows that the compound in question is aromatic
It merely confirms the presence of any ordinary C=C double bond
It indicates the alkyne has been fully hydrogenated
questions.e: Only terminal alkynes (with an acidic ≡C–H) react with AgNO3 to form an insoluble silver acetylide precipitate (RC≡C–Ag↓); an internal alkyne such as CH3C≡CCH3 gives no reaction (NR), making precipitate formation a specific diagnostic test for terminal alkynes.

questions.q: Oxidative cleavage of an internal alkyne with hot KMnO4, or with ozone followed by Zn/H2O workup, gives which products?
o: Two entirely separate aldehyde fragments only
No reaction occurs at all with either oxidant used
Two carboxylic acid fragments, one from each side of the former triple bond
A single 1,2-diol product only, nothing else
questions.e: Both hot KMnO4 and ozonolysis (O3, then reductive workup with Zn/H2O) completely cleave the alkyne's triple bond, oxidising each fragment all the way to a carboxylic acid — e.g. CH3C≡CCH3 + hot KMnO4 gives 2 equivalents of CH3COOH, and a terminal ≡CH carbon is oxidised further, all the way to CO2.

questions.q: According to Markovnikov's rule, when HBr adds to propene, the bromine ends up on:
questions.e: Markovnikov addition places the halogen on the carbon that can best stabilize a positive charge (the more substituted one).

questions.q: Hydroboration-oxidation of an alkene gives which regiochemical outcome?
questions.e: Boron adds to the less hindered carbon, and oxidation replaces boron with OH, giving the anti-Markovnikov alcohol.

questions.q: Complete hydrogenation of an alkyne with excess H2/Pd produces a(n):
questions.e: Excess hydrogen fully saturates both pi bonds of the alkyne, producing the corresponding alkane.

questions.q: Lindlar's catalyst is used to convert alkynes into:
questions.e: Lindlar's poisoned palladium catalyst stops hydrogenation at the alkene stage, giving syn addition and a cis product.

questions.q: Terminal alkynes are more acidic than alkenes because:
o: The sp carbon holds electron density closer to the nucleus
questions.e: Greater s-character in sp-hybridized carbons increases electronegativity, stabilizing the conjugate base.

questions.q: A diene reacting with a dienophile in a cycloaddition reaction describes the:
questions.e: The Diels-Alder reaction forms a six-membered ring from a conjugated diene and a dienophile.

questions.q: An SN2 reaction proceeds fastest with which type of substrate?
questions.e: SN2 requires backside attack, which is sterically easiest at unhindered primary or methyl carbons.

questions.q: Which solvent type favors SN1/E1 mechanisms?
questions.e: Polar protic solvents stabilize the carbocation intermediate and the leaving group through hydrogen bonding and solvation.

questions.q: Oxidation of a secondary alcohol with a strong oxidant typically yields a:
questions.e: Secondary alcohols oxidize to ketones and cannot be oxidized further under normal conditions.

questions.q: The Lucas test is used to distinguish:
questions.e: Lucas reagent (ZnCl2/HCl) reacts at different rates depending on alcohol class, based on carbocation stability.

questions.q: The Williamson ether synthesis combines an alkoxide with a(n):
questions.e: An SN2 reaction between an alkoxide nucleophile and an alkyl halide forms an ether.

questions.q: Tertiary alcohols resist oxidation because:
o: They lack a hydrogen on the carbinol carbon
questions.e: Oxidation of alcohols requires removing a hydrogen from the carbon bearing the OH group, which tertiary alcohols lack.

questions.q: According to Huckel's rule, an aromatic ring must have how many pi electrons?
questions.e: Huckel's rule requires 4n+2 pi electrons in a cyclic, planar, fully conjugated system.

questions.q: An electron-donating group like -OH on a benzene ring typically directs new substitution to:
questions.e: Activating groups increase electron density most at ortho and para positions, directing electrophiles there.

questions.q: A strongly deactivating group like -NO2 directs electrophilic substitution to the:
questions.e: Deactivating groups destabilize the arenium ion least at the meta position, making it the major product site.

questions.q: Friedel-Crafts acylation installs which type of group onto a benzene ring?
questions.e: Friedel-Crafts acylation uses an acyl chloride and a Lewis acid catalyst to attach an acyl group to the ring.

questions.q: Why are halogens deactivating yet still ortho/para-directing?
o: Inductive withdrawal deactivates, but resonance donation directs ortho/para
They are meta directors due to their electronegativity
They have no effect on the ring
questions.e: Halogens withdraw electron density inductively (deactivating) but can donate a lone pair by resonance (ortho/para directing).

questions.q: Aniline is a weaker base than a typical aliphatic amine because:
o: Its nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the aromatic ring
It has no nitrogen lone pair
questions.e: Resonance delocalization of the lone pair into the ring reduces its availability to accept a proton.

questions.q: Which amine classification has three alkyl/aryl groups attached to nitrogen?
questions.e: A tertiary amine has nitrogen bonded to three carbon-containing groups and no N-H bonds.

questions.q: The Gabriel synthesis is a method for preparing:
questions.e: Gabriel synthesis uses phthalimide to cleanly produce primary amines without over-alkylation.

questions.q: Reductive amination converts a ketone or aldehyde plus an amine into a(n):
o: New amine, via an imine intermediate
questions.e: The carbonyl and amine first condense to form an imine, which is then reduced to the new amine.

questions.q: Amine basicity generally follows which order in aqueous solution?
questions.e: Alkyl groups donate electron density (increasing basicity) while aromatic ring delocalization reduces it.

questions.q: The Hinsberg test uses benzenesulfonyl chloride to distinguish:
questions.e: Primary, secondary, and tertiary amines react differently with benzenesulfonyl chloride, giving distinguishable results.

questions.q: Diazotization of a primary aromatic amine with nitrous acid produces a:
questions.e: Primary aromatic amines react with HNO2 (generated in situ) to form diazonium salts, useful in further synthesis.

questions.q: Which carboxylic acid derivative is generally the most reactive toward nucleophilic acyl substitution?
questions.e: Acid chlorides have the best leaving group (chloride), making them the most electrophilic and reactive derivative.

questions.q: Saponification refers to the base-catalyzed hydrolysis of a(n):
o: Ester, producing a carboxylate salt and alcohol
questions.e: Saponification is the classic reaction producing soap (carboxylate salts) from fats (esters) and base.

questions.q: Why are amides the least reactive carboxylic acid derivative?
o: The nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl by resonance
They are the most acidic derivative
questions.e: Resonance stabilization of the amide bond reduces the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon.

questions.q: Fischer esterification is best described as:
o: An acid-catalyzed equilibrium between acid, alcohol, ester, and water
questions.e: Because it's an equilibrium, excess reagent or removal of water is needed to drive the reaction toward the ester.

questions.q: Electron-withdrawing substituents near a carboxylic acid's -COOH group typically:
o: Increase acidity by stabilizing the conjugate base
Convert the acid into an ester
questions.e: Inductive electron withdrawal stabilizes the negative charge on the carboxylate, increasing acid strength.

questions.q: A peptide bond linking amino acids in a protein is chemically a(n):
questions.e: The peptide bond is an amide linkage formed between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amine of the next.

questions.q: Which fatty acid has the highest melting point?
questions.e: Saturated stearic acid packs tightly with no kinks from double bonds, giving it the highest melting point of the four.

questions.q: Which of the following compounds can exist as cis and trans isomers?
questions.e: 2-Hexene has two different groups on each double-bond carbon, allowing cis/trans isomerism; 1-hexene has a terminal =CH2, cyclohexene's ring geometry locks it, and alkynes are linear.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a mechanism by which cis and trans alkene isomers can interconvert?
o: Protonation by a strong acid followed by deprotonation
questions.e: Ozonolysis cleaves the double bond entirely (producing carbonyl fragments) rather than allowing rotation about it, so it cannot interconvert cis/trans isomers.

questions.q: What effect is mainly responsible for terminal alkynes being more acidic than saturated hydrocarbons?
o: Inductive effect (hybridization of the C-H bond)
questions.e: The sp-hybridized carbon of a terminal alkyne holds its bonding electrons closer to the nucleus, stabilizing the conjugate base inductively.

questions.q: What is the shape of the acetylene (C2H2) molecule?
questions.e: Each carbon in acetylene is sp-hybridized with 180° bond angles, making the whole molecule linear.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the ground-state electron configuration of carbon is FALSE?
o: Carbon has 6 electrons: 2 core electrons and 4 valence electrons
All four valence electrons are found in 2p orbitals
The two core electrons are found in the 1s orbital
Carbon's ground state has two unpaired electrons
questions.e: Carbon's ground-state configuration is 1s² 2s² 2p² — two valence electrons sit in the 2s orbital, not all four in 2p, making this statement false.

questions.q: How many pi (π) bonds are present in ethyne (C2H2)?
questions.e: Ethyne's triple bond is made of one sigma and two pi bonds; taken with the C-H sigma bonds, the source keyed this item as three bonding interactions overall.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about cycloalkanes is correct?
o: They can have as few as two carbon atoms in the ring
They have more hydrogen atoms than straight-chain alkanes with the same number of carbons
None of the above statements is correct
questions.e: A cycloalkane needs a minimum of 3 carbons, is saturated, and has 2 fewer hydrogens than the analogous straight-chain alkane — so all three statements are wrong.

questions.q: What is the correct IUPAC name for CH2=CH-CH=CH2?
questions.e: Two double bonds starting at C1 and C3 of a 4-carbon chain give the name 1,3-butadiene.

questions.q: What are the approximate bond angles around each carbon of the C=C double bond in an alkene?
questions.e: The sp²-hybridized carbons of an alkene have trigonal-planar geometry with ~120° bond angles.

questions.q: Cis-trans isomerism is possible for which of the following compounds?
questions.e: Only 2-pentene (CH3-CH=CH-CH2-CH3) has two different substituents on each alkene carbon, allowing cis/trans forms; the others have a terminal =CH2.

questions.q: Which reactant would convert an alkene into an alkane?
questions.e: Catalytic hydrogenation (H2 with a metal catalyst) adds two hydrogens across the double bond, converting an alkene to the corresponding alkane.

questions.q: Markovnikov's rule is needed to predict the major product when HCl adds to which of the following?
questions.e: Propene (CH2=CH-CH3) is an unsymmetrical alkene, so Markovnikov's rule is needed to predict which carbon gets the Cl; the other alkenes are symmetrical (or not alkenes at all).

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) The physical properties of unsaturated hydrocarbons are similar to those of saturated hydrocarbons of comparable molecular mass. (2) Sulfuric acid (H2SO4) is used as a catalyst in the alkylation of benzene. (3) Both PVC and Saran Wrap are addition polymers containing chlorine substituents.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: All three statements are correct as written.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) Terpenes are alkenes containing five double bonds. (2) A vinyl group is obtained by removing a hydrogen atom from propylene. (3) Nickel and platinum are common catalysts used in hydrogenation reactions.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Only statement (3) is true; terpenes vary in double-bond count (not fixed at five) and a vinyl group (CH2=CH-) comes from ethylene, not propylene.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) o-Xylene is benzene with two methyl group substituents. (2) No locant number is needed to specify the position of the double bond in ethene or propene. (3) Hydrohalogenation is an example of a symmetrical addition reaction.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Statements (1) and (2) are true; hydrohalogenation (HX addition) is an unsymmetrical addition since H and X are different groups, so (3) is false.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) Ethene and ethane have the same geometric shape. (2) Allyl chloride contains two carbon-carbon double bonds. (3) Cis-trans isomerism is possible in both 1-butene and 2-butene.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: All three are false: ethene is planar while ethane is tetrahedral, allyl chloride has only one C=C, and cis-trans isomerism applies to 2-butene but not to 1-butene (which has a terminal =CH2).

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) 1,6-Heptadiyne contains four carbon-carbon double bonds. (2) Markovnikov's rule is needed to predict the product when water adds to 2-butene. (3) Benzene contains both localized and delocalized bonding.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: 1,6-Heptadiyne contains triple bonds (diyne), not double bonds; 2-butene is symmetrical so Markovnikov's rule isn't needed; and while benzene does have both sigma (localized) and pi (delocalized) bonding, the source keyed all three as false.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) Alkanes have limited solubility in water and are less dense than water. (2) Propane contains both primary and secondary carbon atoms. (3) Some, but not all, cycloalkanes can exist as cis-trans isomers.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Statements (1) and (3) are true; propane (CH3-CH2-CH3) has only primary and secondary carbons is actually true too by structure, but per the source key only two of the three statements register as true.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) A cycloalkane must contain a minimum of four carbon atoms. (2) 2,4-Dimethylpentane and 2,4-dimethylhexane are constitutional isomers of each other. (3) Every alkane except methane can exist in an infinite number of conformations.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Cyclopropane shows a cycloalkane needs only 3 carbons minimum; the two named compounds have different molecular formulas so are not constitutional isomers; all three statements are false.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) Natural gas and petroleum are the largest natural sources of alkanes and cycloalkanes. (2) The number of hydrogen atoms in an alkane is always given by 2C+2, where C is the number of carbon atoms. (3) Boiling points of unbranched alkanes decrease as chain length increases.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Statements (1) and (2) are true; boiling points of unbranched alkanes actually increase with chain length, so (3) is false.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) Cis-trans isomers have the same molecular formula and the same structural formula. (2) 1,3-Dichlorocyclohexane contains 12 hydrogen atoms. (3) Reaction of ethane with Br2 produces 1,2-dibromoethane.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Cis-trans isomers differ in spatial arrangement, not structural formula; 1,3-dichlorocyclohexane (C6H10Cl2) has 10 H, not 12; and ethane + Br2 gives 1,2-dibromoethane only under specific substitution, not addition — all keyed false.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) Propyl bromide is another name for 1-bromopropane. (2) Compounds with molecular formula C5H10 are alkanes and those with C5H12 are cycloalkanes. (3) Complete combustion of alkanes produces hydrogen gas and carbon.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Only statement (1) is true; C5H10 is actually the cycloalkane/alkene formula and C5H12 is the alkane formula (reversed from the statement), and complete combustion of alkanes yields CO2 and H2O, not H2 and carbon.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) In IUPAC nomenclature, a cycloalkane with only one substituent does not need a locant number. (2) Propane and cyclopropane are both gases at room temperature. (3) Halogenation of an alkane is an example of a substitution reaction.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: All three statements are correct.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) 3-Ethyl-2-methylnonane and 3-propyl-2-methylnonane are both acceptable IUPAC names for the same compound. (2) Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) contain both chlorine and fluorine atoms. (3) Alkanes are the simplest family of unsaturated hydrocarbons.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Only statement (2) is true; the two names in (1) describe different substituent patterns (not the same compound), and alkanes are saturated, not unsaturated, hydrocarbons.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) 3-Ethyl-4,5-dipropyloctane contains 16 carbon atoms. (2) There are two different 3-carbon alkyl groups and three different 4-carbon alkyl groups. (3) A condensed structural formula shows the atoms present but not the bonds between them.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Statements (2) and (3) are true; 3-ethyl-4,5-dipropyloctane actually totals 16 carbons when counted correctly, but per the source key only two statements are marked true overall.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) All halogenated hydrocarbons are denser than water. (2) Substituents are found in some, but not all, branched alkanes. (3) There are two branched-chain isomers with the molecular formula of butane (4 carbons).
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Not all halogenated hydrocarbons are denser than water (fluorocarbons can be lighter); branched alkanes by definition all contain substituents; and butane (C4H10) has only one branched isomer (isobutane) — all three are false.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) Methane is a major component of the atmospheres of Jupiter and Saturn. (2) Solid alkanes are used as skin softeners in cosmetic preparations. (3) Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) are less reactive with atmospheric ozone than chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs).
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: All three statements are correct as keyed in the source.

questions.q: 2-Pentene and 2-Butene are best characterized as:
o: Same number of carbons but not constitutional isomers
One but not the other is capable of cis-trans isomerism
questions.e: Both 2-pentene and 2-butene have two different groups on each double-bond carbon, so both display cis-trans isomerism.

questions.q: 1-Butyne and 1,3-Butadiene are best characterized as:
o: Same number of carbons but not constitutional isomers
One but not the other is capable of cis-trans isomerism
questions.e: Both have 4 carbons, but 1-butyne is C4H6 and 1,3-butadiene is also C4H6 — per the source key they are not treated as constitutional isomers of each other.

questions.q: Cyclohexene and Benzene are best characterized as:
o: Same number of carbons but not constitutional isomers
One but not the other is capable of cis-trans isomerism
questions.e: Cyclohexene (C6H10) and benzene (C6H6) share 6 carbons but different molecular formulas, so they are not constitutional isomers.

questions.q: 3-Methylcyclobutene and 3,4-Dimethylcyclobutene are best characterized as:
o: Same number of carbons but not constitutional isomers
One but not the other is capable of cis-trans isomerism
questions.e: The ring's endocyclic double bond geometry differs between the two substitution patterns, so only one of the pair can display cis-trans isomerism.

questions.q: o-Diethylbenzene and 1,3-Diethylbenzene are best characterized as:
o: Same number of carbons but not constitutional isomers
One but not the other is capable of cis-trans isomerism
questions.e: o-Diethylbenzene (1,2-diethylbenzene) and 1,3-diethylbenzene have the same molecular formula but different substitution patterns, making them constitutional isomers.

questions.q: Which of the following is a correct statement about organic compounds?
o: They can only be made by living organisms
They are always insoluble in water
They can only be obtained from nature
questions.e: The defining feature of an organic compound is that it contains carbon (almost always bonded to hydrogen).

questions.q: The distinction between saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons relates to:
o: The number of carbon atoms present
The types of carbon-carbon bonds present
questions.e: Saturated hydrocarbons have only single C-C bonds; unsaturated ones contain at least one double or triple C-C bond.

questions.q: The four hydrogen atoms of methane lie at the corners of a:
questions.e: Methane's sp³ carbon centre gives it tetrahedral geometry, with the four H atoms at the corners of a tetrahedron.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a possible molecular formula for an alkane?
questions.e: Alkanes follow CnH(2n+2); for n=4 this gives C4H10, not C4H12, so C4H12 has too many hydrogens to be a real alkane.

questions.q: CH3-CH3 written for ethane is an example of a:
questions.e: Writing CH3-CH3 shows how the atoms are grouped without drawing every individual bond — the hallmark of a condensed structural formula.

questions.q: Which of the following is a correct structural formula for an alkane?
questions.e: CH3-CH2-CH3 (propane) correctly places CH3 end-groups on either side of a central CH2, giving every carbon its correct valence of four.

questions.q: Three isomeric 5-carbon alkanes share which set of molecular formulas?
questions.e: Pentane, isopentane and neopentane are constitutional isomers, so all three share the identical molecular formula C5H12.

questions.q: Constitutional isomerism in alkanes is possible only if the number of carbon atoms is:
questions.e: The smallest alkane with a constitutional isomer is butane (C4H10, which has isobutane as an isomer); propane and smaller alkanes have no isomers.

questions.q: How many carbon atoms are in 2,2,4-trimethylpentane?
questions.e: The pentane parent chain (5C) plus three methyl substituents (3C) totals 8 carbon atoms.

questions.q: How many hydrogen atoms are in 3,5-dimethyloctane?
questions.e: 3,5-Dimethyloctane is C10H22, so it contains 22 hydrogen atoms.

questions.q: Which of the following is a pair of constitutional isomers?
questions.e: 2-Methylpentane and 2,3-dimethylbutane are both C6H14, differing only in how the carbon skeleton is branched, making them constitutional isomers.

questions.q: What is the minimum number of carbon atoms needed for a branched alkane, and for a branched alkyl group, respectively?
questions.e: The smallest branched alkane is isobutane (4 carbons), while the smallest branched alkyl group (isopropyl) needs only 3 carbons.

questions.q: Compared to a noncyclic alkane with the same number of carbon atoms, a cycloalkane has:
o: The same number of hydrogen atoms
questions.e: Closing a chain into a ring removes one C-H bond from each end, giving the cycloalkane two fewer hydrogens than its open-chain counterpart.

questions.q: Alkanes are carbon compounds in which:
o: There is at least one carbon-carbon double bond
Carbon is bonded only to other carbon and hydrogen atoms
questions.e: Alkanes contain only C-C and C-H single bonds; carbon is never bonded to anything but carbon and hydrogen.

questions.q: Which formula represents an organic compound?
questions.e: CH4 (methane) is a valid organic (carbon-containing) formula; the other two options are not valid molecular formulas at all.

questions.q: Which of the following is an alcohol?
questions.e: CH3CH2OH (ethanol) carries the -OH functional group that defines an alcohol; the others are a carboxylic acid, a ketone, and an alkyl halide respectively.

questions.q: The term “saturated” in “saturated hydrocarbons” means the compound is:
o: Saturated with water; it is wet
Saturated with carbon atoms in the parent chain
Saturated with hydrogen atoms; it contains only single bonds
Pure, with no other compounds mixed in
questions.e: “Saturated” refers to the hydrocarbon holding the maximum possible number of hydrogen atoms, achieved by having only single C-C bonds.

questions.q: “Saturated hydrocarbon” means the compound is:
o: Saturated with water; it is wet
Saturated with hydrogen atoms; it contains only single bonds
Pure, with nothing else mixed in
questions.e: A saturated hydrocarbon contains the maximum number of hydrogens possible, i.e. only single C-C bonds.

questions.q: Which term applies to alkanes?
questions.e: Alkanes are nonpolar and water-repelling, i.e. hydrophobic.

questions.q: Which of the following is a correct statement about the polyene molecule shown?
o: All the carbons are sp2 hybridized
Two of the carbons are sp3 hybridized
questions.e: Two carbons in the drawn chain sit outside the conjugated system and remain sp3-hybridized, while the rest are sp2.

questions.q: What locant number specifies the double-bond position in CH3CH2CH=CHCH3?
questions.e: Numbering from the end giving the lowest locant, the double bond starts at C2 of pent-2-ene.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of the bromo-substituted methylcyclopentane shown?
questions.e: Numbering the ring to give the substituents the lowest overall locants produces 3-bromo-1-butyl-4-methylcyclopentane.

questions.q: What is the common name of the fluoroalkane shown?
questions.e: The branched CH2 attached to an isopropyl-like group and bearing F matches the isobutyl fluoride structure.

questions.q: What is the common name for 2-bromo-2-methylpropane?
questions.e: Transcribed as circled in the source (note: the compound named is a 4-carbon bromide, though the answer options are oddly built on ‘pentyl’ stems).

questions.q: Which of the following has the highest boiling point?
questions.e: Of these, 1-chlorobutane has the longest unbranched carbon chain, giving it the greatest surface area and highest boiling point.

questions.q: Besides the halogen, what else does a dehydrohalogenation reaction eliminate?
questions.e: Dehydrohalogenation (E1/E2 elimination) removes H and X from adjacent carbons to form an alkene.

questions.q: What is the correct order of carbon-halogen bond strength in alkyl halides?
questions.e: Bond strength decreases down the halogen group as atomic size increases, so C-F is strongest and C-I is weakest.

questions.q: Which reaction results in about 50% inversion of configuration at the reacting carbon?
questions.e: SN1 proceeds through a planar carbocation that can be attacked from either face, giving a racemic (partially inverted) mixture of products.

questions.q: Which of the following is an INCORRECT statement about the SN1 mechanism?
o: It proceeds stepwise through reactive intermediates
Its slow (rate-determining) step is carbocation formation
Its products will always be a pair of enantiomers
questions.e: SN1 products are not always enantiomer pairs — carbocation rearrangements and achiral substrates mean the outcome isn't always a clean enantiomeric pair.

questions.q: Which of the alkyl chloride structures shown is most reactive toward the SN1 mechanism?
questions.e: Structure (a) is the most substituted (tertiary-like) halide, and SN1 rate increases with the stability of the carbocation intermediate formed — favoring the most substituted carbon.

questions.q: What is the minor product when propene reacts with HBr?
questions.e: Markovnikov addition favors 2-bromopropane as the major product, making 1-bromopropane (anti-Markovnikov) the minor product.

questions.q: Which alkyl bromide shown would yield 3-methyl-1-hexene as the major product on treatment with potassium tert-butoxide (KOtBu)?
questions.e: The bulky base KOtBu favors the Hofmann (less-substituted) elimination product; the precursor with Br at C2 next to the C3 methyl branch gives 3-methyl-1-hexene under these conditions.

questions.q: Which alkyl halide would be expected to react by both the SN1 and SN2 mechanisms?
questions.e: A secondary halide like (CH3)2CH-X is reactive enough for SN1 (moderately stable carbocation) while still accessible for SN2 backside attack, unlike primary or tertiary/neopentyl halides.

questions.q: What is the correct systematic name for the trisubstituted benzene ring shown, bearing Br, Cl and NO2 groups?
questions.e: Numbering to give the lowest locant set to the three substituents produces 4-bromo-2-chloro-1-nitrobenzene.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT true of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons?
questions.e: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons are large, nonpolar ring systems and are generally poorly soluble in water.

questions.q: All of the following are aromatic compounds EXCEPT:
questions.e: Pentalene's bicyclic 8-pi-electron system does not satisfy Hückel's rule and is antiaromatic/non-aromatic, unlike the other three.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an activating group in electrophilic aromatic substitution?
questions.e: The nitro group (-NO2) is strongly electron-withdrawing and deactivating, unlike the electron-donating amino and alkoxy groups.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) An allyl group contains three carbon atoms. (2) Alkenes have two fewer hydrogens than the corresponding alkane. (3) Toluene and o-xylene are both monosubstituted benzenes.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Statements (1) and (2) are true; o-xylene is disubstituted (two methyl groups), not monosubstituted, so (3) is false.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) Alkanes have low water solubility and are less dense than water. (2) Propane contains both primary and secondary carbon atoms. (3) Some, but not all, cycloalkanes exist as cis-trans isomers.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: All three statements are correct.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) Natural gas and petroleum are the largest natural sources of alkanes. (2) The number of hydrogen atoms in an alkane is always 2C+2. (3) Boiling points of unbranched alkanes decrease with increasing chain length.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Statements (1) and (2) are true; boiling points actually increase with chain length, so (3) is false.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) p-Xylene is benzene with two methyl group substituents. (2) No locant number is needed to specify the position of the double bond in ethene or propene. (3) Hydrohalogenation is an example of a symmetrical addition reaction.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Statements (1) and (2) are true; hydrohalogenation adds two different groups (H and X) so it is an unsymmetrical, not symmetrical, addition.

questions.q: Consider the statements about benzene: (1) Benzene has 6 pi electrons, satisfying Hückel's rule. (2) Benzene can be described as a hybrid of two cyclohexadiene molecules. (3) Benzene readily undergoes addition reactions.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Only statement (1) is true; benzene is better described as a resonance hybrid of Kekulé structures (not literally two cyclohexadienes), and it strongly favors substitution over addition to preserve its aromaticity.

questions.q: Consider the statements about benzene: (1) All six carbon atoms in benzene are equivalent. (2) All C-H bonds in benzene are equal in length. (3) All C-C bonds in benzene are equal in length.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Benzene's delocalized pi system makes all six carbons, all C-H bonds, and all C-C bonds equivalent — all three statements are true.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) Deactivating groups make a benzene ring more reactive toward electrophiles. (2) Deactivating groups act as nucleophiles toward the ring. (3) Halogens are deactivating groups on a benzene ring.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Only statement (3) is true; deactivating groups make the ring less reactive (not more) and they withdraw electron density rather than acting as nucleophiles.

questions.q: Consider the statements about cyclooctatetraene: (1) It is fully conjugated and planar. (2) It satisfies Hückel's rule for aromaticity. (3) It is a planar molecule.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Cyclooctatetraene adopts a non-planar, tub-shaped conformation with 8 pi electrons, which does not satisfy the 4n+2 Hückel rule — all three statements are false.

questions.q: Which molecular formula corresponds to 2,3-Dimethyl-2-pentene?
questions.e: 2,3-Dimethyl-2-pentene is a C7 alkene (one degree of unsaturation), giving the formula C7H14.

questions.q: Which molecular formula corresponds to 1,3-Heptadiene?
questions.e: 1,3-Heptadiene is a C7 diene (two degrees of unsaturation), giving the formula C7H12.

questions.q: Which molecular formula corresponds to 3-Heptyne?
questions.e: 3-Heptyne is a C7 alkyne (two degrees of unsaturation), giving the formula C7H12.

questions.q: Which molecular formula corresponds to 2-Methylcyclohexene?
questions.e: 2-Methylcyclohexene is a C7 ring with one double bond (two degrees of unsaturation total), giving C7H12.

questions.q: Which molecular formula corresponds to Toluene?
questions.e: Toluene (methylbenzene) is C7H8, reflecting the four degrees of unsaturation of the aromatic ring.

questions.q: How are Pentane and 2,2-Dimethylpropane (neopentane) best characterized?
o: Same number of carbons but not constitutional isomers
One but not the other is capable of cis-trans isomerism
questions.e: Both are C5H12 with different carbon skeletons (straight-chain vs. fully branched), making them constitutional isomers.

questions.q: How are Butane and Cyclobutane best characterized?
o: Same number of carbons but not constitutional isomers
One but not the other is capable of cis-trans isomerism
questions.e: Butane (C4H10) and cyclobutane (C4H8) share 4 carbons but have different molecular formulas, so they are not constitutional isomers.

questions.q: How are Chlorocyclobutane and 1,2-Dichlorocyclopropane best characterized?
o: Same number of carbons but not constitutional isomers
One but not the other is capable of cis-trans isomerism
questions.e: 1,2-Dichlorocyclopropane can show cis-trans isomerism (two substituents on the ring), while chlorocyclobutane (one substituent) cannot.

questions.q: How are 1,2-Dichlorocyclobutane and 1-Bromo-2-chlorocyclopentane best characterized?
o: Same number of carbons but not constitutional isomers
One but not the other is capable of cis-trans isomerism
questions.e: Both rings carry two different substituents on adjacent ring carbons, so both can exist as cis and trans isomers.

questions.q: How are Cyclohexane and Methylcyclopentane best characterized?
o: Same number of carbons but not constitutional isomers
One but not the other is capable of cis-trans isomerism
questions.e: Cyclohexane and methylcyclopentane are both C6H12, differing in ring size vs. substitution, making them constitutional isomers.

questions.q: Which benzene derivative shown corresponds to Anisole?
questions.e: Anisole is benzene bearing a methoxy (-OCH3) substituent, matching structure (c).

questions.q: Which structure shown corresponds to a Benzyl group?
questions.e: A benzyl group is a benzene ring attached to a -CH2- unit (as a substituent), matching structure (d).

questions.q: Which structure shown corresponds to Phenyl?
questions.e: A phenyl group is simply the bare, unsubstituted benzene ring attached at one carbon, matching structure (a).

questions.q: Which structure shown corresponds to Toluene?
questions.e: Toluene is benzene bearing a methyl (-CH3) substituent.

questions.q: The simplest alcohol contains how many carbon and oxygen atoms, respectively?
questions.e: Methanol (CH3OH), the simplest alcohol, has one carbon and one oxygen atom.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name for the structure commonly known as isopropyl alcohol?
questions.e: Isopropyl alcohol has the -OH on the middle carbon of a 3-carbon chain, giving the IUPAC name 2-propanol.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name for the structure drawn as 2,6-hexanediol?
questions.e: Numbering the chain to give the two -OH groups the lowest possible locants converts “2,6-hexanediol” to its correctly numbered form, 1,5-hexanediol.

questions.q: Which of the following is a correct statement about common alcohols?
o: Rubbing alcohol is pure isopropyl alcohol
Wood alcohol is another name for ethanol
Grain alcohol always contains a bittering additive
Absolute ethanol has essentially all water removed
questions.e: “Absolute” alcohol specifically denotes ethanol from which nearly all water has been removed (typically >99% pure).

questions.q: Which pair of compounds both contain two or more -OH groups?
questions.e: Propylene glycol (2 -OH groups) and glycerol (3 -OH groups) are both polyhydroxy alcohols.

questions.q: Alcohols have higher boiling points than alkanes of similar molecular mass mainly because of:
questions.e: The -OH group allows alcohol molecules to hydrogen-bond to each other, requiring more energy to separate them than for nonpolar alkanes.

questions.q: How many hydrogen bonds can an isopropanol molecule form with other isopropanol molecules (donating and accepting through its one -OH group)?
questions.e: An isopropanol -OH group can donate one H-bond and its oxygen can accept up to two, for a total capacity of three hydrogen bonds per molecule in the source's reasoning.

questions.q: What is a general method for preparing alcohols?
questions.e: Adding water across a C=C double bond (acid-catalyzed hydration) is a standard way to prepare alcohols from alkenes.

questions.q: Which of the four butanol structures shown is a secondary alcohol?
questions.e: A secondary alcohol has its -OH-bearing carbon attached to exactly two other carbons; structure (c) shows this arrangement among the four butanol isomers.

questions.q: Intramolecular dehydration of an alcohol produces:
questions.e: Intramolecular dehydration removes -OH and an adjacent H from within the same molecule, forming a C=C double bond (an alkene).

questions.q: Oxidation of a secondary alcohol produces:
questions.e: A secondary alcohol's carbon has only one H to lose on oxidation, so it stops at the ketone stage (it cannot form an aldehyde or acid).

questions.q: Which of the following is an INCORRECT statement about phenols?
o: They are easily oxidized and are used as antioxidants
They are weak acids, unlike alcohols
questions.e: Phenols are only slightly soluble in water (the aromatic ring dominates their character), so “easily dissolve in water” is the false statement.

questions.q: What is the correct IUPAC name for the diiodophenol structure shown?
questions.e: Numbering the ring from the -OH carbon (C1) to give the two iodine substituents the lowest locants gives 2,5-diiodophenol.

questions.q: Which of the following is an exception to the general formula for ethers (R-O-R)?
questions.e: H-O-Ar is actually a phenol (a hydroxyl group directly on an aromatic ring), not an ether, since ethers require two carbon groups flanking the oxygen.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name for ethyl phenyl ether?
questions.e: Naming benzene as the parent with an ethoxy substituent gives 1-ethoxybenzene (the locant is often dropped since there's only one substituent).

questions.q: Ethers resemble which class of compounds most closely in chemical reactivity?
questions.e: Ethers are relatively unreactive, much like alkanes, because the C-O-C linkage lacks an easily removable H or a reactive pi bond.

questions.q: The sulfhydryl (-SH) group is found in which class of compounds?
questions.e: The -SH (sulfhydryl) group is the defining functional group of thiols; disulfides instead contain an -S-S- linkage.

questions.q: Which of the following is the correct structure for 1-propanethiol?
questions.e: 1-Propanethiol places the -SH group on the terminal carbon of a 3-carbon chain: CH3-CH2-CH2-SH.

questions.q: Which molecule contains both an alkoxy group and a hydroxy group?
questions.e: CH3-O-CH2-OH carries both an ether (alkoxy, -O-CH3) linkage and a free hydroxyl (-OH) group on the same carbon skeleton.

questions.q: Which pair of compounds are constitutional isomers of each other?
questions.e: Isobutyl alcohol (C4H10O) and diethyl ether (C4H10O) share the same molecular formula but differ in connectivity, making them constitutional isomers.

questions.q: Which pairing describes the same alcohol by two different names?
questions.e: None of the individual pairings actually match (2-propanol ≠ propyl alcohol which is 1-propanol; 1-propanol ≠ isopropyl alcohol; and 2-methyl-2-propanol ≠ isobutyl alcohol) — so the correct choice per the answer key is (C) alone; see explanation.

questions.q: Which pairing of name and composition is correct?
o: Ethylene glycol; 3 carbons and 2 hydroxyl groups
questions.e: Glycerol is propane-1,2,3-triol: a 3-carbon backbone bearing 3 hydroxyl groups, matching this pairing exactly.

questions.q: How does the water solubility of alcohols change with increasing carbon-chain length?
o: It decreases as chain length increases
It decreases as the number of -OH groups increases
It increases with increasing molecular mass
questions.e: As the nonpolar hydrocarbon chain grows longer, it increasingly dominates over the polar -OH group, decreasing water solubility.

questions.q: In a secondary alcohol, the carbon bearing the -OH group is:
o: Always part of a carbon-carbon double bond
Attached to two other carbon atoms
Unable to bond to any hydrogen atom
questions.e: By definition, a secondary alcohol's -OH-bearing carbon is directly attached to exactly two other carbon atoms.

questions.q: Which dehydration condition (alcohol class and temperature) is needed to produce an ether rather than an alkene?
questions.e: Lower temperature (140°C) with a primary alcohol favors intermolecular dehydration (ether formation) rather than the intramolecular elimination that dominates at higher temperature.

questions.q: Zaitsev's (Saytzeff's) rule is specifically needed to predict the major product for dehydration of which alcohol?
questions.e: Zaitsev's rule applies when more than one alkene product is possible from an unsymmetrical secondary or tertiary alcohol; none of the listed alcohols creates such an ambiguity, so the answer is “none.”

questions.q: Which pairing of alcohol type and oxidation product is INCORRECT?
questions.e: Tertiary alcohols have no H on the -OH-bearing carbon to remove, so they resist oxidation entirely — they do not form carboxylic acids.

questions.q: Which of the following is an INCORRECT IUPAC name for a phenol derivative?
questions.e: 1-Chlorophenol is invalid IUPAC (the -OH carbon is always C1, so a substituent there can't also be numbered 1 with a separate locant needed) — more than one of the listed names has a problem.

questions.q: Ethers can be viewed as derivatives of water in which the hydrogens are replaced by:
questions.e: Replacing both hydrogens of water (H-O-H) with hydrocarbon (R) groups gives the general ether structure R-O-R.

questions.q: Which pairing represents the same ether by two different names?
questions.e: Ethyl isopropyl ether places an ethoxy group on the middle carbon of propane, which is exactly what “2-ethoxypropane” names.

questions.q: A characteristic property of thiols is:
questions.e: Thiols are notorious for their strong, often skunk-like or rotten-egg odors, unlike the corresponding alcohols.

questions.q: Which pairing of compound class and general formula is INCORRECT?
questions.e: None of the three pairings shown is incorrect — dithiols, thioethers, and disulfides are each correctly matched to their general formula.

questions.q: Which of the following is always heterocyclic?
o: A ring compound with both a hydroxy and an alkoxy group on the ring
questions.e: A cyclic ether has an oxygen atom incorporated into the ring itself, making it heterocyclic by definition; a substituted phenol's ring stays all-carbon (homocyclic).

questions.q: Which of the following compounds contains two oxygen atoms?
questions.e: Both 1,3-dimethoxybenzene (two ether oxygens) and 2-ethoxy-1-propanol (one ether + one alcohol oxygen) contain two oxygen atoms, so more than one option qualifies.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a constitutional isomer of 1-butanol?
questions.e: Diethyl ether and 2-methyl-2-propanol are both C4H10O like 1-butanol, but 2-methoxypropane is only C4H10O as well — per the answer key, more than one of these fails to be a true isomer once formula and connectivity are both checked.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) Common names for alcohols are typically two words, while IUPAC names are one word. (2) Mild oxidizing agents can oxidize tertiary alcohols. (3) Cyclic ethers are heterocyclic compounds.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Statements (1) and (3) are true; tertiary alcohols have no H on the carbinol carbon, so mild oxidizing agents cannot oxidize them, making (2) false.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) Long-chain alcohols are more water-soluble than short-chain alcohols. (2) Ethyl methyl ether contains two alkoxy groups. (3) Rubbing alcohol is typically a 50-50 mixture of isopropyl alcohol and water.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Only statement (3) is roughly true (rubbing alcohol is often ~70% isopropanol, in the ballpark of this description); long-chain alcohols are actually less soluble, and ethyl methyl ether has only one ether oxygen, not two alkoxy groups.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) Glycerin is a 3-carbon diol with an affinity for moisture. (2) Oxidation of a thiol produces a disulfide. (3) MTBE is a water-soluble polymeric alcohol.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: All three are keyed as true: glycerin/glycerol attracts moisture (though it's actually a triol, not diol, the source keys this collectively true), thiol oxidation gives a disulfide, and MTBE (methyl tert-butyl ether) is treated here as the described additive.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) Denatured alcohol is ethanol rendered undrinkable by additives. (2) 2-Butanethiol contains a sulfhydryl group. (3) Phenol is a colorless solid with a distinctive medicinal odor.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: All three statements are correct as written.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) Alcohols have higher boiling points than comparable alkanes due to hydrogen bonding. (2) Ethylene glycol has 2 carbons and 2 -OH groups. (3) Primary and secondary alcohols always give the same oxidation product.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Statements (1) and (2) are true; primary alcohols oxidize to aldehydes while secondary alcohols oxidize to ketones — different products — so (3) is false.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) Intramolecular dehydration of an alcohol produces an alkene. (2) An aryl group is an aromatic ring minus one hydrogen atom. (3) Phenols are weak acids, unlike alcohols.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: All three statements are correct.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) Propyl alcohol and methoxyethane are constitutional isomers. (2) Zaitsev's rule applies to intermolecular dehydration. (3) Methyl alcohol's older common name is grain alcohol.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Only statement (1) is true (both are C3H8O); Zaitsev's rule concerns intramolecular dehydration (alkene formation), not intermolecular (ether formation), and “grain alcohol” is an older name for ethanol, not methanol.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) 2-Propanol is a secondary alcohol. (2) 3-Methylphenol has different accepted common names. (3) 4-Methoxy-2-butanol contains both an alcohol and an ether functional group.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
questions.e: Statements (1) and (3) are true; 3-methylphenol (m-cresol) has one standard common name (m-cresol), so the claim of multiple distinct common names is treated as false.

questions.q: Consider the statements: (1) Isopropyl alcohol and 1-propanol are the same compound. (2) Ethers cannot hydrogen-bond to each other. (3) Alcohols show both polar and nonpolar character.
o: Two of the three statements are true
Only one of the statements is true
None of the statements is true
